en: The Verses on the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume One.
Composed by the Venerable Viśākha;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

1. Clarifying the Initial Ordination (*Upasampadā*) and the Essential Ritual Procedures for Bhikṣus, etc. (Part One) Clarifying the Initial Ordination and the Essential Ritual Procedures for Bhikṣus, etc.: He expounds upon the Vinaya, Is well-versed in the meaning of the Vinaya;
Abiding correctly within the Vinaya, He is able to abandon what is contrary to the Vinaya.
I pay homage to such a teacher, to the Dharma, and to the Noble Assembly;
now, according to my own understanding, I shall briefly summarize the Vinaya.
Those who are lazy and of little wisdom feel fear toward extensive texts.
Though one may strive, there is no joy in entering this ocean of discipline;
yet, so that others may enter it without giving rise to great weariness,
I have composed verses as a staircase for superior persons to behold the path to the ford.
One may praise the perfection of wealth, which can lead to rebirth in the sublime Brahma palaces;
yet both meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and *nirvāṇa* are likewise attained through ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Apart from this *vinaya*, no matter how many activities one performs, they cannot be purified.
It is like a garment that has been thoroughly washed, yet not rinsed in clear water;
or like the orb of the moon when it is waning, lacking its brilliance during the night.
So too is it for one who has gone forth in the Buddha’s teaching, if their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is deficient.
Therefore, abandon indolence and take delight in the adornment of the precepts;
desiring to discern what should and should not be done, one should diligently study the teachings of the Vinaya.
A bhikṣu should apply his mind and seek to understand the Vinaya.
One must first clarify this for oneself, and only thereafter should one provide instruction.
Thus, one will receive earnest respect from the fourfold assembly;
the Buddhas of the past, future, and present all hold this person within their inner treasury.
In the diligent pursuit of the True Dharma and for the benefit of sentient beings,
one should guard the aggregate of ethical discipline oneself, protecting it well so that it remains unimpaired.
If others should commit transgressions, they all come to you to inquire about them.
Within the definitive meaning, one attains skillfulness;
one can subdue those who act as enemies, knowing both the Dharma and that which accords with it;
never being despised by others, one is fearless in the midst of the great assembly.
In whatever direction or quarter there may be one who clarifies the teachings of the Vinaya, the Buddha said:
"I have no concern, for through him light shall shine forth.
Thus spoke the Muni: the virtue of the Vinaya is inconceivable.
For this reason, one should diligently seek to receive and uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka.
A bhikṣu who has completed ten years of seniority, who well guards his own discipline and is clearly proficient in the rules and procedures, may grant the full ordination of renunciation.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and its extensive commentary are both excellent in their wording and meaning;
one who serves as a refuge for others is able to instruct them therein.
It is not enough merely to have a slight understanding of the meaning, for those of shallow knowledge harbor many doubts regarding the facts.
One must analyze and discern clearly; the Great Master’s words are never confused.
If one cannot understand the extensive commentary on the *Prātimokṣa*, having been mired in ignorance for sixty years, one will ultimately have to rely on others for one's livelihood.
One should dwell under the guidance of an elder; if there is no elder, one may stay with a junior.
One should not pay homage to a teacher who is younger than oneself; for all other matters, one should act as prescribed for juniors.
Anyone wishing to go forth into homelessness should, according to their inclination, approach a single teacher.
If there are no matters of challenge or dispute, one should accept [the candidate] when the time is right.
Even if they have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, or are those who dwell as thieves, or possess transformed non-human forms,
or belong to the class of outsiders, the deaf, or the mute— [one should still accept them].
If one is a *śaṇḍha* or the like, or has defiled a bhikṣuṇī,
they are like a field of saline soil where the seed of precepts cannot grow.
If a person has committed an offense of the extreme limits (*ānantarya*), or is burdened by debt and afflicted by disease, [they are likewise unfit].
Though appearing now as a king’s minister or general, he was once a great thief and a slave;
born into a lowly station with missing limbs, his ten fingers were stuck together,
his hands and feet were all cramped and lame, his spine was hunched, and his nose was flat and crooked.
Injured by the burden of women, with a long, coarse, and small brain,
as well as excessively decayed teeth, squinting eyes that lack clarity,
eyes of varying sizes with yellow blisters, and those that are red and inflamed;
Those who are thus unattractive are all forbidden from leaving the household life.
To summarize the matters that may be barred, there are essentially only three types:
namely, physical appearance, lineage, and clan; because of these, one defiles the monastic community.
Their physical forms are said to have red hair and the like;
furthermore, they have ears and heads like those of donkeys and the like, yet lack hair on their ears.
They possess the features of elephants, horses, and monkeys, and some have only a single eye.
Those with no eyes, oxen, or horses' teeth, or those who have no teeth at all;
those known as Caṇḍālas, bamboo-workers, scavengers,
and others such as those who walk with a crutch— all these are prohibited by the Vinaya.
If there is one with pure faith, all faults will be absent;
one should carefully examine the entire body and inquire to know whether there are any obstructing factors.
Having observed for eight days, one should maintain mindfulness and skillfully discern the signs.
If one has previously examined [the candidate], there is no need to spend a full day.
First, bestow the Three Refuges; next, grant the Five Precepts.
The candidate should don fresh white robes and stand before the Saṃgha.
Once the Saṃgha has granted permission, one should follow the rules for renunciation:
first, request a preceptor (ācārya), and next, receive the ten precepts (śikṣāpada).
Having received the status of a śrāmaṇera, all lay associates [should be informed].
He should be praised and venerated therein, for he has abandoned the worldly entanglements;
because he has dispelled the obscurations of delusion and donned the robe of the Great Sage,
his radiance is thus magnificent, like the sun at its first rising.
Just as when the leaves of the Pārijāta tree fall in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, so too for one who receives the full ordination (upasampadā), all transgressions are completely eliminated.
In the Middle Kingdom, ten [monks] must be present; fewer than ten bhikṣus is not permitted.
Regarding those who receive full ordination in the border regions, they may remain as they wish for up to five years.
In the eastern region is Pundravardhana; in this realm there is a tree called Śāla;
to the north is the mountain named Uśīra, and the monastery is named Tāmrasaṇḍana.
To the west lies the village named Sthāṇu;
to the south is the city called Śrāvastī.
The Buddha taught that within these boundaries is the Middle Country; outside of this realm are known as the Borderlands.
A bhikṣu whose precepts are pure is worthy to confer full ordination upon others;
he is not like the sound of a conch shell, nor a rotten tree in the sky.
One who upholds the Dharma knows the Vinaya, as do the other four groups of nine who are pure.
The full ordination (*upasampadā*) is worthy of praise; the devas should pay it homage.

When the assembly within the boundary is complete, and those who are pure uphold the Dharma, the *karmavācanā* is virtuous and free from obstacles—these are called the five causes for the attainment of full ordination.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*, there are ten ways of obtaining full ordination (*upasampadā*);
that which the World-Honored One, the All-Knowing One, attained is called "self-awakened acceptance.
With Kauṇḍinya as their leader, the five men attained the path through meditative concentration.
The various pure minds of the assembly of the Noble Ones were all obtained through taking refuge;
the Dharma and the acquisition of the fruits were likewise attained. Through the words "Welcome," they became Bhikṣus;
as for Mahāśāla Kāśyapa, he attained it by means of honoring his teacher.
The youth Udāyin was skilled at giving answers;
he pleased the Great Teacher’s mind, and the Buddha declared that he had attained full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
In the Middle Kingdom, ten persons were required for this.
In border regions, the number [of preceptors] may reach five, or even exceed this; those who uphold the Dharma must know these rules.
Furthermore, because of Gopā, the Great Lady (Mahāprajāpatī), she requested the Buddha;
for her sake, he expounded the Eight Weighty Rules (Aṣṭa-guru-dharma), and by this it is said that she attained full ordination (Upasampadā).
Except for the eight [cases], if one receives [the precepts] otherwise, it is all by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*;
according to what was previously explained, the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*) is permitted in all such cases.
Immediately after having received full ordination, one should inform [them] of the five times for [the distribution of] requisites.
The winter and spring rains last for a long time; their duration is measured by the number of persons [in the assembly].
Winter lasts from the fifteenth day of the ninth month until the fifteenth day of the first month;
spring lasts from the fifteenth day of the first month until the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
Rain begins from the fifth half-month and continues until the middle of the sixth month;
at its conclusion, it lasts for only one day and night, on the sixteenth day of the sixth month.
On the morning of the seventeenth, the long season begins and continues until the middle of the ninth month.
If three months are less by one day, this is called the fivefold difference in time.
At the conclusion of the period, if one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), they are the youngest among those of the same summer (*samanvāgata-varṣa*).
If one receives it at dawn during the long period, they are the most senior among those of the same summer.
One receives full ordination from a bhikṣu; every half-month, one requests instruction.
One observes the summer retreat in proximity to the bhikṣus; within the two assemblies, one may perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
One must not revile a bhikṣu, nor should one interrogate them regarding their violations of the precepts.
If one commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, both assemblies shall perform the half-month penance.
Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been ordained for a hundred years, she must respectfully pay homage to a bhikṣu newly received into the order; this is called the Eight Rules of Respect.
A woman assuming the appearance of a man, or a man taking the form of a woman;
laypeople and eunuchs—these should not serve as preceptors (*upādhyāya*).
Those who are thieves or those with physical deformities, though they may be virtuous, must be excluded.
When conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon them, the entire Saṅgha incurs an offense.
Those who do not desire the full precepts, as well as those who do not understand their year of birth;
one should carefully observe their physical appearance and discern their age by examining their features.
If one has not yet completed twenty years, One may be granted the full ordination (upasaṃpadā);
A wise person should calculate that they have fulfilled it By counting the months of gestation and intercalary months.
If, even when counting the months of gestation and so forth, They have not yet completed twenty years, [they are not ordained].
One should place such a person among the novices (śrāmaṇera); this does not constitute the attainment of full ordination (upasampadā).
If, after one or two years have passed, one then remembers that the age was deficient;
provided the previous years were added and the total reaches the required number, this is called a "well-ordained" (su-upasampanna) person.
If a person hears the proclamation finished, and their ears suddenly go deaf;
this too is called "properly received," for the Buddha permitted it as being without fault.
At the very moment of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), if the male form transforms into that of a female;
This is called "receiving full ordination" (upasampadā), and it should be placed among the nuns.
If the preceptor (upādhyāya) hears the formal announcement and then undergoes a change of gender,
this is not called "receiving full ordination," yet there is no fault for those who performed the ritual.
The candidate for ordination stands upon the ground, while the presiding master remains suspended in the air;
since the physical positions of these two realms are distinct, it cannot be called the formal reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Just as a Wheel-Turning King nurtures his crown prince so that the royal lineage may flourish, [so too must the ritual be performed with proper alignment].
The same applies to protecting a śrāmaṇera, so as to cause the holy teaching to flourish.
Just as when a teacher sent a śrāmaṇera to climb a high tree for some business, he fell and injured his limbs;
it was for this reason that the holy teaching prohibited it.
Therefore, within the Buddha’s teaching, compassion is the foundation for leaving the household life;
even one who is only seven years old is permitted [to ordain], provided they understand the matter of driving away crows.
If one leaves the household and receives full ordination, it is not allowed if they lack an alms bowl.
A vessel for the immortals must ultimately exist; this serves as the cause for begging for food.
As with the Elder Upasena, when a novice was hungry and lacked a bowl, as the time for eating approached, he sought a food vessel from another.
Lending him robes, alms-bowls, and so forth, and granting him ordination and full admission;
do not follow the method of the Brahmins—this is what the World-Honored One permitted.
If a person has not yet received full admission, one must not first explain the four reliances.
Hearing of these difficult practices, the brahmin returned to lay life.
If one performs a single *karmavācanā*, and four persons within a single boundary receive [the precepts];
this is merely the Saṃgha acting for the Saṃgha, and cannot be called "receiving the Dharma."
If two or three persons receive full ordination at the same time,
although their physical appearances may differ, there is no distinction of seniority among them.
They shall receive benefits according to their seating order and should not pay mutual prostrations to one another.
When assigning someone to an office of responsibility, one should act according to the appointment.
For those who are negligent in other matters, one should perform formal acts such as instilling fear;
having rebuked them, one should then expel them properly, so that they may give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
If one understands the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and possesses great renown;
if they can generate vast merit, they should not be driven away.
Because of these heretical deer, the lion cub is terrified.
One who can give rise to a mundane pure mind is like the Great Teacher dwelling in the world;
this dwelling is radiant, like a great bull-king.
To revile such a person is to cause harm to the Buddha’s teaching.
The four grave defiled acts are manifest; with perverse attachments, they maintain a foolish mind.
They do what ought not to be done, and the world universally censures them.
They defile families and give rise to strife; such are those who have broken the precepts.
The great assembly shall together strike the wooden gong, and with one mind, they shall swiftly expel [the offender].
The pillar he embraces must be cut down, and the doorframe likewise shall be hewn;
the monastery should be renovated through exhortation, or else using the *saṃghika* (monastic) property.
One should not keep an image of a bhikṣu for the sake of mockery;
one should earnestly drive it away and not give rise to strife.
Since it has been said that such an object is like a corpse, there is absolutely no sense in cohabiting with it.
The community of monks shall collectively expel this defiled person.
Nuns should not offer him formal salutation, though they may show him reverent respect;
lay followers should not converse with him, yet they should give him alms when he comes for food.
When the disease of envy arises halfway through contact, it is called the "House of Five Halves.
For the sake of those who do not understand, I shall briefly describe its characteristics:
if another comes and embraces one’s body, and the mind gives rise to greedy lust;
The wise should recognize that this refers to one who embraces a eunuch.
"Envy" means that regarding one's own male virility, one feels aroused upon seeing another engaged in sexual union;
"disease" means falling [into impotence] due to illness, or being harmed by weapons and the like.
One born with neither of the two sexual organs manifest from birth is called a "half-eunuch" (ardhapandaka);
such a person is half male and half female.
If, regarding the practice of sexual desire, one is unable to act as a *śaṇḍha* (impotent), [one is so classified].
If both sexual organs are present, one should know this is termed "having two forms" (ubhatovyañjanaka).
With a mind defiled by false and evil views, one should know these are "false outsiders";
having received their teachings from them, such a person is called an "outsider by inclination."
Sometimes one shaves one's own hair, secretly adopts the Dharma, and puts on the dharma-robes;
falsely claiming the understanding of a bhikṣu, such a person is called a "thief-dweller.
One who commits the four pārājika offenses or holds evil views defiles the body of a bhikṣuṇī.
To drink alcohol and disparage the Triple Gem is called a fault of a śrāmaṇera.
If one commits any of these ten matters, that person must be expelled;
if they renounce [the offense], they should be dealt with according to what is appropriate, and the punishment for their transgression shall be imposed.
If one has not committed a pārājika offense, and has properly relinquished the precepts;
having returned to lay life and now coming back again, the bhikṣus joyfully accept him.
If one relinquishes the precepts with an undisturbed mind, in the presence of a person who fully understands.
"You should know that I relinquish you; this is called the training in true relinquishment.
Once it has been received, one should immediately recite the four *pārājika* rules.
A wise person should first inform [the candidate] so as not to let them commit evil deeds."
Because the mind does not conceal [the offense], one confesses it before a single person;
being utterly weary of the extreme [nature of] the pārājika offenses, such a person is called a *śikṣādattaka*.
Next, the rules for miscellaneous conduct are explained; these are the essential protocols for those who have left the household life.
One should take turns teaching one another, so that the honored Dharma does not perish.
As the time of day approaches dawn, one must rise before the teacher;
having chewed a clean tooth-stick, one should first pay homage to the honored image.
Next, one may approach the teacher and arrange the seating materials;
the towel, water, earth, and tooth-stick must be provided according to the season.
At times one should rise early and, having reflected carefully, approach the teacher’s side.
Reverently massaging the body can produce extraordinary merit.
Or, during the first or last watch of the night, one should inquire about doubts before the teacher;
the teacher shall bid one sit down comfortably and resolve those doubts according to the Tripiṭaka.
At dawn, inquire after their well-being and pay homage with deep reverence;
because they provide such great benefit and grace, they are able to personally instruct one on what is right and wrong.
Always maintain the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, and toward them, give rise to a heart of earnest devotion.
Thoroughly sweep the interior of the room and keep the walking path pure and clean.
Construct an altar for offerings, providing incense and flowers as available;
revere the Triple Gem every day—this is the cause for the Four Noble Truths.
At times one pays homage at the incense hall and circumambulates the stūpa;
when encountering those of venerable age nearby, one performs prostrations according to the circumstances.
This is done to seek a firm and enduring body, rather than to employ this fragile frame.
Exert yourself and encourage others; do not follow the mind of the foolish and indolent.
Having made offerings at the appropriate times, settle your mind after recitation and chanting.
Do not think that merely wearing the *kāṣāya* robe is sufficient for your heart’s joy.
On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, one must know it is the time for the *poṣadha*;
the assembly should perform it in harmony, but if there is discord, one should do so individually.
One should examine oneself and seek purity regarding any transgressions.
Even regarding minor offenses, one should always maintain a sense of great dread.
One may go to the monastic kitchen to observe what is being prepared;
if one encounters exquisite fruits or delicacies, having examined them, one should inform the Venerable One.
One should always serve with diligence and respect, performing tasks such as washing the alms bowl;
though one may perform these services for all venerable ones, the teacher should know the proper measure of what to accept.
One should not relieve the fatigue of, nor pay homage to, those who have broken the precepts.
They share in no enjoyment at all, like wood used for burning a corpse.
Even a śrāmaṇera does not pay homage to a layperson who possesses the precepts;
how much less would a great bhikṣu pay homage to a worldly person consumed by lust?
If a bhikṣu, having attained the subsequent fruit, does not pay homage even to one who is slightly inferior;
how much more so within the cycle of birth and death, with a mind that revolves in ignorance and stubbornness?
One who has nothing further to learn (aśaikṣa) is said to be the master; those still in training (śaikṣa) are like a father’s wealth.
For those who are diligent in meditation and recitation, it is permissible according to their needs and is truly without fault.
As for others who are indolent, they are called "those who owe a debt";
those who have broken the precepts are entirely prohibited from using the dwelling place and its appurtenances.
With a faithful heart, one should build monasteries solely for the sake of those who dwell in the practice of the precepts;
those who have committed grave offenses and feel no shame or remorse must never be allowed to set foot there.
If one approaches a latrine, one must not engage in any conversation.
Reciting, washing, dyeing, and so forth—none of these are permitted [in the restroom].
When entering the room for urination or defecation, one must make a sound;
using one or two fingers to distinguish the [excretions] in their respective places—the Great Master has spoken thus.
When passing wind or excrement, exit slowly and make no sound;
when the urge is strong, do not force it to stop, nor should one speak while in the latrine.
Whether using a wooden stick or a clod of earth, first use it to wipe the lower part.
Next, using two or three portions of earth, wash them thoroughly with much water until they are clean.
With the left hand, use seven portions of earth; this is called "cleansing.
Afterward, use seven portions for both hands together; these should all be applied separately.
Furthermore, there is another heap of earth used for washing the *kamaṇḍalu*, as well as for washing the arms, calves, and feet;
this is called external purification (*bāhya-śauca*).
This matter originated with Śāriputra; to act otherwise incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Use both hands with care, washing until they are utterly clean.
The intent is to remove foul odors and allow the body to attain purity;
if one does not follow this method, what is the use of a hundred applications of earth?
It is improper to perform prostrations to the Triple Gem, nor should one accept prostrations from others;
all other such acts are likewise forbidden, as the World-Honored One himself prohibited them.
Furthermore, one should not fail to chew tooth-sticks, nor consume pungent and strong-smelling foods.
These matters are all the same as before, as explained in detail in the Vinaya.
If one does not consult the two teachers, one may perform five things:
defecating, urinating, drinking water, and chewing a tooth-stick for cleansing the teeth.
Within the same boundary, within a distance of forty-nine fathoms, one may perform prostrations before the *caitya* according to one's inclination;
for all other matters, such as washing the hands and feet, one must inform the teacher.
To act otherwise would be to overstep the bounds of propriety.
Before eating anything, one must announce it; whether generally or specifically, this depends on the occasion.
Having performed a single prostration with the head bowed, one should join the palms and make this announcement:
"I announce to the Upādhyāya: I shall wash my hands and eat."
For all other matters, one should proceed by making a formal announcement (*jñapti*) according to this principle;
if one does not consult or inform [the community] at the time [of action], each instance will incur an offense.
At the time of eating, one should apply the mind with care; the giving and receiving must be performed according to the Dharma.
Regarding the distribution of robes and other matters, ensure that no duties are neglected.
Until ten years of seniority have been attained, one must not be separated from one's preceptor;
once five years have passed and one is clearly proficient in the Vinaya, one is permitted to travel as one pleases.
However, wherever one resides, one must still seek a preceptor;
if there is no preceptor, one does not deserve the benefit of food and clothing.
Section One: The Four *Pārājika* Dharmas (Part One) The Training Rule on Impure Conduct (*Abrahmacarya*) The Buddha has taught three kinds of offenses that are incurable and leave no remainder.
Some offenses are to be cleared by the assembly, while the remainder are all to be confessed individually.
The four *pārājika* offenses are most grave and must be treated with reverence;
if one commits even a single such rule, one immediately becomes a monk who has lost his status.
For the first twelve years, he was as pure and clear as autumn water;
at that time, no blemish had arisen. When the thirteenth year passed, Sūciṇḍa committed sexual misconduct with his stepmother for the sake of a son.
Even for a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya, a monkey may commit an offense.
Since the Buddha taught these training rules (śikṣāpada) to eliminate greed and other defilements,
how could you possibly engage in such an act amidst the sinful karma of sexual indulgence?
Seeing ten kinds of great benefit for the welfare and happiness of many people,
the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, extensively established the various śikṣāpadas.
Within the three gates of sores, one seeks entry through the power of craving.
The *pārājika* snake, once its sting has been inflicted, is difficult to treat.
When another forces one into unwholesome conduct, and the one possessing the precepts remains attached;
if defilement arises toward this person, one should know that a defeat (*parājayika*) has been committed.
If one inserts [the organ] into a festering sore, or into an extremely small opening;
or if the male organ does not enter at all—these cases all constitute a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
It would be better to place one’s own organ in the mouth of a venomous snake; [but never to engage in such improper acts].
If one is unsteady within the female organ, the retribution of suffering will be endured without end.
If one encounters the venom of a black snake, only a single body perishes;
but if one violates the grave prohibitions, one shall suffer hardship for eternal kalpas.
The modes of sexual intercourse are manifold; an offense is complete when eight factors are present.
As circumstances vary, the wise should examine them in detail.
A place where a bhikṣu may engage in it is one where neither partner’s organ is damaged.
Entering through the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) beyond the limit, one fully experiences the pleasure with both minds.
Regarding the offenses of the first two preparatory efforts, there are two distinct *thullaccaya* for each;
as for the differences in lightness or gravity of the matters, all are as explained in the extensive text.
Although the question concerns two causes, the answer is given in accordance with the inquiry;
just as that which is not one of the first two causes should be known as not included therein.
Regarding the training rule on taking what is not given: the Bhikṣu Dhanika built a house for his own sake.
If one takes timber belonging to the royal household, thereby creating the cause for an offense; if,
with the intent to steal another's property, one moves it from its original place and regards it as one’s own,
an offense of the highest degree (pārājika) is incurred upon reaching five *māṣakas*.
If the five [types of soil] are passed over, all constitute an offense; for *mṛṣā* (false speech), the rule applies according to the circumstances.
If one forms the intention, one incurs a *tatsvabhāvaka* (reproachful) offense; if one touches the object, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave) offense.
On level ground of a uniform color, dragging [an object] across constitutes merely a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one tears or splits [the net] into different colors, or passes through it when it is free of [living beings], one incurs no offense.
If one destroys a snare with a mind of anger, or a net and so forth, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one releases a sentient being for the sake of merit, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are two ways of contesting land: either at the site of a boundary dispute or through royal decree.
If one gains victory in both places, the bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If he gains victory over the other in both places, that person [the opponent] shall relinquish it by means of a formal act (*upāya*).
The fire of *pārājika* burns the body of this bhikṣu. If, through incantations,
one takes the wealth of others— such as mani-jewels and other objects—
and a bhikṣu sees them from afar with his own eyes, he immediately incurs a root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
For one's own seedlings to flourish, yet not wishing for others' to succeed;
when the water is scarce, one dams the field ridges, fearing loss and thus letting it out.
One’s own seedlings attain fruition, while the seedlings of others are ruined.
One should know that according to the actual substance of the act, it may be grave or sometimes light.

To declare what is Dharma as non-Dharma, and to declare what is non-Dharma as Dharma;
to declare that which is disciplinary as non-disciplinary—such matters as these should be recognized.
These are disputes concerning verbal censure, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal matters.
Among these, the wise one of awakened intelligence should know the four kinds of disputes:
namely, various verbal expressions, discord within the assembly, differing minds;
based on these, strife arises, which is called the dispute of formal accusation.
If a person, out of anger and affliction, speaks with words that are contrary to the Dharma, conflict arises therefrom;
thus, this is called a dispute over what is right and wrong.
Regarding body, speech, and mind—these three each constitute one kind.
Whether two, three, or more types, briefly stated there are six conditions.
When a bhikṣu and a woman do not know they are staying in the same room;
from one night up to the third night without being fully ordained—this constitutes the offense of bodily association.
When speaking five or six sentences to a woman while preaching the Dharma to her,
if the sentences are increased intentionally, one should know that it constitutes a verbal offense.
When questioned during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if one conceals a fault, [it is likewise an offense].
This is called a mental offense; one should know that it incurs *dukkaṭa*.
When there is both a body and a mind, and one intentionally takes the life of a living being;
or when one takes what is not given, such as alcohol and so forth—this offense is incurred through these two.
Having spoken five or six phrases, one further increases the words with a deliberate mind;
this is called the duality of mind and speech. False speech is likewise the same.
Thus, with a deliberate mind, one instigates killing and says, "Strike that person's body."
It is said that body, speech, and mind—through these three, one commits offenses.
How can a bhikṣu commit an offense while in a virtuous state of mind?
It is by removing weeds from atop a Buddha hall so that they do not grow.
Furthermore, if one acts with a virtuous intention for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha,
one incurs an offense by stringing garlands, yet there is no fault in arranging them in rows.
One must not intentionally contravene the words of the Sage nor the regulations established by the Saṃgha.
This is said to be indeterminate (avyākṛta), because it lacks an evil mind.
Therefore, those mental states that transgress [the ethical norm] are all unwholesome (akuśala);
the opposite of these should be known as wholesome (kuśala). This refers to the meaning of the "side-vehicle" (pratyekabuddha-yāna).
In such immeasurable ways, one commits transgressions;
from these, disputes arise—this should be known as "dispute arising from an offense.
Such matters as formal announcements (*jñapti*) and the like are said to be "not virtuous" and so forth.
Quarreling gives rise to clamor; one should know that such matters constitute strife.
If one intends to cause a schism in the Saṃgha out of ignorance, it incurs the offense of duṣkṛta (wrongdoing).
If, after being admonished separately, one does not desist, this constitutes the fault of duṣkṛta.
Declaring "I do not relinquish" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as does the recitation of the first *karmavācanā*;
likewise for the second, until finally obtaining the formal instruction of the Saṃgha.
Those who follow and assist in the schism of the Saṃgha, and those who turn toward this position within the community of monks—these are the sinful bhikṣus.
The distinctions such as private admonition and so forth are all exactly as before.
Regarding the training rule on defiling a household (*kuladūṣaka-śikṣāpada*): if there is one who defiles a household, two kinds of defilement are taught;
the first is called "living in confusion" (*miśravāsa*), and the second is called "enjoying [the offerings]" (*paribhoga*).
Dwelling together with women, engaging in play, agitation, and the like;
enjoyment refers to eating together, as well as gathering flowers, fruits, and similar things.
One should know that these consist of the three—seeing and so forth—arising from the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and mind.
The distinctions regarding formal admonition (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*) and so forth are as previously explained for the offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding this training rule on the stubborn refusal of admonition: one who speaks such evil words incurs the offense of communal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*);
knowing that they are unwilling to comply with virtuous speech is what is meant by "evil speech."
Thoroughly training in the defeats (*pārājika*) and so forth is called the "places of training" (*śikṣāpada*);
one should receive the words of instruction in accordance with the pure Dharma.
Having explained the equality of the Dharma and so forth, one follows the teachings of the Great Master.
If one does not relinquish [the offense] despite formal admonition and so forth, the gravity of the offense is the same as previously stated.

2. The Two Indeterminate Rules (Part One). The two indeterminate rules are briefly summarized from among the various categories of offenses;
having already explained those that correspond to the minor [rules], I shall now set forth the indeterminate ones, as the Great Teacher spoke of these two rules.
The bhikṣu Udāyin was intimate with Guptā;
because this matter was indeterminate, the Saṃgha established a comprehensive rule:
if one bhikṣu and one woman sit together in a secluded place...
Engaging in sexual acts, or the absence thereof, These are called the two *aniyata-dharmas*.

Walls, fences, darkness, curtains, and screens, And dense thickets as the fifth.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, a bhikṣu should speak according to the facts;
as one of pure faith relates it, his transgressions should be dealt with in accordance with the matter.
If, during walking, standing, and so forth, he does not speak according to the facts;
One should grant the formal procedure for seeking the nature of the offense, performing the *jñapti* and so forth as previously described.
If one receives the disciplinary measures, they shall not go forth or receive full ordination;
nor shall they walk for exercise together with others, nor share in dependence and other such matters.

When a transgression is not definitively adjudicated, The name "Two Indefinites" (aniyata) arises.

**Third Section: Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas (Part One)** **The Training Rule on Keeping Extra Robes Without Distinguishing Them:** If a bhikṣu, beyond ten days, keeps an extra robe without distinguishing it [as such], [he commits an offense].
The dust of the *naiḥsargika* offense defiles the body of the transgressor.
Once the robe has been sewn, stitched, and dyed, it is said that the robe is "completed.
What is called "keeping and possessing the robe" means to take it as one's own property.
When the *cīvara* has been completed, but the *kaṭhina* has not yet been removed—one should know that such cases constitute four permutations.
[The materials are: wool, hemp, and *śāṇa*; *karpāsa* and silk.
Kauśeya, kṣauma, and so forth—these are called the seven kinds of robes.
What is meant by the "distinguishing of property" regarding the minimum measurement?
If the length and width reach one cubit, the offense constitutes *naiḥsargika*.
That which should be relinquished is not relinquished; one does not confess and repent for transgressions;
furthermore, one does not create a separation [from the offense]. Thus, the fallen offense cannot be removed.
If one commits even one of these three, or two, one is not pure.
Only after all three matters have been performed is one called a person free from fault.
Regarding this offense, which has not yet been mentioned— whether it concerns the bowl,
the bag, or other items— if they are later obtained, they are all equally *naiḥsargika*.
Because one possesses wealth that can be relinquished, yet is further wounded by falling into an offense;
because one falls into the evil realms, it is called a *pāyattika*. Regarding the training rule on staying apart from the three robes:
one should always remain together with the three robes; unless there is a valid reason, one must not stay overnight apart from them.
One performs the ritual for the sake of the community; otherwise, one incurs an offense.

Whether there be one, two, or many dwellings, surrounded by moats and ditches outside the village, or enclosed on all sides by walls and fences, they possess one or many spheres of influence (*sīmā*).
The "common sphere" (*sīmā*) refers to open gardens, temple sites, and the like;
whether distinct or unified, it is called a single common sphere.
Because they are connected as a single continuous line, one should know that this constitutes a single dwelling (*śālā*).
Villagers and bandits, though distinct, are like those of one community;
two houses separated by two rows are like a brahmin and a villager;
when established with many gates, these are called "many houses."
Regarding the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*) herein: its outer perimeter extends one fathom wide;
or it is the area where a chicken falls when dropped, or as far as the place of threshing, and so forth.
This includes houses, shops, stalls, towers, fields, as well as the dwellings of non-Buddhists.
A boat, a tree, a carriage, a garden, or a dwelling— these constitute a single or multiple *sīmā* (territorial divisions).
If brothers do not demarcate them, or if there is only one person [inhabiting them],
because they constitute a single residence, they are said to form a single *sīmā*.
As previously explained regarding the sphere of influence (*pradeśa*), many spheres of influence arise;
because they exist through distinct individual gates, one should know that the gates themselves are shared.
The same is held to be true for many houses, storerooms, and so forth.
One should know that all functional domains (*pradeśa*) are distinguished by identity and difference.
If non-Buddhists perceive them as distinct, they distinguish between the functional domains of identity and difference;
these differing functional domains refer to such things as the wearing of skins and garments.
In the dwellings of musicians and the like, all matters are exactly as previously described;
outside, there are flagpoles, drums, and the like, as well as places where bamboo has been split.
If tree branches are interlaced, this constitutes a single boundary.
Within the shadow and the reach of raindrops, extending one fathom outward,
the person and their robes share the same boundary; if one wears the three robes within this area,
or if a bhikṣu sleeps anywhere therein, there is no offense whatsoever.
In places such as deva-temples, where the main gate is common to all;
if one stays overnight there apart from one's robes, one will not be harmed by transgression.
When traveling on the road, the permissible distance is forty-nine fathoms.
When sitting, standing, or lying down, one must remain within one fathom of one's robe; there is no fault if this is not exceeded.
Regarding the training rule on the *māsa-cīvara* (the robe expected for a month): although one has obtained a *cīvara*, if there is still expectation for another, one may keep it for up to one month;
provided it is not formally designated as one's own, there is no offense.
From the eighth day of the bright fortnight until the middle of the next, this one month is the time for robes;
thereafter it is called the improper time, though one may hope for them from relatives and others.
At a *śmaśāna* (charnel ground), if there is the clothing of a deceased person;
Clothing obtained from funeral processions on the way to or from them, Cast-off rags discarded by others,
Rags from a charnel ground or a forest hermitage, Discarded on the road and perforated by ants and insects;
Furthermore, there are five other distinct types of tattered garments.
Burnt by fire or submerged in water, Or discarded by a wet-nurse;
Torn by rats or chewed by oxen— One should know there are five such types.
Having concluded the discussion on robes, The three robes shall now be explained according to their specific functions.
The sequence should be understood as explained; its characteristics of manufacture will now be set forth in detail.
New items and those previously used—these are called the two kinds of robes.
When a bhikṣu wishes to make one, this rule shall now be stated.
If one makes a new *saṃghāṭī*, it should be cut into two layers;
the same applies to the *niṣīdana*. As for other robes, they may be made according to one's preference.
After wearing them for four months, if one makes a *saṃghāṭī*;
This robe should be made of four layers; other robes should be made of two.
If they are further increased in thickness, one should pluck them apart so that the layers are separated.
Once separated, it may be worn, but after ten days, it must be formally designated.
The great robe (saṃghāṭī) has unequal strips; from nine strips, there are nine grades.
The latter consists of twenty-five strips; these shall each be explained separately.
The three grades have two and a half lengths; the three grades have three and a half lengths.
The final three grades of robes are four and a half [units] for the maṇḍala.
Among these three grades, they serve as the partitions for the great robe-altar (*mahācīvara-maṇḍala*).
These robe measurements should be explained: the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is three or five cubits (*hasta*).
The smallest is four and a half cubits; those between these two are called medium.
As for the seven-fold and five-fold robes, their measurements are all similar.
Furthermore, it is said that the five-fold robe has four or five horizontal strips and two vertical ones.
It is difficult for the poor to obtain [the required materials]; out of compassion, he granted permission.
This refers to those of standard proportions; the measurements mentioned here are in *cubit* units (*hasta*).
For those who are exceptionally tall or short, the dimensions of the robes may be adjusted according to the individual's body.
Regarding the three robes—upper, middle, and lower—one must recognize the measurements of their patches:
two finger-widths wide and four finger-widths long; those within these dimensions are called "middle.
If they fall short of such cubit-measurements, they do not conform to the rules for formal possession.
Whenever one wears a woolen garment, one must not enter a village,
nor go among the assembly, nor perform the ritual of eating at a stūpa;
regarding it as the property of a donor, one should distinguish [the matter] in this way.
One should not enter a village without having hemmed one's saṃghāṭī robe;
violating this incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense, though it is permitted in cases of difficulty.
One should not revile those who are untrustworthy, nor dwell with those who are fond of quarreling.
One who has been expelled or is about to be expelled should not be entrusted with [one's belongings].
Even if the monk to whom one entrusts them resides across the sea, he may still be considered a kinsman;
thus, one should distinguish such a person as a friend for the purpose of managing extra robes (*atirekacīvara*).
Whether in one's own country or another land, if one knows that the person to whom the entrustment was made has died,
one should designate another bhikṣu as the person to whom the entrustment is now made.
When the robes are being distributed, if one is not near the person to whom the entrustment was originally made;
One should not [entrust] items to a śrāmaṇera or others, nor to those who are not trusted confidants.
If someone requests that you hold an object for them and entrusts it to that bhikṣu,
and if one knows that the person has died, this robe should be given to the Saṃgha.
On the borders of all robes, one should apply ink dots;
this prevents the robes from becoming disordered, making them easy to identify without requiring much effort.
Should a bhikṣu pass away, his six personal items may be taken [by the community].
Those who have tended to the sick should be rewarded; the remainder shall be distributed among the other monks.
The three robes must be cut and sewn with patches; the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is likewise.
As for the thirteen requisites, here are their names listed in brief:
The three robes together with the sitting mat, the two kinds of *nivāsana*,
the two types of *saṃkakṣikā*, and the two towels for wiping the face and body,
as well as the garment for shaving the hair, and the cloth for covering sores and scabs;
The thirteen medicinal requisites—these are all held by name.
As for all other extra robes, each should be distinguished;
according to what is appropriate, a bhikṣu who requires them may hold them.
If one has no *saṃkakṣikā* within, one should not wear the upper robe;
one should use things with care and protection, and the same applies to all other items.
Those that ought to be dyed should be dyed, and those that ought to be sewn should be sewn.
Those who are permitted to possess [robes] may do so, provided they distinguish them according to the prescribed rites.
When a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should apply three types of discoloration—
blue, red, or from tree bark— in order to eliminate the mind of greedy attachment.
Madder, indigo, saffron, vermilion, *mahānīla*, and red lac, Minium, *suvarka*,
and the eight major colors— A bhikṣu should not use these to dye his robes.
Layered blankets, high-folded *kṣomā* cloths, woolen shawls, and felt rugs,
as well as light and thin fabrics— these should be kept without cutting [the fringes],
except for those with hair; all of those should be held with attached patches.
Do not cause those of few desires to suffer the toil and hardship of sewing and stitching.
If one covers the body with five strips [of cloth], one may attend to communal tasks;
if one wears seven strips in a pure place, performing work is permitted without restriction.
When among the assembly, during meals, and when performing prostrations at a caitya;
likewise, upon entering a city or a walled town—in these places, one should wear the saṃghāṭī.
It may be folded, worn with high pleats, or used as a mattress; it may also be made of wool or camel hair.
When folding various layers of clothing, do not strain water containing insects.
When lying upon another’s mats or bedding, use a spare *saptaka* (seven-strip robe) as a liner;
it may be folded into four layers, and one should remain vigilant against sleep during the night.
Staying overnight apart from one's robes in another location, or wearing another person’s robe that has not been cut;
even if it is not a dyed garment, temporary custody is permitted.
To wear only a single robe while not ill, one is not allowed to consume food or drink.
One may go without robes and even refrain from bathing; in times of difficulty, one should act according to the circumstances.
Having carefully sent one person to borrow *śāṭaka* cloths, *saṃkakṣikā* vests, and so forth, these should be used equally by all;
they are not for the exclusive use of the person who borrowed them.
One's own white woolen blanket should be used for daytime naps to conceal the body from view;
when using property belonging to the Saṃgha, both the inner and outer layers must be concealed.
When wearing a *kambala* (woolen cloak), the hair should face outward; one should not wear it while traveling.
If one fears fleas and lice, one may sit or lie upon a *sūcaka* (a coarse woolen cloth).
The *ārya-kaṭhina* (noble woolen blanket) may be kept only with the permission of the Saṃgha;
because it originated in this country, it was named after that land.
The Saṃgha has a rule of conduct: it is appropriate to use the *kaṣāya* robe;
as for other various patchwork garments (*cīvara*), individuals may all possess them.
To ensure the lower garment remains secure, the Buddha permitted the fastening of a waistband.
One should recognize three types of borders: circular, square, and those with triple stripes.
If one’s own bedding is new, or if it is another’s object—regardless of its quality—one must place a cloth underneath; sleeping naked is not permitted.
A bhikṣu who possesses robes should not hire others to wash them;
if he does so himself or employs a skilled person, he should wash them slowly in a basin.
He should not beat the robes until they are damaged, nor cause their dye to fade.
If one were to quickly destroy [the robes], it would ruin the purpose; for this reason, the Great Teacher prohibited it.
If there are those who possess ethical discipline (*śīla*) and properly utilize their robes, he causes their giving to be uninterrupted, so that the increase of merit flows forth constantly.
The width shall be no more than one and a half cubits, and the length shall be three cubits;
this is the measure for a bag for the three robes, and to exceed it is improper.
When a bhikṣu obtains another's robe that has been worn until it is polished with a luster, [he may accept it].
Sprinkle water to diminish its luster, only then conforming to the decorum of one who has left the home life.
When Sundarī received her robe, she beat it for the sake of Nanda;
it was for this reason that the Great Teacher established the rule, fearing the arising of a mind of pride and indolence.
The width should be only the span of one's own hand, and the length about one cubit and a half;
it should be dyed with red earth and sewn onto the *saṃghāṭī*.
This article should be fastened upon the shoulder.
Fearing that sweat might soil the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), one should use it with a heart of reverence.
If the edges of the robe are near breaking, one should recognize this subtly;
one should then sew them with thread so as not to let the practice of maintaining it fall into neglect.
While the body of the deceased has not yet decayed, do not take its clothing;
for to do so would be improper and cause injury, as they are intended to become *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) raiment.
When a bhikṣu takes the garments from a corpse, even if they have been damaged down to the level of insects and ants;
Dry it for seven or eight days; when washing and dyeing it, use materials appropriate for the purpose.
Those who wear the shrouds of the deceased must not use the bedding of the Sangha;
when begging, stay outside the gate and must not enter other households.
If another person arrives, one should inform them that the body is there;
they must then be invited with great earnestness to enter the house and sit together.
If performing a circumambulation of the caitya, one should maintain a distance of one *vyāma* all around it.
One does not eat fish or meat, nor does one dwell in a house.
If it is a robe from the Saṃgha, one wears it without dyeing or mending;
as for robes offered at Jetavana, dyeing them is not permitted.
If it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, there is no offense of Naiḥsargika;
if it is the robe of an individual, there is an offense, and when relinquishing it, one should follow the prescribed rule.
Regarding the training rule on having a nun who is not a relative wash one's robe: while looking at the robe, one sees impure semen.
From this, desire arises; thus Gupta obtained a son.
If a bhikṣu has a non-relative bhikṣuṇī wash his robes, or if she dyes or beats them, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that harms the body.
If one causes a nun to wash [the robes] and so forth, a single offense is incurred;
if she is not a relative and there is doubt, this incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one strikes with the palm of the hand once, or rubs the garment once in dyeing liquid;
Even though a bhikṣu possesses a virtuous mind, he may still fall short regarding the training rules.

Regarding the rule on taking the robes of a nun who is not a relative: if a bhikṣu takes the clothing of a nun who is not a kinsman, because he lacks compassion, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon receiving it.
Neither giving nor taking, there is no fault in exchanging;
when purchasing, one should follow the proper price, or otherwise act according to one's own inclination.
If a bhikṣuṇī possesses wealth and resolves to offer it as a gift, [one may accept].
Whether listening to subtle and wondrous teachings with joyful devotion while serving the Dharma Master;
or at times seeing one receive full ordination and bringing offerings to provide assistance;
or giving when being robbed by bandits—accepting these in all such cases constitutes no offense.

The training rule regarding begging for robes from the wife of a householder who is not a relative: When a bhikṣu already possesses robes, yet begs for more from a layman who is not a relative, or from the wife of such a layman, he incurs an offense.
If one asks for a lower garment or thread, one obtains a superior upper robe;
if seeking a small amount, one receives a complete robe—there is no fault in accepting it when received.
Regarding the training rule on begging for excessive robes: if a bhikṣu’s robe is lost or stolen, and someone offers many robes as a gift;
One should take only the upper and lower robes, and must not accept them in excess.
The upper robe measures eleven cubits, and the lower robe reaches seven cubits in length;
these refer to the garments of laypeople and are termed "upper and lower robes."
The outer robe (saṃghāṭī) is three or five cubits; two layers constitute the upper garment.
The lower garment (antarvāsaka) is two or five cubits; these are called the upper and lower robes according to the Noble Teaching.
When begging for robes from others, if one obtains an excess, [it should be shared].
"It is fitting that [the robe] be returned to its original owner; furthermore, one may accept gifts as permitted by the rules.
Regarding the training rule on a householder’s wife who is not a relative jointly preparing a robe:
if a lay couple intends to provide the price for a robe, and a bhikṣu seeks it from them—if he incurs an offense, he violates the precept."
If one receives seven kinds of robes from someone who is not a relative, as described above,
and the substance of the robes is durable, they are said to be "pure items.
If one begs for the price of a robe from another, whether it be five [units] up to ten;
Regarding the *kārsāpaṇa*, its color and dimensions are as previously described.
If one seeks such robes, begging for them incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if they are obtained, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. However, if many are obtained, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu lacks robes, his deportment will not be dignified;
therefore, by the instruction of the World-Honored One, he is ordained to wear the three robes.

Regarding the training rule on laywomen who are not relatives each providing robes—the matters concerning the robes are all as previously stated—with the exception that the price for the robes is provided separately.
One should observe the conditions of dependent origination regarding what is blameworthy and what is blameless.
Regarding the training rule on ministers and kings sending the price for robes:
if it is a consecrated king, or a brahmin, or a high minister, or a general, who commands that the price for a robe be brought;
Seeing the messenger delivering the price for the robe, he told him that it was not what was appropriate;
"I accept only pure robes," he said, thereby enlightening the messenger.
He should have told the attendant that this person was one of faithful heart.
A bhikṣu may seek robes up to six times; if he obtains further robes beyond that, he may accept them and they shall be pure.
To seek more than this limit constitutes a fundamental offense (pārājika).
If it exceeds six times, he shall come in person to deliver the robe;
saying, "I have ceased [my practice]," one should then return it to the owner.
If he is exceedingly earnest, one may respectfully and joyfully grant it to him.
These items should be accepted; there is no fault in using them.
There are four distinct types of dwellings: namely, open houses, fields, shops, and "open" (cāṭaka) structures;
"open" refers to those made of tiles and the like.
A "house" refers to a domestic dwelling;
a "field" refers to a place for cultivating crops, namely rice, sugarcane, grain, and wheat;
a "shop" refers to a place where goods are stored—these should be understood as the locations subject to interrogation.
It is said there are six methods of interrogation; wait for their words and answer slowly.
If one speaks with haste, one will incur the fault of *duṣkṛta*.
When they see a bhikṣu approaching, they should say, "Welcome, O Venerable One."
Some say, "Welcome most excellently; you should sit here.
Some say, "Eat rice," or at times, "Please eat cakes";
or drink non-timely gruel—briefly stated, these are the six kinds.
If a donor employs a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), these three persons are pure;
if there is a non-human being present, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a *bhikṣu* sends away a robe entrusted to him, giving it to someone he holds dear;
Regarding property entrusted to another person, one may use it as if it were that of a close friend without fault.
If one learns of the death of the owner while on the road, the property then belongs to the deceased;
if no claimant appears for a long time, the matter is to be settled according to the rules for property from other locations.
The Training Rule on Using Wild Silk for Bedding: If one makes a new silk mattress, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) upon completion;
there are two types of such work: making a bag and making a quilted coverlet.
To make both [types of bedding] constitutes an offense; if another provides them for use, there is no fault.
Because it benefits the donor, it causes their merit and lifespan to increase.
Regarding the training rule on making bedding from pure black wool: one should not make a new bedding cover using exclusively pure black wool.
It is difficult to obtain when seeking, and it further hinders correct practice.
Regarding the training rule on the excessive use of wool for bedding: for example, if using sheep’s wool, four *liǎng* (jin) shall constitute a sleeping mat;
two parts black and one part each of the other colors—this is in accordance with the Dharma and incurs no offense.
"Black" refers to hair that is naturally black; "white" refers to that which reaches the nape of the neck.
That which is on the head, belly, and feet should be known as the "places of movement.
If white or brindled hair is deficient, even by half a *liang*, [the animal is not pure]."
If one has finished making this mat, it must be known as a sinful object.
Black is easy to find while other colors are difficult to obtain; thus, even a purely black one is permitted to be made.
If it is obtained from another source, one may use it according to one's own inclination.
The Training Rule on the Six-Year Retention of Bedding: If one makes a bedding mat oneself, one must compulsorily retain it for six years;
if one has another make it within those six years, an offense is committed, except when the Sangha acts as the legal authority.
If a bhikṣu, within one year, begins to make a second mat, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for undertaking the work;
when it is finished, he incurs the primary offense (*maulāpatti*).
This applies likewise for a second, third, fourth, or even up to the end of five years.
If one enters the six-year period, even if one commits what is prohibited, there is no limit [to the offense].
Regarding the training rule on the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat): when making a new sitting mat, one must apply a patch of the Buddha’s one span of hand;
this patch should be placed upon the new mat, dyed a different color, and made secure.
If, within the span of a hand, one intentionally reduces it by even a fragment’s measure;
one shall again encounter the punishment of the original offense, and this person's body will suffer excruciating pain.
The old parts will utterly rot and decay; being worn out for so long, nothing remains fit for use.
If there is only new [wool], and one does not apply it [to the garment], there is no offense at that time.

Regarding the training rule on carrying wool: if one does not carry wool oneself while traveling more than three *yojanas*, or carries a small amount for a hat or similar purpose, holding it secretly is not a transgression.
If one carries [wool] across half a village, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); likewise for half a *krośa*.
If it exceeds a *krośa*, having crossed the village, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
Regarding the training rule on having a non-relative nun card wool: if a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash [the wool], and so forth.
If one uses hair from that [robe] for washing, it constitutes a violation of the Śikṣāpada.
If one instructs another to wash it separately, or if one does so collectively;
the offense incurred corresponds to what is appropriate, while failing to do so results in a mere duṣkṛta.
Regarding the training rule on handling money and precious objects: The Buddha prohibited bhikṣus from grasping or holding gold, silver, and the like;
however, one may carry along the three robes, provisions for the journey, and medicine for illness.
A bhikṣu should have few desires, Acting little and seeking little;
Keeping his mind set on delighting in nirvāṇa, He should receive [offerings] with moderation and at the proper time.
The training rule regarding seeking profit through lending: Engaging in trade for the sake of profit, And the receipt and disbursement of wealth, grain, and so forth.
Seeking a sharp vajra-club, one strikes down the body of the greedy;
seeking afar, setting a deadline, demanding interest, and providing collateral—
whether the venture succeeds or fails, there are four such distinctions in engaging in trade.
Or going elsewhere to seek it, preparing boats, carts, and the like,
as well as seeking traveling companions— this is called "seeking afar.
Only after obtaining a sevenfold profit and so forth does one finally give the wealth to others.
When a document is written with a guarantor, this is termed a "term contract.
When one originally intends to seek interest on a loan, and the interest increases by double or more;
when the document specifies the time for collection, this is called "accumulated interest" (*vṛddhi*).
Storing up treasures such as mani-jewels and coral, or pearls and other goods;
making a formal agreement through a clear pledge—this is called "pledging collateral.
If the profit has not yet arisen, one has already incurred the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one gains profit from such production, it immediately incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Accomplished" refers to that which has already been made; "beaten" refers to [metal] fashioned into ornamental objects.
"Unaccomplished" refers to gold and the like; all these cases are as previously explained.
If one seeks profit through expedient means for the sake of what is required by the Triple Gem, one should appoint a person to oversee the affairs; do not contravene worldly laws.
The king and his various officials should have no dealings with the donor.
If it is difficult to pursue and reclaim [the goods] at the proper time, one may not recover them at all.
By taking a pledge, one can observe the situation well; one should deliberate on whether the items may be returned.
If the person is virtuous and worthy of entrustment, there is no need for a pledge, and there will be no injury.
Regarding the training rule on buying and selling: if there is no other person to conduct the transaction, the bhikṣu must buy it himself;
he should carefully examine the object and state his price, but the final bid shall be limited to three times the initial offer.
If there should be buying or selling, one must not originally seek profit;
if there is something else required, there is no fault in buying or selling at that time.
If it is for the sake of the Three Jewels, buying and selling must indeed take place.
The administrative officials should act in such a way as not to conflict with worldly customs.
If someone provides offerings, they should not go to the monastery to trade;
rather, they must grant a reduction in price so as to increase that person's faith.
If sesame, grain, beans, or the like, with insects emerging within them,
are placed in a cool and shaded location, they are left to follow their own conditions.
Even though they are kept in the shade, the insects that have been produced still remain.
Place it within a room, a jar, or similar vessel, and seal it tightly so that it does not suffer damage.
Regarding the training rule on keeping an extra alms bowl: there are two kinds of bowls, namely those made of iron and those made of clay;
if one keeps one for more than ten days, it will certainly constitute a transgression.
If a bowl is of the proper measure or smaller, one may store it as an extra;
for the sake of providing for those receiving full ordination, there is no fault in not making a distinction between them.
Regarding the training rule on begging for a bowl: one may repair it in five ways, but one must not beg for another bowl.
The intention is to prohibit the pursuit of excellence; if one purchases [a bowl] for that purpose, it is not an offense.
When a bhikṣu mends a crack in his alms-bowl, he should not use substances that melt;
molasses, tin, purple minerals, clay, and wax are all prohibited.
There are five ways to mend a bowl: by attaching strips of metal, by attaching rivets;
with iron nails and iron filings, as well as by using fish-teeth stitching.
If one repairs it according to the rule and replaces it when necessary, there is no offense.
If one begs for it otherwise than this, there is an *dukkaṭa*; when it is obtained, there is *naiḥsargika*.
The extra bowl that has been acquired must be relinquished to the Saṃgha;
having transferred the possession to the last [monk], one should hold and use it in accordance with the Dharma.
The finger-hook does not touch the food; receiving two *śīrṣa* of rice along with room for vegetables is called a "large bowl";
receiving one *śīrṣa* of rice along with condiments and vegetables is called "small."
Among these two internal names, these are called the three kinds of bowls.
If a bowl has cracks or holes, one may repair it with patches while maintaining a sense of propriety;
however, any necessary tools for making repairs must be kept within the monastic storehouse.
One must possess a bowl before traveling; one does not receive the formal authorization of the assembly [to go alone].
Except when there is fear of bandits, and provided that one intends to return.
Regarding the training rule on begging for thread and having a non-relative weave it: if it is a non-relative weaver, and one has no price paid for the weaving of the robe, an offense is committed.
To pay the price and involve one's kinsmen, or to send someone to have it woven at an improper time, is not an offense.

Regarding the training rule concerning a householder’s wife who employs non-relatives to weave: if a layperson instructs a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should not go to that person’s side and, with a sycophantic mind, offer words of affection.
If one causes [the wool] to be combed, clipped, or beaten, and entices the weaver with food;
if that person acts accordingly, the [offender] incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Elder" (*gṛhapati*) refers to one of great means; "combed" (*saṃvāhita*) means made soft and smooth.
"Shaving" means removing the knotted threads; "beating" means beating it to make it firm.
"Begging cakes for weavers" refers to the five types of primary food and other such meals.
"Giving them grain" should be understood as rice, beans, and so forth.
The Training Rule on Taking Back Robes: When a bhikṣu has given a robe to another, he must not take it back out of anger;
there is no fault in doing so out of compassion, as his intention is to benefit the other person.
Moving the body constitutes bodily karma; speaking words constitutes verbal transgression.
Within these two types of karma, committing either one brings about guilt.
This applies even to a corner of one’s robe: as long as it has not yet been separated from the body, [the act is not complete].
One should know that this constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); if one departs from the body [of the robe], one commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Regarding the training rule on robes offered in haste: these are benefits exclusively for those who have spent the rains retreat;
they should be divided among those who have completed the retreat. This does not extend to others; to divide them prematurely incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
In the summer, there is no one to manage robes; therefore, it is not permissible to accept robes from others.
However, if there is a robe offered due to a difficult circumstance, gold and other such items may all be accepted.
There are five kinds of urgent offerings: namely, those given for the sake of the sick, for a sick person; and so forth.
Desiring death or intending to depart, one practices giving before setting out.
One may remain for ten days at will; during this time, one should accept material goods.
If one exceeds the period permitted for robes, it is then improper to possess them.
If a donor says, "I shall give with my own hands," and [the recipient] receives it and performs the formal act of holding (*udgrahaṇa*), all offenses are cleared.
If one obtains benefits at will, they belong entirely to those who have completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
It also applies to those who do not spend the rainy season retreat; they likewise perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together.
Regarding the training rule on being separated from one’s robes while in an *araṇya*:
if there is danger in the forest hermitage, one may leave one of the three robes behind at a layperson’s house in order to prevent such calamity.
Regarding staying apart from one's robes overnight: it is permitted for six nights without fault;
when the seventh dawn arises, one must return to the araṇya.
This is not the preceding summer retreat; this is called the subsequent summer retreat.
In this context, if there are bandits, one should know that this refers to what constitutes a "danger.
What is called a place of "doubt and fear" refers to lions, tigers, and the like;
"fear" refers to gadflies and such, which cause distress and are full of many poisons.
The Training Rule on Rain-Bathing Garments: When one month remains of spring, from the fourth fortnight until the fifth fortnight;
if one requires a rain-bathing garment, it is appropriate to request one at this time.
When the day of the commencement of the *pūrvavarṣā* retreat has passed, one month still remains;
during this month, one should maintain the vow, and upon entering the summer, one may use [the rain-cloth] as desired.
For one and a half months, a *bhikṣu* may use the rain-cloth.
If one seeks to keep [the robe] before the *pārivāsika* period has passed, this incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
However, if on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one receives excellent robes or wealth as a gift,
one should perform the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and accept them in the presence of the assembly.
Once the assembly of monks has reached a common agreement, let each apply themselves with earnest diligence;
in a single day the work shall be completed, and the substance must be made firm.
Having fashioned the robe according to the Dharma, it should be beautifully adorned with flowers and fragrances.
Placed within the assembly, let those who know the Dharma take heed:
by spreading the kaṭhina, the bhikṣus obtain great benefit;
that is to say, within ten days, there is no need for separate possession of robes.
Although one lacks the saṃghāṭī, one may go about at will among people;
eating separately from the community and passing food along—none of these constitute an offense.
Although one does not inform the bhikṣus, one may enter within the village.
The full account contains ten [periods], but here I have briefly mentioned five.
That is, from the middle of the eighth month until the middle of the first month;
within these five months, it is called the *kaṭhina* season.
One who has traveled with a downward intention and has completed [the journey], one who has practiced the *pārivāsika* (probation) and the *nissāraṇa* (release);
one whose summer retreat was incomplete and one who broke it; one who arrived after the summer retreat—these are not permitted.
This applies to those who have sent a messenger, as well as *śrāmaṇeras*, and those undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇā*).
If one does not accept the *kaṭhina*, all remaining benefits must be granted [to others].
One whose morality is broken and whose conduct is ruined, whom the Great Assembly has placed under suspension,
or who has joined the faction of the unrighteous, shall not receive [the benefits] even if they spend the summer retreat in another location.
These five kinds of people bring neither profit nor benefit;
because they cannot digest the offerings, they should instead be [the objects of] those who uphold the precepts.
Regarding the training rule on diverting communal property into one's own possession: if property belonging to the Saṃgha is present before them, one diverts it to make it one's own.
The benefit of others is most difficult to digest; one shall suffer the pains of hell.
When clothing, gold, and the like are given by others, as well as various foods and drinks—to obstruct these two kinds of things is known as "misappropriation" (parivartana). One should know this.
If the benefits generated for this assembly are diverted to another saṃgha, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) will certainly be incurred; one should know that this is not a fundamental offense.
Alternatively, if the benefits intended for another assembly are collectively diverted to this saṃgha, [the same applies].
If an object belongs to this [monastic] community, the entire assembly incurs an offense of transgression (*āpatti*).
Regarding images of the Buddha, reliquaries (*caitya*), persons, or even animals;
as well as ascending or descending stairs, eaves, and so forth—if one diverts these for personal use, it is all an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the precept on seven-day medicines: having received ghee, honey, and so forth from a bhikṣu, one may take them for oneself and consume them as desired;
this is without transgression provided it remains within the seven-day limit.
The *naiḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished; this should be done by a virtuous bhikṣu.
After an interval of at least one night has passed, the offense must be confessed.
On the second day, the robe should be returned; the original owner should then request it back.
If one with a stingy mind does not return [the robe], it may be forcibly taken back.
If any one of these three conditions exists, and one further obtains another robe,
because it is not yet purified, accepting it at that time constitutes an offense in every case.
Because one must relinquish robes and other items, the term "relinquishment" (niḥsarga) arises;
furthermore, because one falls into the three miserable realms [due to such transgressions], it is called "relinquishment and falling" (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 2. The Ninety *Pāyattika* Dharmas (Middle Section). Regarding the training rule on intentional lying (*saṃprajñāna-mṛṣāvāda*), the thirty matters associated with forfeiture and falling (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) have already been explained.
Now, following the sequence, the ninety simple *pāyattika* offenses shall be explained.
The multitude of people from Rājagṛha, as well as the bhikṣus, inquired of Rāhula: "Where is the Buddha now?
