He replied: "The World-Honored One is here; he is in that place."
On account of this matter, the Great Master spoke two verses:
"The person who speaks falsehood violates the single Dharma of Reality;
having committed many evils in the present life, they shall suffer the retribution thereof in the future."
It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, terrifying with its fierce flames,
than to use a mouth broken by precepts to consume the food of others through unrighteous means.
Because of the false speech of bhikṣus, the Buddha established this training rule (śikṣāpada).
There are nine distinctions, ranging even down to two types.
Regarding the five rootless factors—the *pārājika* offenses and so forth;
discipline, view, conduct, and wrong livelihood—these nine kinds should be known.
The five dharmas, such as defeat (pārājika), differ in three ways: view and so forth;
to speak of differences therein, one should know that eight forms of falsehood are established.
These concern precepts, views, conduct, and livelihood, as well as what is seen, heard, and suspected.
When a bhikṣu speaks falsely, there are seven such instances:
three times when what has already been said, what is currently being said, or what is yet to be said is untrue;
furthermore, there are the three cases involving what is seen and so forth—thus, there are six ways of speaking falsehoods.
In this way, each [of the five] is subtracted; the wise should reflect upon this:
if one’s speech is known by another, it becomes two kinds of falsehood.
What are the five kinds of falsehood?
One should know that these constitute *parājika* (defeats) and so forth;
when one speaks of having attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), it is called entering into a *parājika*.
If, regarding two kinds of slander, one deceives another with what is untrue;
The distinction between having a formal basis (*mūla*) and lacking one is what defines entry into the various categories of instruction.
If, before the Saṃgha, one declares the Dharma to be non-Dharma,
because of the gravity of addressing such a public assembly, it is termed an offense of Thullaccaya.
If, during the *poṣadha* ceremony, one is asked, "Are you pure?
and remains silent while concealing a transgression, this is called entering into wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*).
When such a false speech is uttered, it constitutes four distinct types of offenses.
All other false teachings are subsumed within these [other] categories of downfall.
These five types of false teachings differ in their gravity and lightness;
because they do not overlap or intermingle, each is presented with its own specific terminology for inclusion.
In cases where one has not seen and so forth, yet speaks of having seen and so forth through inversion;
thus, when one speaks of another’s understanding with a defiled mind, one falls into the offense of injury.
Regarding the training rule on disparaging speech: even if one disparages an animal by calling it "hornless" and so forth, [it constitutes an offense].
Feeling shame, one cannot bear it; how much less could one destroy another!
For this reason the World-Honored One taught that one should always benefit sentient beings;
if a bhikṣu utters words of destruction, he immediately incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, asks about the Brahmin caste—
“You have gone forth as a brahmacārin”— this constitutes an *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he asks about a kṣatriya with a playful mind, it likewise constitutes an *duṣkṛta* offense.
Vaiśyas and Śūdras— if questioned, they constitute the root [offense].
Hair-cutters, carpenters, weavers, itinerant tailors, bamboo-workers,
and those of such various kinds— if questioned, they incur a *pārājika* offense.
"You, a brahmin, are skilled in crafts; you ought to study purity.
What use is a śramaṇa to you?"—by saying this, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"You are a kṣatriya; [tasks such as] wielding the spear, the bow, and archery—these are what you ought to do. To speak [of them] now would be an evil deed.
Likewise, the tasks performed by śūdras and vaiśyas..."
If one engages in various crafts such as weaving bamboo, one incurs a root offense.
Regarding begging for alms, teaching, reciting, and so forth—
if you perform such acts, you incur an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), just as before.
Lame, blind, crippled, and hunchbacked; dwarfs, deaf, and mute—to speak thus in disparagement of others, one falls and is immediately scorched by fire.
You, with your scabies, leprosy, and abscesses; your itches, sores, hemorrhoids, and nausea;
By speaking such words as these, this person shall fall into transgression.
Your offense is not purified; you possess doubt, regret, and misdeeds.
You harbor anger, resentment, and vexation; your guilt is likewise as described before.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind intent on disparagement, utters evil speech, abuse, and the like;
if his words correspond to base expressions, he falls into an offense and brings harm upon himself.
This applies likewise to [deriding] one’s lineage, craft, occupation, physical appearance, or illness.
Words concerning offenses and afflictions are all termed "destructive speech.
If one intends to distinguish the person before them, asking, "Which one is the Buddha-protected?
and answering, "A Kṣatriya," and so forth—there is no fault in such cases.
The Training Rule on Divisive Speech: If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, Intending to cause a rift between others, And does so with a mind of malice, He will certainly incur a pāyattika offense.
"You lowly person who has shaved your hair, when asked 'Who told you?', you replied, 'So-and-so said so'; this incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
In the preceding training rule (*śikṣāpada*), [the objects] such as clans and craftsmen were mentioned."
One should know that such offenses are similar; the wise should not commit them.

Regarding the *śikṣāpada* on the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for exposing and settling disputes: when the harmonious Saṃgha performs the ritual and unanimously consents to the matter, should one further violate it, one falls into an offense and thereby brings harm upon oneself.
The great assembly, with one mind, acts according to the Dharma and according to the rules;
they should know how to eliminate the four kinds of disputes, such as those concerning formal discussion (*sāmghika-vivāda*).
With a single heart, they uphold the Dharma together, remaining free from hesitation regarding their affairs.
If one says it is "not good" at the time [of the formal act], one incurs the offense of *karmabheda*.
If one perceives what has not been done as already done, or destroys it out of doubt, this constitutes the offense of *dukkaṭa*; otherwise, there is no fault.
If one performs this formal act of adjudication while perceiving it as another formal act of adjudication,
one should know that whether the matter is resolved or not, the offense incurred is the same as before.
This applies equally when the host presides over the *karmavācanā*, or when holding the consent (*chanda*) or the view (*dṛṣṭi*), and so forth.
Together with visiting bhikṣus, these are called the five distinctions.
One who recognizes the beginning, middle, and end is called the host;
herein, the person who performs the ritual act is the one who presides over the *karmavācanā*.
One who intends for another is called a "holder of desire";
one who dwells before the assembly is called a "seer of equality.
I cherish such a view and engage in such deliberation.
If one does not recognize the beginning, middle, or end, it should be known that this is termed "adventitious.
If the first three are violated, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if the latter two are violated, both result in a *duṣkṛta*.
The training rule concerning teaching the Dharma to women for more than five or six words: When teaching the Dharma to a woman, one must limit it to exactly five or six words;
except when a man of intelligence is present, exceeding this limit constitutes a root offense.
All forms are impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
These five aggregates should be understood by those of clear wisdom.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all impermanent.
This is called the "six-word" [offense], which the wise should recognize.
When intending to speak five phrases, one intentionally utters the sixth;
or when intending to speak six, the seventh is likewise the same offense.
If one stammers without fault, or speaks with haste;
if a wise woman asks again and one explains at that time, there is no offense.
To recite the Dharma phrase by phrase together with one who has not yet received full ordination—
To speak [of another's faults] as one hears them brings about an offense; reciting together [the same words] is permitted and free from fault.

Regarding the training rule on speaking of another’s grave offense to one who has not yet received full ordination: if one knows that another has committed a grave transgression, one incurs an offense by informing an unordained person;
however, there is no fault in speaking when the Sangha is bestowing a formal act (kamma).
What is called a "grave offense" (*sthūlātyaya*)?
It refers to the *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; one should know that it does not refer to other matters.
If a monk speaks of such an offense to someone who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*), [he incurs a fault].
If one falsely claims to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If it refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), which are commonly known as the dharmas of ordinary people;
one who is not such [an ordinary person] is called a "superior person," referring to the spheres of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth.
The training rule concerning the misappropriation of communal property: To speak of goods given to the community as being for an individual, and to divert them accordingly;
when such false speech is uttered, one incurs the offense of *pāyattika*.

Regarding the training rule on disparaging the precepts: when the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra is recited for the fortnightly purification (*poṣadha*), if one speaks with contempt or disdain, one will certainly incur the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Why is it necessary within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra to speak of these minor and very minor precepts that cause people to give rise to vexation and regret?
This is called the transgression of the light and contemptuous precept.
Giving rise to weariness, doubt, and affliction, and burning with the heat of sorrow;
these can cause remorse to arise—whatever one says in such cases incurs transgression.
This applies to all the minor precepts contained within the Vinaya teachings.
If a bhikṣu speaks with contempt, he likewise incurs the original offense.

Regarding the training rule on destroying seeds: all types of seeds and the "villages" of sentient beings—whether roots, stems, joints, buds, or fruits—to damage them oneself or to cause others to do so constitutes an offense.
If they grow from roots, these are called root-seeds;
one should know that these include nut-grass, ginger, taro, and the like.
Stem-seeds emerge from stems; once planted in the earth, they immediately sprout.
One should recognize that the *bodhivṛkṣa*, the pomegranate, the willow, and so forth all belong to this category.
As for those propagated from joints, one cuts off a joint and plants it in the ground where it can grow;
because of this, plants such as reeds, *naḍa*, sugarcane, and bamboo receive their names.
The splitting of seeds refers to peaches, almonds, hemp, beans, and the like; the term "grains" refers to rice, wheat, and so forth.
There is an interpretation that distinct seeds arise from cow dung and the like producing lotuses, and that fine awns grow from wool; this is the specific explanation of one master.
Sentient beings such as insects and ants encompass all forms of life.
"Village" refers to trees and the like, which serve as the dwellings for sentient beings;
to damage them with a thought of doubt incurs the offense of a downfall (pārājika).
Thus, regarding seeds, fruits, and the like, one incurs a transgression if they correspond to the object;
it should be known that one likewise incurs a fault if there is a different seed, a different perception, or doubt.
When a bhikṣu takes the five kinds [of grain], places them in a mortar, and pounds them;
If the seeds are damaged, the five offenses are incurred simultaneously;
if they are not damaged, one incurs only the five *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doings).
Placing them in fire or throwing them into boiling water is, as before, a fundamental offense (*pārājika*) in all cases.
If one acts with the intention of damaging while walking upon green grass, one falls into an offense when the damage occurs; if no injury is caused, it incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one drags an object across green grass and causes damage...
Or if one pours out broth, rice gruel, or the like,
the transgression is the same as that of pouring [water]. If, by a single means,
one cuts down a single tree, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* and one *pāyattika*.
If one uses two means of action to cut down a single tree or the like,
one should know that two *duṣkṛta* offenses are incurred, and one *pāyattika* offense.
According to the number of means employed, that many *duṣkṛta* offenses shall be obtained.
According to the specific nature of the act, one incurs the fundamental offense in every case.
Regarding leaves, fruits, unopened flowers, various lotus roots and tubers,
lotus stalks, water lilies, and duckweed— the gravity of the downfall depends on the degree of destruction.
Wrinkled bark and yellowing leaves, lotuses and the like have already blossomed;
if one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense, the Buddha taught that the gravity of the transgression varies.
If one requires tooth-sticks, as well as bark, leaves, flowers, or roots;
When gathering [vegetation], one should speak of it as "pure"; one must not say "cut" or "break.
Regarding water-weeds, duckweed, pond-scum, *dìjī* (earth-chicken), salt-encrusted soil, green moss, white mold, and *gé* (knotweed)—one should not pull or drag them about.
What is pure speech? It is that which you should know as such;
understanding this as being equal to purity, one realizes that all things are entirely without fault.
There are two types of purification, distinguished by five pairs: fire, knife, withering, bird, and nail;
dropping, breaking, pulling out, twisting off, and splitting—these are not permissible.
When constructing or felling a tree, one should make a request to the tree deity.
With various flowers, fruits, and food, one may perform sacrifices according to the season.
One should recite the True Dharma, such as the *Triśaraṇa-gāthā* and other sūtras;
it is fitting that one should fully explain the retributions for the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome deeds.
Practicing virtue invites pleasant fruits; otherwise, one is born in the evil realms.
To manifest the merit of giving, he further spoke of the sins of stinginess and greed.
Within the gardens of Nandana and the like, celestial maidens constantly sport.
The fruit of supreme bliss for a long duration can be summoned only through giving.
Constantly harboring the fires of hunger and thirst, one does not even hear the names of water or broth;
wandering through the various realms of saṃsāra, one undergoes suffering without end.
Habituated since beginningless time, repeatedly oppressed by afflictions,
Bringing no benefit to self or others, all because of being entangled by stinginess;
Even after seven days, there has been no change, nor any shedding of blood and the like.
A great tree should be cut down; one that is different should not be harmed.

Regarding the training rule on disparaging, reviling, and treating others with contempt: when a bhikṣu utters words of disparagement or uses coarse and abusive speech, the light and heavy offenses incurred therein shall be briefly stated according to their general outline.
The assembly performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one announcement) to appoint those who shall distribute the rice and gruel;
those who shall assign the rooms and distribute the cakes and fruits; and those who shall distribute the remaining miscellaneous items.
[They also appoint those for] the *kaṭhina* utensils, and those to store and guard the *cīvara* robes.
As well as those who distribute robes, and those who guard the rain-cloths;
the *vihārapāla*, and the messengers sent by such persons;
those who carry vessels and poles for water, and those who drive away crows.
If one is sent to distribute bedding, to distribute cakes, or to distribute profits;
if the community appoints such a person, then when others feel resentment, it constitutes the fundamental offense in all cases.
Regarding these twelve types of persons, one who harbors resentment or reviles them incurs the fundamental offense.
Other instances result in minor offenses; one should carefully examine the specific circumstances.
Regarding the training rule on violating and disturbing [another's] speech: violating the instruction incurs the primary offense. "Instruction" refers to the time when another person questions you;
"disturbing" refers to speaking evasive words rather than providing a definitive response.
When he asked such questions, wishing to provoke me, I gave other answers;
except when a hunter came to inquire, fearing he might harm my previous lives.
I look upon the sky and my own fingernails; in ultimate reality, sentient beings do not exist.
When this person speaks with skillful means, replying to others does not constitute a fault.
If, when questioned by another, one remains silent out of resentment, one will thereby fall into the evil realms;
only when tormented by suffering and pain will one speak.

The Training Rule on Not Putting Away Reclining Utensils: If one places monastic beds, seats, or the like in an open space, unless someone has been entrusted with them, one incurs an offense for departing while leaving them behind.
If one leaves one's original residence and intends to travel outside the boundary,
yet has not yet moved beyond the space occupied by the bed or similar furniture, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one abandons the residence and departs while it is raining, one likewise incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If there is water that is moist and clear, one incurs the offense of a downfall (pāyattika).
It is said that there are three kinds of deterioration: namely, by insects, wind, and rain.
When both the exterior and interior are damaged, this is called deterioration by insects.
When it is blown by the wind and folded back, this is called destruction by wind;
when the second layer is soaked by rain, one should recognize this as destruction by rain.
If it remains inside a room and is damaged by insects and the like, [it is destruction by creatures].
One incurs offenses such as *dukkaṭa*; the rules for these are all the same as previously explained.
If one departs without initial reflection and suddenly remembers while on the way, one should reflect upon one's own delusion and the like, and must sternly reproach the mind.
If you encounter other bhikṣus, upon seeing them you should approach them;
for the sake of protecting your bedding and requisites, you should earnestly and kindly entrust them with your care.
If they have taken charge of it, do not hide or move it from its place wherever you go.
The arrow of the *pāyattika* strikes one immediately, yet one does not remember the person [who sent it].
When a layperson comes to invite one for a meal, one must lend them a seat;
if a *śrāmaṇera* or others take it away, the *bhikṣu* should not carry it himself.
When lay associates visit the monastery to provide food offerings for the community of monks,
one should grant them seats and assign guards to protect the property.
This applies even if they are caregivers, or if they are elderly, infirm, or have broken the precepts.
Furthermore, those who are not yet fully ordained must never be entrusted with the supervision [of robes].
If two people sit on the same seat, the junior one should fold and put them away;
if their seniority in the *varṣa* is equal, the one who rises last should take charge of them.
When listening to the Dharma and other teachings, if the Elder is advanced in years and frail,
the younger monks should take turns assisting him by lifting and arranging his monastic seats and mats.
The Buddha ordained that all Bhikṣus must provide service and attendance to their elders and seniors.
One should rely upon these matters, benefiting both oneself and others.
If a difficult situation arises—whether at the foot of a wall or the root of a tree—one may sit there without incurring fault;
yet one must not break the fast without a valid reason.
When traveling with one's *cīvara*, its protective perimeter remains as it was;
even if there is no one to guard it, one should understand that the same principle applies to bedding.
When reciting the True Dharma, one should ascend a high seat.
One’s dwelling should be made secure and peaceful, and one should revere the words of the Great Master.
A high seat should be prepared with four legs shaped like lions;
its height and depth should be appropriate to the occasion, and it should be well-crafted and perfectly square.
A walkway is installed on the sides, with a flower-patterned footstool placed in front;
one sits cross-legged to recite the words of the Honored One, and when reading, a desk is set before him.
Behind him, a flower-screen is installed, with silk streamers hanging freely from both sides.
The upper canopy, according to the proper occasion, Is placed beneath the long corridor.
A long rope hangs from the eaves below, Intended for suspending flower garlands;
Those who come with a sincere heart to hear the sutras Should stand or sit in the rows before them.
A layperson may prepare a precious seat; those who wish to sit may do so as they please.
One should dwell there with mindfulness gathered, contemplating the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena.
One should attend to it thus: "This is the property of a donor."
Although it is adorned with jewels, there is no fault in sitting upon it.
Whether in the palaces of yakṣas and nāgas or in the heavens, sitting is permitted;
this teaching causes their merit to increase—this is the instruction of the Muni.

The Training Rule on Not Putting Away Grass Mats: If one uses a grass mat belonging to the community within a monastery, and there is no obstacle to departing, one must put it away oneself or entrust someone else to look after it.
This is also explained as before; it is no different from [the rules regarding] mats and bedding.
One should know that the offense is the same as that; those who guard the precepts should recognize this.
If one does not remove [the bedding] from the house, or if the owner forbids its disposal;
If one spreads [a rug] within a vihāra without removing it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
For those practicing meditation who perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), the rug should be twelve cubits long;
for those diligently engaged in recitation, it should likewise be known to be twelve [cubits].
If the ground is hard, one should spread grass; failing to do so will lead to illness.
To prevent calamities, one should provide partitions; without these, there is no cause for distress.
Regarding the training rule on dragging others out of the monastic quarters: if one is angry with another bhikṣu, one drags him out from his dwelling place.
That person incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*), except in cases where there is a compelling reason.
Even if one does not pull it with one's own hand, but causes another bhikṣu to pull it, both persons incur an offense; that is to say, a *pāyattika*.
If one causes a śrāmaṇera or the like to pull a bhikṣu out of the monastery, the bhikṣu incurs the fundamental offense (mūlāpatti), while the śrāmaṇera incurs a minor transgression (duṣkṛta).
Regarding the training rule on forcibly causing distress or contact with another: if one uses food that is good or bad, or that is cold or hot, etc.;
Therefore, to annoy another bhikṣu and cause him to eat [only] what he has invited constitutes a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Whether it be a dining hall, a warm shelter, a bathhouse near the door,
a gallery, or the eaves— none of these locations are appropriate for such a division [of food].
Regarding seats and bedding, one should not move them without the intention of another;
when a previously resident bhikṣu arrives, do not allow a latercomer to displace him.
Therefore, regarding the training rule on sitting or lying down carelessly on a bed with detachable legs: if one dwells in an upper room, one must not sit on a bed with detachable legs.
To support the legs of a bed with wooden planks, there is no fault when sitting upon it.
As for what is called "the feet coming loose," it refers to pulling them out from the holes;
this occurs when one stays in an old dwelling where the rafters have long been decayed and rotten.
If there is no object to support the feet, one may place them upward upon the bed;
provided it does not harm others, one should use it after considering the time.
Alternatively, at times, one may use iron nails to fasten the feet so they do not slip off.
One may, according to one's inclination, insert wedges for stability or wrap them with grass ropes.

Regarding the training rule on using water containing living beings: if one pours water containing life onto the ground, trees, or other objects—whether acting oneself or commanding another—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If there are insects in the water and one perceives them or suspects they are there, one incurs the original offense;
if there are no insects but one perceives them or suspects they are there, one incurs the fault of *duṣkṛta*.
If one borrows a jar or a rope from another, there is no harm in using what the other provides.
Filter it well so that it may be clearly observed; when it is turbid, place a black fruit within.
If the water contains suspended impurities, one cannot see one's reflection in it;
therefore, filter it with diligent care, for only when it is pure is there no fault.
If a well or spring is known to be pure, and the dharma-vessel and other implements are well-sealed;
for the community or for an individual, the five kinds of water may be used as desired.
There are five types of filters: namely, the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) and the *kamaṇḍalu*.
The dharma-flask along with its water-strainer, And the folds of one’s robe— With a settled mind,
one should inspect them well; If there are insects as small as a hair-tip,
One must examine them according to the instructions, Without the need for constant scrutiny.
One should observe the water to the extent that it would take six oxen to pull a cart;
this measurement of bamboo [length] for Magadha is called the limit of observation.
If, regarding a vessel of water, one gives rise to the thought or doubt that there are insects therein;
One should examine it thoroughly once more; only when there is no doubt may it be used.
Even if it is a distance of one *krośa* or perhaps a single *yojana*, provided one knows for certain that there is no *nīla* (mud/slime) there, one may proceed.
If one is permitted to return immediately, there is no fault in traveling half a *yojana*;
if there are acquaintances among the merchants and travelers, one may proceed at will by means of their escort.
When traveling along a riverbank following the current, for every *krośa*, [one must remain mindful].
One should carefully examine whether it is fit to drink; otherwise, one should not drink.
When taking water upstream or from its source, one should examine and filter it as usual;
for water from a pond or lake that does not flow, one should examine it within a distance of one fathom.
At places for drawing water, such as wells, one should recite the verses spoken by the Buddha;
wherever there is a deity, one should make a request of them.
One should not bring the *kuṇḍikā* (water flask) to the mouth to drink water; the Buddha did not permit this.
If leaves and such are certainly absent, a secluded place is not a restriction.
One should appropriately use silk or cloth to tie the mouth of the *kuṇḍikā* with leaves, as well as to cover jars and vases; otherwise, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If there is grime or grease on jars and the like, one should diligently wash and clean them;
they may be dried in the sun at the appropriate time, desiring to make them pure.
What is done by laypeople, a śrāmaṇera should not do.
What is done by a śrāmaṇera may not be appropriate for a bhikṣu;
regarding a bhikṣu’s conduct toward a bhikṣuṇī, there are matters that constitute an offense and those that do not.
One must carefully examine all such cases and act in accordance with the teachings.
In ponds, wells, and the like, if one sees cakes, vegetables, or other such things, one may drink from them after filtering as desired; know that this is called "pure.
At places where laypeople offer water, one must carefully inspect it according to the rules.
Even though it is not the proper time [for meals], one may drink or use [these liquids] according to one's needs.
In places such as cowherds' settlements where bhikṣus lack water,
they may likewise use curd-juice, milk, and so forth for washing their feet as the occasion requires.
If wine has been stored in large or small vessels, these utensils should be discarded;
if they have held oil or similar substances, they should be treated by heating with fire or scrubbing with water,
or by having fish or turtles lick them clean, so that all grease and grime are entirely removed.
Place water within this vessel; its use at improper times becomes pure.
When a woman requests water, a bhikṣu may grant it to her;
however, he should not pour it in a continuous stream, lest a mind of deluded attachment arise.
The Training Rule on Building a Great Monastery Beyond the Limit: When constructing a great vihāra, one should establish the foundation and install drainage conduits;
One may then attach doors and bolts, And likewise install bright windows.
If one wishes to erect a wall, one should mix grass with mud;
when piling it up to the level of the horizontal bolt, do not exceed two or three layers.
If one adds more on top, one will incur the offense of a *pāyattika*.
Constructed of brick, stone, or wood, though many such cases exist, there is no offense.

Regarding the training rule on not appointing one who has not been authorized to instruct bhikṣuṇīs: One who possesses the full precepts and is learned in the teachings, who has reached twenty years of age and twenty years of standing as a monk;
whose speech is excellent and complete, and who has never personally defiled a bhikṣuṇī.

He who skillfully explains the eight *pārājika* offenses, can expound upon the eight points of respect (*gurudharma*), and possesses the seven qualities required for appointment—such a person is fit; otherwise, it is not appropriate.
He must be well-versed in the *sūtras*, the *vinaya*, and the *mātṛkā*.
This combined instruction for nuns, which can resolve disputes and bring about subduing—
apart from this, there is another, a second brief instruction:
if the great assembly has a teaching, the Elder may transmit the words.
"Is the community of nuns pure? And is it harmonious?
There is no bhikṣu here to provide instruction to the nuns."
Sisters, in the teaching of the Muni, you must always be heedful;
do not let your precepts decline, for this is the cause of the three miserable realms.
Because you have honored twenty years of seniority, you are able to discipline those beings who are to be converted.
One who is well-versed in the Vinaya teachings, O King, should recognize this as the training rule for the instructor:
once appointed to act as an instructor, although one may be fully endowed with ethical discipline (śīla), one must return by daybreak;
it is not permitted to let the sun set while away.
If the sun has set and one perceives it as having set, or if one entertains doubt;
yet one still performs the act of instruction, there is no doubt that one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If the sun has not yet set but one perceives it as having set, or if one gives rise to a doubting mind; [and one still instructs, one likewise incurs an offense].
Struck by the arrow of misdeeds, one shall undergo great suffering.
If the nunnery door is not closed, or if it is situated nearby;
or if there is much instruction, there is no harm even when the sun has set.
A nun may perform offerings according to her own ability;
the honored one should accept the food so that her merit may increase.
Regarding the training rule on disparaging others for the sake of food and drink: if, with a mind of resentment or jealousy, one treats the instructor with contempt and deprecation.
By giving rise to an unwholesome mind, one shall encounter the flames of hell.
He who possesses a mind stained by greed and instructs a nun to seek food and drink—
yet speaks according to what he has actually seen— is truly without fault.
The training rule concerning giving robes to a nun who is not a relative: If she is a nun who is not a relative, it is improper to give her clothing;
because of her greedy desire to obtain them, she does not consider the source from which they come.
Regarding the training rule on making robes for a nun who is not a relative: one should not make a robe for a nun who is not a relative;
because doing so results in improper appearance, it causes the laity to give rise to reproach and contempt.
The Training Rule on Traveling with a Bhikṣuṇī on the Same Road: When a bhikṣu travels toward another place, If he travels as a companion with a bhikṣuṇī;
In times of great fear from bandits and the like, There is no fault in traveling together.
If one is ill and has no one to carry them, they must not be abandoned on the road;
bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should carry each other in turn.
A bhikṣuṇī may carry her own provisions for the journey, which are deemed pure for a bhikṣu.
A bhikṣu may accept purification from a bhikṣuṇī; in these matters, do not harbor doubt.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī board a boat to travel up or down a river, this is not permitted;
however, there is no fault if they cross directly across.
The training rule concerning sitting alone with a woman in a secluded place: Because Udāyin sat with a woman in a secluded place, he incurred public censure;
therefore, the Noble One decreed that such a thing should not be done.
The training rule on sitting in private with a nun: Furthermore, sitting alone in a secluded place with the nun Guptā;
based on the circumstances, this constitutes one offense, while the remaining three cases all result in a downfall.

The training rule concerning knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has praised [the donor] in order to obtain food: If a bhikṣu knows that the bhikṣuṇī obtained the food because she praised [the donor], except when the donor had a prior intention [to give], eating it incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
There are two kinds of praise: for those who possess the precepts and for those who are learned.
Those with the precepts range from stream-enterers up to arhats;
those who are learned are masters of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā-śāstras.
If one truly possesses such virtues, praising food for them incurs no fault.
If one truly lacks such virtues, yet accepts praise from a nun for the sake of profit;
if one eats knowing this to be so, one immediately incurs the root offense.

Regarding the training rule on eating in succession: if a bhikṣu is not afflicted by illness, and it is not the time for traveling without robes, yet he develops further greed after having already had enough, he incurs an offense at the moment of eating.
If one cannot find peace with even a single meal, this is described as being "ill";
when one obtains a robe merely the size of a square cubit, this is called the "time for giving robes.
In the monastic quarters or at a caitya, the ground is like a small mat.
Sweeping, wiping, sprinkling, and smearing—these are called "labor.
If a bhikṣu travels half a yojana and then returns;
this is called "conduct on the road," and there is no offense in eating again.
If one has received an invitation for robes, yet subsequently accepts an invitation for those without robes;
after having accepted it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense, and at the time of eating, one obtains the original [offense].
If one first receives an invitation for those without robes, and later there is a *cīvara*;
Even if one partakes of food at both locations, this meal is not subject to restriction.
If there was an invitation with robes received first, and a subsequent invitation also includes robes;
eating at both places according to one's inclination—in all these cases, there is no fault.
If one abandons a place where there is no clothing and goes to a household that has clothing,
this should be understood as applying only to circumstances of difficulty and regarding robes, and not for other matters.
If it is known that at a layperson's house, the entire Saṃgha is being invited, [one may go].
The administrative official and others, when the time arrives, shall sound the *kaiṇḍa* gong.
If a bhikṣu from one's own group or a guest has newly arrived, one should instruct them on where to take their seat; one should not depart in silence.

The training rule concerning accepting more than one meal: When a bhikṣu stays at a dwelling place of non-Buddhists, he may eat there for one day provided he is not ill; otherwise, it is not permissible.
If one stays apart from the sick on another day, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense;
if one receives food from another again, swallowing it brings about the primary transgression.
This applies unless the donor’s intention is impartial, or if it is in the case of a relative.
Even if one eats for many days, this shall not be considered a transgression.
Regarding the training rule on receiving food beyond three bowls: if the donor does not act according to one's wishes, yet one obtains rice, parched grain, or other such foods;
having taken two or three full bowls, if one exceeds that limit, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If taking three from the large bowl, they are two large and one medium;
or two large and one small; or two medium and one large;
or two medium and one small; or filling the bowl to take it back.
All these incur the original offense; the three minor [offenses] are entirely without fault.
If kinsmen joyfully offer [food], there is no fault in accepting much;
having accepted it, one should take it away and distribute it equally among the bhikṣus.
The Training Rule on Sufficient Food: Once a bhikṣu has finished eating his fill, it is not permissible for him to eat again;
if he does so without performing the remaining formalities, a transgression arises with every swallow.
The five kinds of *khādanīya* (hard foods) do not constitute a sufficient meal;
once the *bhojanīya* (soft foods) have been sufficiently consumed, these too should not be eaten.
The five kinds of *bhojanīya* are: rice, barley, and bean porridge.
Grains, meat, and various cakes—these should be known as the five *bhojanas* (solid foods).
Roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits are called the five *khādanīyas* (chewable foods);
this is based on the meaning of "chewing and biting," whereas the five *bhojanas* generally include both chewing and swallowing.
Knowing this is *prāsaṇika* food, and that there is someone nearby who has offered it;
having performed the ritual of refusal (*pratikṣepa-dharma*), one leaves the seat and abandons the dignified posture (*īryāpatha*).
One who acts thus in these five respects is called a bhikṣu who has finished his meal (*paryāpta-bhukta*).
In this context, if even one [of the requisites] is lacking, it is not called "sufficient.
When the sufficiency has ceased and one departs, this is termed "cessation of sufficiency";
if one speaks of the path provisionally, the Noble One declares that there is no fault.
If one performs the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-vidhi), one should not sit at the side nor behind [the teacher];
one should not place it in the lap, nor hold it in the air, nor set it on the ground.
Having washed both hands thoroughly, one may then receive the food.
Having finished eating, one should not leave the seat; this should be known as "not yet satisfied.
While holding the food, one may squat and address a bhikṣu:
"I am performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa* rite; you, sir, should bear this in mind."
That person should take some food, whether two or three mouthfuls;
saying, "Please take this and go," he may eat it as he pleases.
Even if that person has already finished his meal, provided he has not yet left his seat;
One should proceed before that person, performing all the ritual procedures as described above.
Since that person is not permitted to eat it, one should say to the person who will eat it:
"Take it and eat it as you please. This is called the second *śeṣa-dharma* (rule concerning leftovers).
If one obtains what is not considered formal food— namely, things such as milk,
curd, thin gruel, or thin flour porridge— these do not constitute a completed meal (*pūraṇa-bhakta*).
If a spoon held upright does not remain standing [in the vessel], this is called "thin gruel."
The trace of a finger-hook is not seen; one should know this refers to thin flour.
If one forms the thought that one has eaten enough, or if doubt arises, eating will incur the fundamental offense and open the gates to hell.
If one has not yet eaten enough, yet forms the intention that one has eaten enough;
or when a state of doubt arises—these all incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the training rule on encouraging another to eat their fill: knowing that another has already finished eating, and not performing the *atirittakaraṇa* (the rite of leaving food remaining);
Harboring an evil mind within, one incurs sin by urging another to eat.
If one suspects that another has already eaten their fill, yet persistently urges them to eat more;
desiring to cause another to commit a transgression, one will wound oneself with suffering in the future.
One should not tread with both feet upon leaves used for food;
this is not a transgression for one who is ill, but for one who is healthy, it gives rise to censure.
If a bhikṣu is not ill, he should not eat while wearing his sandals.
If one is ill, it is permissible to draw out the foot; treading upon a shoe is not an offense.
When food is offered from behind, or from a distance, or across a barrier, or when the hand is not held palm-upward, in all such cases, the acceptance is not valid.
The giver stands nearby, directly in front without any obstruction;
both must receive with palms turned upward, and one should request with the utmost attentiveness.
Pointing to the food, have it placed in the bowl, just as if it were falling onto a leaf plate.
This is what is called "receiving"; one should eat it without hesitation.
There are many kinds of minute particles: flowers, fruits, food, drink, and clothing;
they are distinguished as being tangible or intangible, and pure or impure.
There are many kinds of soil and dust, both pure and impure;
if the appearance of the color is not distinct, one need not laboriously accept it.
If the characteristics of the dust are distinct, one should neither accept nor eat it.
If food soils one’s robes, they must be washed; failure to wash them gives rise to transgression.
If one has finished distributing salt and other items, one should not rise even if the meal is small;
one should sit at the proper time and follow the order of precedence without jostling others.
When the young dwell above the old, one’s perceptions may give rise to doubt;
The *tūṣṇīka-śailpasthānika* [defilements] increase day by day.
If one gives food to another while harboring a mind of expectation, [the fault is incurred].
If a person offers food again, it is impure and should not be eaten.
If one has definitively renounced it and abandoned all hope, yet later obtains it from another, this is called pure food; there is no fault in accepting it.
Do not say to those who bring food, "Give me such food as this";
one may eat whatever is obtained along the way, for there is no prohibition against the sick.
If a bhikṣu has finished eating, he may set aside a single large spoonful.
One should give universally to all sentient beings, without making distinctions.
If a guest arrives who is about to depart, or if there is a steward or one who is ill,
as well as those tending to the sick, they may eat before others according to their needs.
Because Kaṇḍina opened the rice gruel, the assembly of monks all followed his example;
because of this, King Bimbisāra offered land, which the Buddha permitted them to accept.
Because of discussions concerning the rules for food as well as matters pertaining to medicine, [the regulations were established].
The essential gateways for purifying the ground and so forth must be understood according to each specific case.
Rice, cakes, meat, fish, bean porridge, parched grain flour, and the like—
these are called "medicines for the proper time" (kālabhaiṣajya), which must be consumed constantly to sustain life.
Grapes and plantains, sour fruits and black raspberries;
dates and the like, as well as the udumbara fruit—these are all called "non-time liquids" (vikāla-pāna).
Laypeople and śrāmaṇeras should soften them thoroughly and filter them clean.
Curdled milk, sugarcane juice, and vinegar—these are not to be consumed outside of the proper time.
It is taught that there are seven-day medicines: ghee, oil, honey, various sugars, rock sugar, and granulated sugar; it is permitted to take these without fault.
Furthermore, there are medicines for the duration of one's life, namely roots, stalks, and so forth;
these should be formally accepted and maintained according to the Dharma, and may always be consumed without limit.
Roots include clove, ginger, and the like; "stalks" refers to the *amṛta* creeper.
Turmeric and the like may be understood, as well as various fragrant substances mixed with water;
the seven-leaved plant, *kaṭuka*, and *vijaka* sprouts; fruits such as black pepper and the like;
and the three types of myrobalan—these are all permitted for consumption according to the specific illness.
Lac and asafoetida, yellow wax and various tree resins;
the five substances such as sesame ash, and furthermore the five kinds of salt.
*Amla*, *kṛtavedhana*, the seven-leaved tree (*saptaparṇa*), and *śirīṣa*.
The bark of such trees as these is all termed "medicine for the duration of life.
These various types of medicine are not intended to serve as food;
they are merely used to dispel hunger and thirst, with the aspiration of the mind directed toward Nirvana.
Grapes and pomegranates, mangoes and plantains;
roots such as lotus tubers—these should be known as medicines taken at specific times.
When such time-medicines and others are mixed with one another in succession, [they must be consumed accordingly].
Each according to the potency of the previous medicine, those who consume them will suffer no harm.
The fat of bears, cubs, tortoises, turtles, and likewise that of wild boars—
these may all be used to treat illnesses as they arise and may be consumed at any time.
The physician said that one may eat raw meat, provided it is not from humans, snakes, or elephants;
if fish or meat is brought forth, one should ask whether it is pure and then eat accordingly.
At the gate is the caitya-shed, the open-air pavilion, and the water hall.
Neither under the eaves nor within the rooms should food be cooked.
There are five kinds of purification, following rules such as the mental resolve;
if a kitchen is constructed for the purpose of cooking, the community of monks shall collectively establish it as a purified site.
When marking out the site with strings and ink-lines, and when first establishing the foundation,
the person skilled in the methods of construction should give rise to the thought and perform the ritual:
"At this very spot, I shall now establish a communal kitchen for the purification of food."
With threefold mental reflection and verbal recitation, one says: "This is the purification of the mind.
When half of the monastery has been completed, the administrator stands before the Saṃgha and makes this general announcement; it should be stated thus three times.
"I maintain this place as a site for pure food";
making such a formal declaration is called "common authorization.
If one constructs a monastery, the doors and rooms may be opened at random.
When the dimensions of the rooms are unequal, this is called "purification by the reclining of oxen.
If there is a monastic residence that has been abandoned by bhikṣus for a long time,
and no transgression occurs upon later arrival, this is called "purification by disuse."
If the Saṃgha performs the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and the assembly grants its detailed consent;
if they know the Dharma and are of one mind, this is called "purification by formal act" (*karmavācanā-śuddhi*).
These five types of purified kitchens are not established by the Bhikṣus through formal ritual action.
Setting food aside and cooking it both result in impurity;
yet for the sake of purification, there are two sets of five exceptions: using a knife, fire, withering, birds, or shells;
and when food is dropped, pulled out, cut, split, or broken—those who perform these acts incur no fault.
If burned by fire, all five types are pure; for the remaining [defects], if the seed is damaged, they are all considered formed.
If the skin is injured, some are not formed; therein one should verify the nature of their growth.
One should do so in the presence of the senior monk (sthavira), and the one serving the food should say:
Third, *pātra-dharma*: this is called the method for distributing food.
The senior monk (*upādhyāya*) should announce:
"It should be distributed equally."
One should eat with a focused mind and recite the concluding verses of aspiration.
While the verses on merit are being recited, a bhikṣu should not eat;
however, if he does not hear the sound, there is no fault in eating at that time.
While the verses are being recited, one should listen attentively;
once the stanzas are finished, one may eat as desired. Thereafter, further discourse is not prohibited.
Those who are capable should speak—either the head of the assembly or another person.
One should expound the Dharma in accordance with the needs of the time, following the expectations of the donor.
All who preach the Dharma must have companions and assistants;
for it is not through being alone that the Dharma is made to shine.
When reciting sutras for the assembly, it is not permitted to do so at night without a lamp;
to protect against insects, one should use a "hundred-eyed" screen or perhaps a cage to shield the light.
As for the fish, meat, and other foods consumed, these are the same as those of worldly people and eminent figures.
If another holds out an alms-bowl for one to receive, it is permissible to eat from it without fault. However,
if meat has been prepared specifically for oneself, and if there is seeing, hearing,
or suspicion regarding its origin, one should not consume it out of compassion for sentient beings.
If one obtains the remains of tigers, wolves, and the like, or if there is doubt or suspicion regarding them;
because of such thoughts, one must not abandon [the resolve for non-harming], and none of these should be eaten.
It is not permitted to lack compassion and indulge in flavors by taking the lives of others.
In accordance with the Dharma and relying on the three types of purity, eating meat is permitted without fault.
Medicines such as garlic and scallions are allowed at one's discretion when one is ill;
to preserve one’s life and body, these are called the vessels of the Dharma.
When a sick person eats garlic, they should guard against its foul odor;
they should select a secluded place for rest and act in private.
Once the medicinal garlic has been consumed for the sake of illness, they may wash their body to become clean.
Once all odors have been eliminated, one may then enter one's own room.
If one has consumed garlic, scallions, or leeks, for the sake of purifying the body, one should observe a period of seven, three, or two nights respectively; this is how it should be understood.
When wandering from house to house to beg for food, one must remain mindful as there are many potential distractions;
one should keep track of the alms-food received so as not to lose one's way.
When begging, one should hold the sounding staff (khakkhara) to let those who would give know of one’s presence.
Furthermore, one should not fear dogs or oxen, nor is it permitted to strike them.
When a bhikṣu eats cakes, fruits, or roots in a layperson’s house,
he should not chew with a loud noise, nor should he drink the juices at such times.
Unless there is a matter of great necessity, one should not eat while touching others;
when eating, one must be mindful and ensure that food does not splash onto those nearby.
If one obtains food during a time of scarcity, the donor will joyfully grant it according to their generosity.
One may also take much and distribute it among the bhikṣus.
If the elder (sthavira) accepts an invitation, he should give half of his food to others;
this is for the sake of relieving times of scarcity and sustaining all fellow practitioners of the holy life.
If one wishes for a long life, others should receive their due portion of food;
yet within the teaching of the Muni, even a single day is truly difficult to encounter.
If, within the seams of the alms-bowl, one sees that there is some remaining food left over;
One should remove [impurities] by picking them out with an object; washing three times, there is no fault in its use.
After eating, one should purify the mouth using tooth-sticks, earth, and so forth;
rinsing with pure water three times, though more may be done according to one's inclination.
When a bhikṣu has received food, if he suspects it has been touched by another person,
he should seek out one who is not yet fully ordained and receive it again from them to eat as he pleases.
If there is business requiring him to travel and no one is available to carry his provisions for the journey;
If one carries it oneself with the intention of exchanging it, there is no fault in eating it.
If there is no one to exchange it for, one should not eat for a day;
on subsequent days, one may eat "tiger-claw" [food], provided one does not exceed this limit.
For three days, practice the tiger-claw fist; thereafter, you may act as you please.
You should eat what you have prepared yourself, hoping thus to preserve your life.
If you seek the roots, you may dig the earth; if you desire the fruit, you should climb the tree.
A bhikṣu should take [food] himself; by removing hunger, he may prolong his life.
These are prohibitive precepts, temporarily permitted in times of difficulty;
if they were natural offenses (prakṛti-sāvadya), one should not commit them even at the cost of one's life.
When relatives or acquaintances come from afar, one should eat together in a secluded place;
for a śrāmaṇera, eating together is permitted in a location where there is cause for fear.
Having received the food, do not set down the vessel; hold it firmly with the left hand.
Place your hands together when you are ready to eat; at the time of eating, one must be attentive.
If the food is not covered, it will be left for crows to devour;
remove the portion near the mouth and eat the remainder as you please.
Regarding the *Saṃghāṭī* robe, or items such as ghee, oil, and granulated sugar,
if one should happen to touch them by mistake, they should not be discarded immediately.
Whether it be the property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters or the food of an individual, [one should handle it with care].
If one knows it is pure, it should be accepted; otherwise, it should not be.
If food is mixed with granulated sugar and the like, it should be eaten after washing it with water;
even if consumed outside the permitted time, there is no fault of impurity.
When sugar and parched grain flour are mixed together, one should add pure water;
the bhikṣu must filter it thoroughly, and it is permitted to drink even at improper times.
When a bhikṣu prepares sugar for his own use, he should maintain it with mindfulness.
It is permitted for these five types of persons to eat from one another when they know each other’s circumstances:
those who are ill, those who have fasted, those who have eaten very little, those who are suffering from heat and faintness, and those who are traveling on the road.
For these five, it is allowed; for others, it is entirely improper.
Supreme fruits are difficult to encounter, as are superior foods and the like;
though a bhikṣu has eaten his fill, he may still eat if the proper ritual is performed.
If a bhikṣu who begs for alms wanders from house to house and obtains food;
If someone invites you into their home, comply with their request so that merit may increase.
If there is leftover food remaining in the house, and the donor sends it back for you to take, you should eat it even if you have already finished your meal;
this is permitted during times of famine and is not a transgression.
The temple provides food at the three times of day to sacrifice to those deities who protect the monastery;
likewise, the yakṣas who dwell there—whether at their appointed time or not—should be fed as is appropriate.
To the children of Hārītī, the Buddha has commanded that many offerings of food be presented.
To protect the dwelling place and cause the teaching to shine brightly,
one should not eat a separate meal (*pṛthag-bhaktika*) except on account of illness or other such circumstances;
taking a small or large portion from within the Saṃgha, or having it sent there, involves no offense.
Even with as little as a single spoonful of salt, or a handful of grass leaves;
if these are sent to another location, one may thereby express conciliation.
If not all members are assembled, four persons constitute a "separate assembly" (pṛthag-saṃgha).
When traveling for the sake of illness, the matters are as previously explained.
If one travels by boat and reaches half a yojana,
or even returns before that point, there is no fault in consuming food.
If many donors each separately provide offerings to the bhikṣus,
according to the intention of those respective donors— this is called the distinction of time.
If various non-Buddhist śramaṇas should offer food to the Saṃgha, [the same applies].
One should accept [the food] out of compassion, because of their lack of faith.
Regarding eating in a separate group within a monastic community, if there is the perception or suspicion that there is another bhikṣu present, an offense is incurred;
however, if there are three [or more], there is no fault in eating.
There is a specific case belonging to the benefit [of others]: when eating at a time that differs from the assembly;
this accords with the donor's intention, so even if one eats, it does not constitute an offense.
Regarding the training rule on eating at improper times: from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light.
A bhikṣu should not eat; if he eats, sin will invade his person.
When one has an illness at an improper time, a physician may order him to eat;
this should be done in a secluded place so that laypeople do not see it and mock him.
Regarding the training rule on consuming food that has been touched: a bhikṣu who has touched food and so forth should not consume it;
since there is a distinction between before and after eating, "touched" is said to have two different meanings.
If one receives [the food] before a meal, it is a transgression to eat it after;
if one receives and holds it after a meal, it is improper once the night has passed.
If the hands are stained with various impurities, this is excepted when there are various unavoidable circumstances.
One should not touch the key, nor touch one's robes or bowl.
Regarding the training rule on receiving food: if food is not received, one who fears transgression shall not eat;
for if food is swallowed without being received, the offense is incurred, with the exception of water and tooth-sticks.
Leaves and tooth-sticks that have sap must still be accepted;
if they are raw seeds, they must be purified by fire.
When a bhikṣu goes begging for food, if there is a remainder that is not yet cooked:
One should cook the food oneself; having accepted it, one should eat it.

If fish, meat, fruit, or the like are obtained that have already changed color through prior cooking, or cow’s milk and so forth that have been boiled three times, there is no fault in cooking them again oneself.
When others come to provide food, if one has business and must leave,
one should regard it as being from the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and take the food oneself after observing the proper time.
When using medicinal oil for nasal irrigation, if it is swallowed, it must be accepted [as food].
If one is able not to swallow it, there is no harm in not consuming it.
If there are flies, ants, or the like upon food, they do not constitute contact if they merely touch it;
one should eat after removing them from the spot of contact. One should know that this applies to mice and birds as well.
If hand receives from hand, or if an object is offered while requesting with the hand;
or if the hand offers an object while requesting, or if an object is received from an object.
If one enters a country where [receiving] is loathed or despised, even placing it at a distance constitutes a valid reception.
There are further instances of receiving [food], namely from elephants, horses, and monkeys.
Regarding the training rule on seeking choice food: a bhikṣu who is not ill should not, for his own sake, beg for fresh butter, milk, curd, various meats, or fish.
If one begs for food because of illness, even if one eats it, there is no offense;
if one begs while not ill, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), and if one eats it, the fault is incurred.
When wandering for alms at the houses of laypeople, one should stand silently holding the bowl.
He asked, "What do you require?
Speak according to your wishes.
Regarding the training rule on using water containing insects: if one knows that water contains insects, it is entirely improper to use it.
It should be understood that there are two kinds: external and internal, namely bathing and drinking.
Regarding water with or without insects, these are all as previously explained;
one must filter it according to the rules, for this constitutes a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

The training rule concerning sitting down forcefully in a family’s dining quarters: A bhikṣu, when in a family’s dining quarters, should not sit in a secluded place, thereby causing others to feel disturbed; unless there is a reason involving danger or fear.
Regarding the training rule on standing at a house where food is being eaten: if a woman or a man, out of lustful desire, takes pleasure in mutual attachment;
this is called "eating. To stand in a secluded place [with such a person] also incurs an offense.
The training rule concerning giving food to male or female members of the Nirgrantha sect: A bhikṣu shall not give food with his own hand to those of the Nirgrantha sect;
he may break it apart and give it to them, provided it is for the purpose of causing them to abandon their wrong views.
If that vessel is on the ground, one should offer it with a compassionate heart;
out of a sense of pity for the living being, one must not display formal reverence.
Regarding the training rule on observing an army: if one observes an army engaged in battle, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to do so in any case.
If there is a necessary reason to go, this is permitted according to the circumstances.
Regarding the training rule on staying more than two nights among the military: when one must go for a necessary reason, one may stay for up to two nights;
if one stays longer than that, except in cases of hardship, it constitutes an offense.
Regarding the training rule on military forces in turmoil: when one sees an army in motion—whether it be elephants, horses, or multitudes; banners, kings, or military strength;
or a sovereign and his ministers—one incurs an offense immediately upon seeing them.
"Army" refers to being fully equipped; "military power" refers to being valiant and brave.
If one stands where the signal flags are planted, one is here called the King of Banners.
When requested by a sovereign or a great minister, there may be obstacles, difficulties, or fears.
Even if one remains for a long time, this does not constitute an offense.
Regarding the training rule on striking a bhikṣu: without a mind of anger, one strikes another bhikṣu;
thus violating one's original vow and failing to follow the Noble Teaching.
Even if one were to strike with a single finger, one would incur a transgression;
how much more so when using hands, feet, fists, staves, or wooden implements to inflict harm?
If one strikes with a broom, for however many stalks there may be [of hair], [so many are the offenses].
Touching the body of that bhikṣu likewise incurs such an amount of offense.
Know that the same applies to striking with beans and the like;
if they do not fall upon his body, the number of offenses corresponds to the count, all being *duṣkṛta*.
If one is struck by another, or perhaps due to the recitation of mantras, or if a bhikṣu strikes with an object—none of these constitute an offense.
Regarding the training rule on threatening a bhikṣu with the hand: if, toward a bhikṣu, one makes a threatening gesture with the hand;
Even if one incurs a *pāyattika* offense, it is treated as explained under the rule on striking.
Regarding the training rule on concealing another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*): knowing that another has committed a grave offense, one is fundamentally not permitted to conceal it;
however, if there is fear for one's safety, concealing it even then constitutes no offense.
From the *pārājika* offenses down to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, as well as the grave preparatory acts (*prayoga*), one incurs a fault by concealing them until dawn.
Regarding the training rule on not refusing food when visiting a layperson’s home: without harboring a mind of resentment, one intentionally causes another to be deprived of food.
That person shall have no illness, yet they will certainly incur the mark of transgression.
Regarding the training rule on touching fire: unless it is an occasion for an exception, lighting a fire is not permitted;
likewise, extinguishing or touching a fire constitutes a fault, except when there is an emergency.
Fur, skin, claws, mucus, and saliva— If these are thrown into a fire to be burned, Or if one does not mindfully guard hot coals, Touching them all incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the training rule on obstructing after having given consent: When the Saṃgha has business to attend to, A bhikṣu first gives his consent; [if he later obstructs it...]
Later, this was prohibited; the offense of falling into sin will surely invade one's person.

Regarding the training rule on staying overnight for more than two nights in the same room as one who has not yet received full ordination: if one stays in the same room with a person who has not yet attained full ordination, this is permitted only for two nights;
on the third night, one falls into the offense.
It is said that there are four kinds of dwellings:
(1) those with a double roof and many partitions; (2) those with a triple roof and many partitions; (3) those with a quadruple roof and many partitions;
and (4) those with a quadruple roof and many partitions.
When a bhikṣu sleeps within these four types of dwellings, he incurs offenses according to their gravity.
Regarding these four kinds of houses, until the appearance of the three signs of dawn,
those who guard the precepts should understand the varying degrees of offense therein.
There are three kinds of signs of dawn: namely, blue, yellow, and red;
as soon as the blue light appears, one incurs the root offense.
If one is on a high terrace and the sound of speech cannot be clearly understood;
Furthermore, it is not an offense to sleep together in other houses;
however, two persons should not lie down on the same bed.
It is permitted as a temporary concession to share a mattress, provided that clothing or similar items are placed between them.
One may lie down in a room lit by a lamp; this is permitted for those who are ill and for those attending to the sick, but it is not allowed for others.
To sleep during the day when not ill is forbidden for those who are lazy and indolent.
If one diligently practices meditation and recitation, one may lie down for a short while as one pleases.
When paying homage to the Venerable One in the dark, one should not let the head touch the ground;
rather, with a heart of reverent devotion, one should utter the words "vandana."
When traveling together with a śrāmaṇera, one should share the same bedding but remain vigilant;
if one is too weary to do so, one may sleep while remaining in a seated posture as the situation permits.
At all times, one must diligently protect the śrāmaṇera.
Just as the prince of the wheel-turning monarch, so is this the sprout of the Buddha-tree.
Not abandoning evil views despite being exhorted against them—this training rule for bhikṣus who engage in improper conduct and claim that sensual desire is not an obstructive dharma;
this can indeed act as an obstacle, arising from delusion and a lack of knowledge.
Even up to three admonitions, if one does not relinquish that view;
this is the ultimate of transgressions, and one should swiftly expel them.
Regarding the training rule on those who persist in their refusal (*pratikṣepaṇīya*): one should know that such a person of evil views has not yet conformed to the Dharma.
And those who do not abandon evil views—none of these should be lived with.
One should not engage in recitation or study with them, nor should one act as their friend;
if one partakes of the Dharma-food together with them, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
To sever such evil views, whether it be for one's kin or for the sick, reciting [the scriptures] is permitted at will, but their use is not allowed.
Regarding the training rule on receiving those with evil views who seek the status of a śrāmaṇera: if one is not yet fully ordained, yet intends to go to a place where full ordination is sought;
The ignorant preach the dharma of desire, which does not obstruct the path;

such persons should be expelled. A bhikṣu who stays away from evil factions and takes the welfare of beings as his heart's aim will incur a downfall even by merely lodging with such a person of no wisdom.
The Training Rule on Wearing Garments of Altered Color: When a bhikṣu obtains a new garment, he must alter its color.
"New garment" refers to one that is white. There are three ways to dye it for alteration:
"blue" refers to a dull blue; "mud-colored" refers to red ochre.
Bark, flowers, leaves, and the like, dyed, are called the *kāṣāya*.
Regarding the training rule on handling jewels:
it would be better to touch an angry snake whose fierce venom is difficult to treat; [but not to handle jewels].
He does not touch precious gems, nor those adorned with jewels;
pearls and mani-jewels, coral ornaments, swords, spears,
and various weapons, as well as drums and the like— he touches none of these.
Precious objects such as pearls and the like—by touching them or piercing them, one incurs a downfall;
if one touches them but does not pierce them, this constitutes a transgression of the Dharma.
This applies to drums, musical instruments, strings, and flutes, as well as the category of swords, staves, bows, and arrows.
Whether [the weapon] is completed or not yet completed, touching it in either case incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one touches a bow made of hair or sinew, one likewise incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*;
how much more so for swords, spears, and the like—would not the transgression of holding them be severe?
If a statue or the like contains relics, touching it incurs the root offense;
if it contains no bodily bones, touching it constitutes a minor transgression (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding such things as dancing, singing, and chanting, neither watching nor listening is permitted.
Engaging in conversation and wrestling is not a condition for tranquility;
performing songs and dances for one's own pleasure or wandering about at a stūpa—
by failing to guard the sense doors, every single step incurs transgression.
Because of such a distracted mind, one must not crave sounds or forms;
seeking only liberation from the three realms of existence, one ultimately hopes to proceed toward Nirvana.
Seeing discarded wealth within the monastery—namely gold, silver, and the like—
One should cover it with grass and the like, guarding it for eight days.
If an owner comes seeking it, one should give it back provided the identifying marks match;
if there is no owner, it should be stored in the monastery treasury, kept safely so that it does not diminish.
If the latter owner comes to demand it back, one should transform that person of little wisdom;
whether by paying half the price or the full amount, if they ask for more, one must not grant it.
Regarding the training rule on bathing at improper times: unless it is one of the permitted exceptions, one should not bathe within the interval of a half-month.
When one is ill, traveling on a journey, or engaged in work, as well as during times of wind and rain—
if not washing leads to discomfort, these instances of illness shall be granted an exception;
for traveling and performing tasks, these cases are all as previously explained.
When a sudden gust stirs the hem of one’s robe, this is called the time of wind;
when raindrops moisten the body, this is what should be recognized as rain;
if wind and rain are mingled together, this is called their conjunction.
For two and a half months, this period is known as the "Hot Season.
Beginning from the time one removes one's robes until the water has not yet reached the navel, bathing incurs a light offense;
once the water passes the navel, it incurs a *pārājika* (defeat).
Crossing a river is not an offense, nor is it when one faints and water is poured over the body;
or if one may cross a pond or embankment, there is no offense in all such cases of distress.
When a bhikṣu walks within the water, or when riding in a boat;
If one is in the great ocean, there is no offense in discharging excrement or urine.
If there are women washing, or the king and his military forces,
or if there are cruel and wicked people present, one should avoid them from afar and not bathe there.
One should not play in the water, swimming or submerging;
nor should one splash or throw water at others, or make sounds by splashing the water.
This applies unless one is learning to swim, or requires medical treatment.
In a secluded place, even if one is floating, one must not obstruct [the flow].

Regarding the training rule on killing animals: if a bhikṣu kills an animal, whether acting himself or sending another, he shall encounter a place of extreme suffering, where the fires of the evil realms burn.
Therefore, regarding the training rule on causing distress to a bhikṣu among fellow practitioners of the holy life, one must not cause them to feel regret;
if one acts with the intent to cause distress, one commits an offense, whereas in cases other than this, it is permitted without fault.
If you are not yet twenty years of age, you do not accomplish full ordination;
your preceptor has broken the precepts and the assembly is incomplete.
If one speaks with a mind of wrongdoing, one incurs an offense at that very moment.
If one speaks of actual facts, this is established as being without fault.
Regarding the training rule on poking others with a finger: although it may be just a single finger, poking someone brings about an offense;
yet, if there is no intent to mock, pointing out a mole is permitted and is not a transgression.

The Training Rule on Sporting in Water: When a bhikṣu sports in water, crossing back and forth between this shore and the other, there are both permissions and prohibitions regarding this matter, all of which have been explained as previously stated.
The training rule on sleeping in the same room as a woman: One should not share a room with a woman unless there is a partition;
if the door is securely locked, this constitutes no offense.
Regarding the words of a woman, whether good or evil, one must understand both the names and their meanings;
this gives rise to grave offenses, while other cases incur minor transgressions.
As for "completely concealing" and "completely obstructing," the characteristics of the dwelling are as previously explained.
One must wait until the body is fully reclined; this is what is meant by "sleeping," which you should know.
If one falls into a deep slumber, the wind of *pāyattika* will blow through the iron beds amidst the fires within the hells.
If there is a woman in a multi-storied pavilion, one should remove the ladder;
or else, one may send a bhikṣu to keep watch, and even if one lies down, it constitutes no offense.
If one lies down during the daytime, it is the same as the matters mentioned above.
One must also fasten the lower garment; otherwise, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the training rule on terrifying bhikṣus: out of respect for the Buddha’s teaching and to avoid distressing sentient beings, whether acting oneself or employing another, one should not cause terror.
Some manifest in the forms of various ghosts, or like the images of rākṣasas and the like;
others use sound, breath, or touch to terrify those whose bodies are invaded by sin.
There are also pleasing lords of men, devas, gandharvas, brahmins, and so forth.
To say, "I have come to harm you," incurs the fault of *duṣkṛta*.
If one wishes for another to gain benefit, even if one manifests extreme suffering to terrify them and speaks of the three evil realms, there is no harm despite the fear it may cause.
The Training Rule on Storing Another’s Robes and Alms Bowl: One should not store another’s robes, bowl, or other belongings out of mere playfulness or for the sake of laughter;
if one does so, it is a transgression that brings harm upon oneself. However, there is no fault if it is done for the benefit of the person.
The training rule concerning wearing a robe sent by another without inquiring of the owner: if one first gives a robe to a bhikṣu and uses it without informing him, one incurs an offense;
however, if the person is of like mind, there is no fault in using it.

The training rule concerning slandering a pure bhikṣu with a formal offense of the Saṃgha: If one slanders another pure person with a formal offense of the Saṃgha, this constitutes the transgression of "being burned and boiled"; all other [instances] incur an *dukkaṭa*.
The training rule on traveling with a woman on the same road: If there is no male companion, traveling the road together with a woman constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
