the distance in *krośas* is as explained in the regular [rules].
Upon reaching each village, one immediately incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if the village has not yet been reached, it should be known that an *dukkaṭa* offense occurs.
If on a dangerous path, a woman acts as a guide, [one incurs an offense].
Or if one acts as a protector or ally, none of these involve any fault.
Regarding the training rule on traveling with bandits: if one travels together with bandits, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
however, the circumstances under which there is no offense have already been explained previously.
A merchant who evades taxes on the road is still called a thief;
how much more so one who plunders villages and commits highway robbery?
Regarding the training rule for conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon those under age: if a person is less than twenty years of age, it is not appropriate to grant them full ordination.
Because of hunger, thirst, and the like, they are unable to endure [the discipline].
If one is actually not yet of full age, yet later speaks with the intention that they are;
this is not called "full ordination," and all such bhikṣus incur an offense.
If one has a doubtful mind, yet perceives oneself as not having reached the age [of twenty],
and says "I have reached the age," there is an offense at the time of receiving [the precepts].
If one perceives oneself as having reached the age and says, "My years are sufficient";
Or it may be spoken through confusion; in all such cases, there is no offense.
Full ordination is not a single matter, as its explanations follow many different approaches.
One who guards the precepts should maintain mindfulness and, in principle, inquire with careful scrutiny.

Regarding the training rule on destroying uncultivated ground: when one intends to work upon the earth, whether digging it oneself or instructing others to do so, damaging moist soil incurs the root offense, while damaging the outer crust incurs a minor transgression.
It is said that there are two kinds of ground: that which is productive and that which is not.
If it is moistened by rain and water, it is called productive ground after three months;
if it is not moistened by rain, it must remain so for six months.
This refers to ground that has already been tilled and ruined; for other lands, the timing is not considered.
One who causes [a plant] to grow incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*); for others, one incurs a minor transgression (*duskṛta*).
Regarding gravel, sand, soil, and mud, one must recognize the varying degrees of gravity in both cases.
If one drives a stake into the ground, one incurs a root offense;
to pull out the stake or disturb the mud, these all incur an *dukkaṭa*.
To cause a wall to collapse or a riverbank to crumble, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one causes damage or breaks [the ground], all such acts constitute a transgression of the Dharma.

If one acts with the intention of wandering about—such as by collapsing cliffs or stirring up mud—one incurs the offense of damaging the earth for every count; if there is no damage, there is no fault.
If one cultivates a garden or orchard for the sake of the community, one may command others to dig the earth using pure speech;
it is permitted provided there are no insects, but it is improper if any living beings are present.
Regarding the training rule on seeking food beyond the four-month period: if there is an invitation for four months, a bhikṣu should accept it.
Excluding the "extreme invitation," the "repeated invitation," the "constant invitation," and the "individual invitation.
What is called the "constant invitation" refers to the regular invitation for meals;
therein, the "individual invitation" should be understood as giving to a specific person.
"An 'extreme invitation' refers to one made with great earnestness; a 'repeated invitation' refers to eating on successive days.
Apart from food received through such invitations, all other food incurs an offense.
If one is invited to receive superior and exquisite food, yet the bhikṣu requests coarse food instead,"
If one asks for food and receives only a small offense, yet eats it, there is no fault.
If invited to eat coarse and inferior food, but then begs for something superior and exquisite;
if one asks for it, one incurs a minor transgression, but at the time of eating, the offense is grave.
To ask for meat when given milk, or to seek butter when offered curd;
to beg for light food when it is fundamentally a transgression—these do not apply to those who are ill.
Whether through faith or wealth, if the donor possesses a generous intention;
To cause their merit to increase, they may endure it for a long time without fault.

Regarding the training rule on obstructing the transmission of teachings: you, within this training rule, having been told to be sent away for study, spoke contemptuously before the bhikṣus, calling them "fools" and "younglings."
This will cause one to fall upon the sword of transgression, Self-slaying the body of ignorance;
Falling into the evil realms, One undergoes suffering, constantly burned and boiled.
"Stupidity" refers to wandering thoughts and conjectures; "Ignorance" refers to failing to understand the sūtras.
If one speaks words that are unclear and unwholesome, failing to understand the Sūtras and Vinaya,
uttering such foolish speech— whether speaking word by word or as a whole—
if the person before hears and understands it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
One who asks a person learned in the Tripiṭaka, seeking understanding, commits no offense;
the wise say such speech should be employed like a lamp in a dark place.
If that person speaks falsely, one should cross-examine them.
Even if one says, "I am foolish," etc., the truth of the Way remains unimpaired.

Regarding the training rule on silently listening to criticism while not enduring it: if one seeks out faults and vulnerabilities in others, or silently goes to eavesdrop, one incurs an offense at the very moment of remaining there.
If one speaks in a private room, one should listen without making a sound;
to understand the meaning incurs the full offense, whereas merely hearing the sound constitutes a minor transgression.
If one is within a gabled pavilion, whether standing still or walking about;
To listen with an evil mind constitutes an offense; for one with a virtuous mind, there is no transgression.

Regarding the training rule on departing in silence when not granted permission: if one speaks words that are in accordance with the Dharma, or performs the *jñapti* (single motion) and so forth, yet does not inform those nearby and departs in silence, [it is an offense].
Do not perform the ritual for a separate assembly; when departing, you may speak to others.
Because you have not made an entrustment, you enter alone into the boundless ocean.
One who does not respectfully abide among the community or with individuals shall not perform acts of reverence.
If one treats the assembly with pride, one incurs the fundamental offense; if one treats an individual so, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
The same offense applies for violating the instructions of those who guard the monastery for the assembly, as well as for an elder within the assembly, or one’s own venerable teacher.
If another speaks with opposition and their heart is unwilling to comply, one should skillfully provide instruction;
in this case, it is permitted and without fault. Regarding the training rule on drinking alcohol:
if any kind of liquor causes intoxication, not even a drop the size of a blade of *kuśa* grass should be taken into the mouth.
One should neither drink it nor give it to others; this is due to the fault of negligence.
If a bhikṣu has an ailment in the mouth, a physician may instruct him to hold it in, and there is no offense;
even if his life were to end immediately, he must not swallow it.
Various substances such as fermenting agents, when brewed together, achieve their effect;
that which is universally accepted by the multitude is called "great wine.
If it is accomplished using the juices of bark, fruit, or flowers, [it is likewise so].
This is called "mixed liquor," and all of these can intoxicate people.
Whether made from sugar, honey, grapes, or other ingredients,
they are all included herein because they cause one to become dazed and drunk.
Just as with the substance of wine, if it has not yet formed or is still subject to decomposition,
there is no fault in drinking it, for it is not a cause of intoxication.
This applies to all types of fermented gruel and the liquid from curdled milk as well.
If water is clear and filtered, there is no fault in drinking it even outside of the proper time.
When various wines have turned into vinegar, drinking them constitutes no offense;
one should know that vinegar made from fermented grain-liquor, even if stored for a long time, is likewise vinegar.
Millet beer and the like are not prohibited; one should know that two types of liquor are spoken of:
those that have changed or are yet unformed, which clarify that they lack the nature of intoxication.
Liquor possesses color, aroma, and flavor; it can intoxicate and incurs a grave offense.
If it cannot intoxicate a person, it incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses;
likewise for two or one [measures], drinking at such times all constitutes an offense.
Depending on whether one, two, or three [measures] are incurred, if it does not intoxicate, it is not the fundamental offense.
If skins, flowers, fruits, and the like, which can serve as conditions for intoxication and affliction, are mixed with yeast and such, this likewise incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the training rule on entering a village at an improper time without informing a bhikṣu: if there is a bhikṣu present at an improper time, one enters the village without having informed him.
If there is a valid reason, one commits no fault; if there is no such matter, one incurs transgression.
From the time after midday until the first appearance of light at dawn—this is what is called "the improper time," so the Great Master has taught.
If a bhikṣu enters [a house] at an improper time, he incurs an offense if he harbors doubt;
if he acts at a proper time while perceiving it as improper, or if he harbors doubt, he incurs a minor transgression.
Regarding the training rule on visiting other households before or after a meal: when a bhikṣu is the primary guest invited by a layperson, he may go to that household for a meal.
If this person has not granted permission, one should turn away and go to another house. If,
regarding those who have accepted an invitation, one says,
"Eat as you please," or if the host allows one to leave, it is no fault to go elsewhere.

Regarding the training rule on entering the royal palace: if one reaches the king’s gate, the palace gate, or the vicinity of such gates before the appearance of the dawn light, one incurs the full offense.
The city gate, the royal gate, and the threshold of the palace gate—
the area not far from these gates is called the "sphere of influence" (sīmā).
If one arrives at the city gate before dawn, yet still maintains the perception that it is not yet dawn;
If one crosses the threshold of the door, one immediately incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If it is done with another intention or out of doubt, one likewise incurs *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the phrase "the treasure has not yet been hidden," this refers to that which has not yet been lifted up and set aside.

Regarding the training rule on not listening attentively and claiming ignorance: Although I have already listened extensively to the Pratimokṣa Sūtra over the past fortnights, to say "I only now understand" implies that all the categories of the precepts are contained herein.
This Dharma was taught by the World-Honored One who attained self-awakening within the sūtras:
first one must cause [the offender] to feel remorse and weariness, and only then should one send them forth to confess their transgression.
Regarding the training rule on making needle cases from bone, ivory, or horn: needle cases made of horn, ivory, or bone are not permitted for use.
This person shall then enter [the assembly], yet the transgression of violating the teachings remains within the needle-case.
The needle-case must be broken; that offense must be confessed.
Abandoning these conditions of arrogance and negligence—if one retains them, repentance will not be achieved.
There are four kinds of syringes: made of brass, red copper, or iron;
the lancet should be made of iron, and it should be known that there are three sizes:
the large is eight finger-widths long, the small is six, and the rest are intermediate.
It should be shaped like a crow's beak, or curved like a chicken feather.
Even if a bhikṣu is in urgent need while traveling to another village or similar place,
he must carry at least one needle for the purpose of sewing his robes.

The Training Rule on Making Beds Exceeding the Proper Measure: When a bhikṣu makes various beds and seats for the sake of the Saṃgha, the height should be eight finger-breadths of the Sugata; beyond this, one should not make them.
The Sugata’s [fingers] measure eight finger-widths; this is equivalent to one cubit for an average person.
Those who are tall should have [the bedding] trimmed accordingly; the confession of the offense follows the standard procedure.
Regarding the training rule on bed-covers stuffed with grass, wood, or cotton: one must not store various types of cotton within the beds and bedding belonging to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, if you wish to vex another person, the arrow of sin will come to strike you.
Whether it be mats of *pūtīka* grass or reeds, cotton, wool, or the like—all these must first be removed;
only then should the remaining offenses be confessed.
What is meant by "storing"?
It refers to spreading [the cloth] upon a bed, causing it to stick to the robes of a bhikṣu, thereby displeasing others.
Regarding the training rule on making the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) of excessive size: if one makes a *niṣīdana*, its length should be three spans of the Great Awakened One’s hands.
It may be as wide as one hand and a half; beyond this, one should not make it.
If it is too long, it should be cut short, and the offense must be confessed.
One should then ask: "Has it been removed?"
Only then can one's transgressions be expiated.
If making a wound-covering cloth, it should be four spans long according to the Buddha’s span and two spans wide;
exceeding these dimensions will result in the incurrence of a fault.
If one makes a rain-cloak, it should be six spans long according to the Buddha’s span and two and a half spans wide; otherwise, it should not be made.

Regarding the training rule on making robes equal in size to the Tathāgata’s: one must not make a robe that exceeds the prescribed measurements. The Tathāgata’s robe is not permitted to be made in a different measure.
Ten spans in length and six in width—this is called the measurement of a Buddha’s robe.
Born into a place of bitter suffering, where there has never been even the slightest joy;
constantly scorched and boiled by fire—this is the etymological explanation.
If those who violate the precepts fall into the three evil realms, and the fool does not repent for their transgressions, by this means the meaning of "falling" is established.

Part Four: The Four Rules for Individual Confession (Pratideśanīya-dharma). Regarding the training rule on receiving food from a nun who is not a relative, the offenses involving falling (pārājika) have already been explained; now the four rules for individual confession are set forth.
To briefly state its specific characteristic, one should understand it in full detail:
if a bhikṣu who is not related by kin receives food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī while in a village at a place for alms-gathering, he incurs the offense of *pāyantika*.
The Training Rule Concerning Receiving Food Directed by a Nun: If, while a bhikṣu is eating in a layperson’s house, a nun comes and directs him, he may give her such things as ghee and curd.
The entire assembly must respond:
"Sisters, do not speak such words";
if even one person does not stop her, the whole assembly incurs an offense.
In the three dwellings—inner, middle, and outer—the bhikṣus eat at these three locations.
If the senior monk makes a prohibitive statement, it extends even to the lowest-ranking monk:
"For now, do not speak; wait for a moment until the meal is finished."
One may inquire among those inside and outside: "Is there anyone preventing the *niṣadyā*?
If one eats without asking, one incurs the original offense within the household;
if there was no one to prevent it at all, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* outside.
From the very beginning among the assembly, all have committed offenses requiring individual confession;
these distinct transgressions differ from the previous *pāyattika* rules.
If one is within a nunnery, there is no fault whatsoever in giving or receiving.
One should give away one's own wealth, doing so with profound faith.

Regarding the training rule on receiving food from a family under discipline: if it is a family under discipline and one knows that the assembly has performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), a bhikṣu, even if oppressed by hunger and thirst, should not eat if he has been invited [to do so].
Flowers, fruits, leaves, and such items—even if accepted, they cause no harm;
accepting a seat and reciting the sūtras are both permitted and not a transgression.
If one eats at another’s house, it is permissible to give cakes to the children of a family in training.
Break it apart and then let him eat; do not allow him to remain in vain expectation.

Regarding the training rule on receiving food outside the dwelling of an araṇya: if one is in an araṇya, where there is much fear and terror, a bhikṣu should not go outside the monastery to receive his meal.
If there is no one to oversee the forest, and a bhikṣu goes out to receive food and eats it elsewhere within the monastery, he incurs the offense in every case.
Once the bhikṣu has committed the offense, he should return to the monastery.
One should reply to those people, saying:
"I am speaking of base and lowly matters.

Section Five: The Rules of Training (Madhyama), Part One. The Fourfold Rules for Individual Confession within the Section on the Rules of Training; as the nature of the offenses has already been set forth.
The remaining rules for the *śikṣamāṇās* shall now be explained in sequence:
One should wear the lower robe neatly and evenly, neither too high nor too low;
it should not resemble an elephant’s trunk or a snake’s hood, nor should it be made like a *tāla* leaf.
Nor should one form it into a bean-shaped ball; thus should one train.
When putting on the saṃghāṭī robe, one should know how to wear it properly and neatly:
neither too high nor too low, wearing it well and covering the body correctly.
One should speak with few words and not look far into the distance;
one should gaze only at a distance of six feet, no more than a fathom.
This is the manner for entering a layperson’s home; thus one should train.
In lay households, one does not cover the head, nor does one partially tuck up the robe,
nor double-tuck it up; one does not cross the hands over the waist or rest them on the shoulders,
nor walk while squatting, nor point with the toes as one departs.
One should not leap, nor stamp the feet; one should not walk with the body acting as a pillar, nor walk with the body swaying.
One should not go with arms flailing, nor enter with the head shaking, nor push with the hands or shoulders.
One must not sit down without permission; when sitting, one must observe carefully.
If one lets the body fall heavily, this can give rise to great faults.
One should not cross the feet or overlap the ankles, nor should one curl the legs too tightly.
One must not stretch out one's legs, nor expose one's body.
The following clarifies respectful eating: one should not fill the bowl to the brim;
one should leave space for a finger’s breadth, and eat the rice and soup in proper sequence.
Before the food has been served, one must not extend the bowl in advance;
the bowl should not rest upon the food, but one may eat with a respectful mind.
The morsels should be neither too small nor too large, and one must not open the mouth in anticipation.
If one has food in the mouth, one should not speak at once;
one should not cover the soup with rice, nor hide the rice with vegetables;
to harbor further expectations in this way only increases the mind of greed.
One should not suck, nor slurp, nor smack the lips; one should not hiss or blow upon the food.
One should not place rice between the lips, nor should one disparage the meal.
One should not bite with puffed cheeks, nor should one protrude or flick the tongue.
One should not eat from a stūpa; nor should one eat after breaking it apart.
One should not lick the hands or lick the bowl, nor shake the bowl or shake the hands.
One should maintain the perception of the bowl as a vessel for food, and with mindfulness focused, one may eat.
One should not, out of a disrespectful mind, look at the bowl of another sitting nearby;
with defiled hands, one should not grasp a vessel, nor should one sprinkle water on others.
One must not discard foul or filthy water within a layperson's house.
One should not leave food remnants in the bowl; one should not set it down without a replacement base.
One should not wash the bowl while standing, nor place it where it might fall and break.
One should not scoop water against the current; these are the rules for protecting the bowl that should be known.
Next, the matters of preaching the Dharma are clarified: if one stands while the other sits;
or if one sits while the other lies down—provided there is no illness—these are all improper.
Likewise, it is improper for one to be in a lower position while the other is in a higher position, or for oneself to remain behind while another is in front.
If he says "it is not the Way" when it is the Way, his head is covered just as before.
If he rides on elephants, horses, or carriages, or wears shoes and the like, or wears crowns and hats tied upon his head,
or adorns himself with flower garlands— [in all these cases, his head is likewise covered].
Carrying a parasol, bearing a sword, or wearing armor—these are all modes of arrogance;
to preach the Dharma while removing one’s belt or while ill is to incur an offense.
One should not stand while defecating or urinating, nor upon green grass.
One or two finger-breadths of nasal mucus or saliva, Removing [mucus] except when ill, both incur transgression.
Do not climb trees taller than a person, Except when there is an emergency;
These *śikṣamāṇā* rules Are all that one should train in.

2. The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes (Middle Section). Having already briefly stated the general outline of the rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*), I shall now explain in their proper sequence those [rules] associated with the seven methods for settling disputes.
Regarding what are called criticisms and the like, there are methods for their removal according to the Dharma;
these seven types of skillful means differ according to the distinctions among persons.
One should appoint impartial and upright individuals who have restrained their body and speech.
Within the assembly, one should be appointed; resolving the dispute in accordance with reason.
One who is free from desire, hatred, and delusion, and likewise free from fear, who can move that which cannot be moved—such a person should be appointed to eliminate the dispute.
If a dispute regarding criticism should arise, it may be settled through the presence [of the parties];
furthermore, by means of the presence of the Dharma, one should rely upon the Teacher’s instruction.
Because it can be settled through such presence, it is called "presence" (sammukha).
For those of limited wisdom and mindfulness, I shall briefly set forth one corner [of this matter].
If nine or ten people are dispatched, it is a dispatch by a large assembly;
if five or more than five are dispatched, it is called a "double dispatch."
Whenever one appoints a person to resolve a dispute, they must be upright and clear regarding the three baskets;
the senior monk (sthavira) must not be partial to any side, for he is the one capable of extinguishing the contention.
If he lacks these five virtues, even if already appointed, he should be withdrawn.
One endowed with virtue should be appointed to act as the distributor of voting sticks (*śalākā*).
He shall prepare two kinds of sticks: those representing the Dharma and those representing non-Dharma.
The stick for the Dharma should be straight, fragrant, smooth, and pleasing to the mind.
The illegal voting tally-stick must be curved, foul-smelling, rough, and unpleasant;
it should be cast while covered by the left hand. The legal voting tally-stick should be displayed openly.
The Saṃgha should assemble in its entirety, and the sticks should be distributed in order, beginning from the first.
First present the voting-slips for the Dharma; give them with three earnest words.
If those who take up the slips for the Dharma are more numerous than those for what is not Dharma, this is called the extinction of the Dharma; know that through this, disputes shall cease.
When a bhikṣu breaks [the settlement] at that time, he incurs the offense of a pāyattika;
if the illegal voting sticks are more numerous than these, it is called "settling a dispute through illegality.
Although the dispute is settled through illegality, the one who breaks [the settlement] incurs a minor transgression.
This is indeed for many people; it is the Vinaya that extinguishes disputes.
Having already explained the dispute of censure (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), two methods should be applied to eliminate it;
the detailed account of its causes is fully set forth as in the extensive text.
Next, the non-contention regarding speech is explained as being settled by three methods:
namely, when one uses an objectionable matter to interrogate another person who is pure;
that is to say, the matter is before one's eyes, or it concerns recollection, or it concerns being free from delusion.
The first case has been explained above; the remaining two shall now be analyzed.
One should know that mindfulness is a form of discipline, like the bhikṣuṇī Suvarṣā;
it was because of her slandering the Venerable Sthūlanandika that the Great Teacher established this precept.
One should apply the disciplinary procedure of *smṛtivinaya* (reinstatement through recollection) to Śrīgupta;
having him stand before the elder monks, he should be made to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"Because he falsely accuses me, I request that the Saṃgha grant me the *smṛtivinaya*. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, listen to my plea.
Having made this request three times, they should instruct a single bhikṣu:
For that person, one who upholds the Dharma performs the *smṛti-karman* (act of restoration of mindfulness).
Next, one performs the *amūḍha-dharma* (the rite for one no longer insane), as in the case of the Bhikṣu Pāpa;
because he was previously deranged, he now upholds the matter of being no longer insane.
He approached the elder and said: "In the past, I was afflicted by madness;
I committed what was wrong without being aware of it.
He then questioned him repeatedly, saying, "I have committed evil deeds."
I now beg for non-delusion; the Vinaya should be granted to me.
Regarding the disputes arising from offenses, they can be resolved through four methods:
confession (*pratijñā*), presence (*sammukha*), the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*), and seeking the true nature of the matter (*yadbhūyaḥ*).
Once a transgression has been committed, whether it be questioned or not questioned,
one should stand before the bhikṣus with palms joined to eliminate that offense,
saying: "Venerable sir, please attend to me!"
"I have now committed this offense.
When asked, "Do you recognize the offense?",
he replied, "I now recognize it."
"Will you not commit [such an offense] hereafter?
He replied, "I shall not commit it.
He said, "Avusika," and he answered, "Sādhu."
When one commits a defeat (*pārājika*) or other such offenses, confessing them before the assembly—
this is what is meant by "speaking for oneself," which can cause disputes to be extinguished.
As in the case of the bhikṣu Kāla, who was caught in the words of another;
Because of a robe, he was subjected to censure; proceeding toward the city of Śākya, he was able to settle the dispute in their presence.
This is called the "Procedure in Presence" (*sammukhavinaya*);
this too is "in presence," and the method is stated once more.
Now I shall explain the method of "covering with grass" for those who engage in mutual strife and contention:
the Elder should approach them and instruct them according to the correct principle, saying:
"The Dharma is difficult to encounter; why do you form two factions?"
To engage in strife and contention for no reason, and to treat the words of the Great Master with contempt—
by speaking of such deeds, both you and I have committed an offense.
Since this constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat) offense, you should pray that it may be cleared away.
When these words are spoken, if they do not oppose them, this is called abiding in one’s original nature; those in such a company should likewise be so.
When the minds of others are stilled and they do not utter words of contradiction, [the assembly is harmonious].
Therefore, this dispute can be eliminated; it is called "extinguishing by covering with grass.
One confesses having committed this offense, yet before the assembly one says there is none;
just as the Bhikṣu Hastaka claimed something exists when it does not.
Having performed the formal act of seeking out the nature of the offense, the Bhikṣu causes that minister to [confess];
the Great Sage’s instruction was given with intimate words, precisely because he possesses a compassionate nature.
He, too, before the Elder, should likewise beg for it from the assembly.
The great assembly should act accordingly here; the ritual procedure is the same as before.
To extinguish a dispute arising from formal acts, the entire community must assemble.
If there is no refusal or opposition, it should be known that this dispute has been settled.
The above two fascicles clarify the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Next, the following fascicle clarifies matters such as the *Bhikṣuṇī-kaṭhina*.
This concludes the middle fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kārikā*.

Among the seventeen *vatsadūta* [narratives], the essential matters are recounted (Part II). This explains the essential matters recounted among the seventeen *vatsadūta*, wherein *vatsadūta* refers to these events.
If one is a caṇḍāla, a public crier, a tavern keeper, a prostitute,
or a queen’s attendant— these five are not proper spheres of activity.
To study and recite the various scriptures of non-Buddhists, regarding them as superior;
For those who have frequently committed offenses, whatever they eat becomes poison.
One should constantly recite the Buddha’s teachings; these are the excellent physicians for the evil realms.
It is permitted to read non-Buddhist texts, however, only for the purpose of knowing their faults.
The speech of the All-Knowing One is exquisite and rich in parables;
how could it compare to the treatises of the non-Buddhists, which are irrational, coarse, and shallow?
The accumulation of various utensils and their elaborate ornamentation are all forbidden.
If one paints the legs of a seated bed, these are all the customs of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
If a bhikṣu is aged or ill, he may use a palanquin as permitted;
staffs, carrying-nets, and leather garments—all these are within the scope of what is allowed.
At the request of Śakra, he then opened the bathhouse;
those diligent in meditation and recitation were all permitted to partake of a light meal.
He did not pour [water] over his eyes or mouth, nor did he perfume his robes with incense.
One should not paint parasols or leather shoes, nor should one polish the nails until they are bright and clean.
There are two kinds of parasols: those made of leaves and those made of reeds or bamboo;
when entering a village, one should not carry them held upright.
If one makes a handle for a parasol, it should be made of the same material as the canopy;
when yawning with the mouth open, one should cover it with the hand and robe.
When there is a reason to smile, one must not expose the gums and teeth.
Praising the virtues of the Great Master and preaching the Dharma are not transgressions;
yet one must not make a long-drawn sound when proclaiming the scriptures of the Muni.
One should recite according to the established rules, and do not let them be contradicted in any place.
If one studies the sounds of praising virtues, it should be done in a secluded place;
for the purpose of proclaiming the True Dharma, one should not give rise to defiled thoughts.
Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and the other five assemblies are permitted to observe the summer retreat.
When the summer retreat has concluded, the fivefold assembly gathers for the *pravāraṇā*.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must study all the precepts;
śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs should know that they receive the ten precepts.
Not alone on a journey, nor alone crossing water;
not intentionally touching a man, nor sleeping with a man;
not acting as a matchmaker for marriage, nor concealing another's faults.
These are known as the six rules, which a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā) should know:
she should not handle gold or silver; she should not remove the hair from her private parts;
she should not dig the earth; and she should not cut green grass.
One must not accept food that has been stored overnight, nor food that was left over from a previous meal;
these are called the six *anuvartakas*, which one must train in for two years.
The *sthavira* must clearly remember and know the number of days.
The administrator, standing before the assembly, shall announce it every day.
Within the six periods [of the day], one day is to be subtracted at each half-month;
when the subtraction of days completes a month, and this occurs six times, a leap month is formed.
Just as when a king intercalates a month, the lunar count becomes irregular;
the bhikṣus should likewise conform to this, for the king possesses great power.
Whether it be at the place where one washes hands or the bowl, or if one constructs a maṇḍala;
It should not resemble the shape of the sun or moon, nor should it have the form of a stupa.
When a bhikṣu travels along a road and passes by a shrine or temple hall,
he should snap his fingers upon entering and recite the words of the Buddha.
If one arrives at a shrine, one should neither cause harm nor offer benefit;
if a bhikṣu violates this instruction, he incurs the offense of duṣkṛta.
Bhikṣus and the other five assemblies do not make offerings to celestial deities.
Whether performing it oneself or causing another to do so, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If there are other necessary circumstances, the offering of incense, flowers, and food is permitted;
however, one must not contravene local customs, nor should one perform acts that would cause harm or benefit [to others].
The benevolent deities who serve the Buddha should be honored with offerings according to one's inclination;
if commissioned to perform tasks within the context of the great sūtras, there is no transgression.
Toward all classes of sentient beings, one should always provide protection and practice loving-kindness.
Because they possess the seeds of compassion, they are not reborn in the miserable realms.
Those who love and revere the celestial deities always delight in making offerings;
this is so for all in the world, as they crave the pleasures of birth and death.
All seek worldly fruits, and for this reason they sacrifice to false deities;
they afflict and kill sentient beings, leading others to the evil realms.
Having already taken refuge in the Buddha, they now turn back to serve celestial gods.
The fruit obtained from making offerings is meager, for they do not know the place of reverence.
Those who break the precepts yet wear the kāṣāya, deceiving others with the mere appearance of a bhikṣu;
shamelessly consuming the food of others, they are like glowing embers of fierce fire.
One should copy the Vinaya teachings and so forth; their dissemination can generate merit.
One should cause those who have forgotten to remember, while personally reciting and upholding them as well.
When a bhikṣu enters the bathhouse and must scrub his body;
One should cause those who possess reverence and faith to act, and not allow those who lack faith to do so.
Among all those who uphold the precepts, one should not provide support for those who have broken them;
one must not allow a lion to serve a jackal.
This is a thorn in the Buddha’s Dharma, a corpse within the True Teaching;
to dwell with such a person or to follow them in their travels makes one unfit for the Dharma.
Even when one's preceptor, instructor, parents, or other teachers are ill, [one must not associate with such a person].
Even if they have broken the precepts, one may provide for them all.
When parents are old, poor, or ill, one should offer them half of whatever alms one has received;
because they have bestowed such great kindness, they should be cared for and supported.
Whenever one perceives a lack or deficiency, one should provide for it according to the need;
even down to oil for anointing the feet, or bathing and washing them so that the body is clean.
If a bhikṣu uses a brick, he may only rub his ankles with it.
Other parts of the body are not permitted [to be adorned], yet all are allowed if for the sake of illness.
One should not draw three lines on the head, nor wear a comb, nor carry a mantra-thread;
however, it is permitted as an exception for treating disease that it be tied to the left arm.
When the illness has been cured, one should place [the medicine] back into the hole in the pillar;
if a physician instructs one to do so, there is no offense in anointing the body with incense.
If one anoints the body with incense, one should not go outside the room.
Do not cause others to feel disdain or increase their lack of faith.
If there are those with pure faith, for the sake of merit, offer scented clay;
it should be applied to the edges of the door panels, for smelling it can benefit the eyes.
With pure faith, one may smear the feet of a bhikṣu with fragrant clay;
for the sake of merit, this should be accepted, but it must be washed away upon departure.
If there are exquisite fragrant flowers, and the bhikṣu wishes to smell them, [they may be accepted].
One who desires to be clear-sighted should not give rise to thoughts of attachment.
One may be permitted to hold an iron key for the sake of protecting robes and medicine;
do not harbor afflictive thoughts, nor should you ever seize or strike sentient beings.
Whether for the great assembly or for an individual, it is permitted for all to hold the seal;
it should be made of copper, iron, wood, mineral stone, brick, tin, or similar materials.
For an individual, there may be an image of a skull, or perhaps one carved as a white bone.
The great assembly takes the form of a Dharma wheel; this is the manner of forming the mudrā.
Whenever one eats small fragrant fruits, one must always wait until the seeds are formed;
if one wishes to cause their merit to increase, the fruit of the Saṃgha must ripen.
One should not look at the reflection of one's face in water or a mirror out of a mind of attachment;
however, there is no fault in looking while reflecting on impermanence for the sake of illness.
One must not cut off one's own genitals, nor strike them with bricks or stones.
One should employ the contemplation of impurity to wash away the mind stained by lust.
The basin for washing the feet should be high, its shape like an elephant’s footprint;
one should carry two kinds of fans: those made of bamboo and those made of *tāla* leaves.
If one wishes to ward off mosquitoes, five kinds of whisks are permitted:
branches, cotton, *karpāsa* cloth, hemp, wool, and torn rags.
If it is necessary to climb a high ladder, one should tie the lower hem of the skirt.
A bhikṣu should not carry heavy loads; he should seek out a layperson to hold them.
Such is the protocol for bhikṣus: they differ from the laity in all respects.
Using combs or similar items to scratch the head—none of these things are permissible.
If there is dust or grime on the hair, one may scratch the itchy head with the hand;
or at times, using an old garment—none of these constitute an offense.
In the northwestern corner behind the monastery, one should establish a chamber for defecation.
As for small practice rooms, they must all have shop-style doors and panels.
In the lower room at the northwest corner, one should place the large communal water jar;
this is based on the assumption that the door faces south—the other orientations should be understood accordingly.
If one sees a layperson or an elderly bhikṣu sneeze, one should say, "May you live long";
if one does not speak, one incurs an offense.
When an elder sees a junior sneeze, he should say, "May you be free from illness."
A junior, toward those of seniority, must immediately say, "I pay homage.
This applies whenever one is eating, or when one has just relieved oneself and has not yet washed;
or when wearing only a single garment while on the road, or standing in a place that is defiled or crowded.
Or again, even if one has finished eating, if the mouth has not yet been rinsed;
in such cases, one neither performs prostrations to others nor accepts the prostrations of others.
If, at the time of rising in the morning, the mouth has not yet been cleansed with a tooth-stick;
To perform a prostration to another or to receive a prostration from another both incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
One should not prostrate to those undergoing the *parivāsa* probation or similar disciplinary measures;
one should prostrate only to these two: the Buddha and the great *bhikṣus*.
Within this holy teaching, there are two kinds of prostrations:
the first is performed with the five limbs, and the second is by clasping the calves.
One who upholds the precepts should not bind a snake’s neck with a cord of hair.
If it is unwilling to leave, one should skillfully drive it away.
One may use a soft rope to gently tie its neck and discard it;
it should be placed in a secluded thicket, not in the presence of many people.
In this way, one may arouse compassionate thoughts even toward mice and the like;
whether they are bound or released, do not let them be harmed, applying oneself with diligent and skillful mindfulness.
For the one who guards the precepts, compassion extends even to fleas and lice, maintaining constant mindfulness toward them.
Place it inside an old cloth or felt mat, or set it within a crevice;
if one wishes to eliminate the fleas, one may place them among green grass.
Let them go wherever they please, and do not cause them any suffering or harm.
There are three types of oil vessels:
the large holds one handful, the small half a handful, and the rest are intermediate; they may be carried and used according to one's convenience.
For those on the path of practice, there are two methods: speaking the Dharma or maintaining noble silence.
While staying for the night, one should recite verses; at the place of rest, one should chant the Threefold Homage.
One may use three kinds of cords:
a long one of one hundred and fifty cubits, a short one of one hundred cubits, and those of intermediate length; these should be used according to the circumstances.
If the well or pond is shallow, the water may flow level;
one may hold it according to its length, or at times not use it at all.
If for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, one expounds the teachings on the Vinaya discipline;
One should screen the area with a curtain; otherwise, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* offense.
One must not take items left behind by thieves, but should instead observe them carefully;
if many people are entrusted with the knowledge of the item, there is no fault even if one takes it.
If a bhikṣu plants trees intended for a monastic fruit orchard, he must guard them for five years;
when departing, he must entrust them [to another].
If a bhikṣu does not take an oath, yet acts as if he were speaking falsely, [he incurs an offense].
Nor should one gamble with robes and the like; such games of chance are not the śīla.
When a bhikṣu sees a woman and a defiled mind arises, or if the woman conceives a defiled intent, he should leave his dwelling and depart.
If one sees a bhikṣuṇī coming for the purpose of listening to the Dharma,
one must not have her stand; rather, one should provide her with an object so that she may sit comfortably—
such as a brick, a wooden stool, or a cushion of grass or straw.
Only this [seating] shall be provided for the nuns; no other items are appropriate.
When a nun arrives at the monastery, bedding and mats should be given to her;
she should be provided with those of middle or low quality, as it is not fitting to give her superior items.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should not fail to confess their offenses when facing one another;
because of the transgressions they have committed, they may feel such shame that it is difficult to speak of them.
If a bhikṣuṇī has doubts, her offenses must be resolved.
A nun must give rise to respect and never harbor thoughts of contempt.
When a nun enters a monastery belonging to the monks, she should send someone to inquire at the gate;
once it is reported that she is without fault, she may be allowed to enter as she pleases.
One who wishes to dwell in an araṇya should first become proficient in the Tripiṭaka;
the movements and sequences of the sun, moon, and stars should all be known through careful discernment.
If one resides in an araṇya, one should keep items such as oil.
He may accept whatever can be offered as provisions, so as to cause the thieves to rejoice.
Previously, those who were artisans were not permitted to keep their tools;
however, physicians and those skilled in writing are permitted to keep needles, pens, and the like.
A bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya should apply himself with diligent effort;
for one who has left the household life, diligence is paramount, while indolence brings about fault.
Even if one practices with vigor, one must still seek the True Dharma.
Deprived of this vision, one lacks clarity; faith is lost and cultivation goes astray.
If one is separated from authentic instruction, it is not fit to practice the gateway of meditative concentration;
it can give rise to a deranged mind and damage the path of the factors of dhyāna.
In the dwelling where one resides, incense, flowers, and the like should be fragrant;
bedding and clothing should likewise be so. Otherwise, the mind will find it difficult to attain concentration.
When the Sangha constructs wooden items, they must not be used for burning or dyeing.
If it is bent or rotten, its use is permitted provided it causes no harm.
If one seeks to relieve another's fatigue, one must observe the proper rules and regulations;
if that person has companions or associates, one must investigate and question them before granting admission.
If a bhikṣu sees a woman being swept away or harmed by water, fire, or the like, he should rescue her;
because it is out of compassion, there is no offense.
If someone comes and asks, "What are the means for sustaining life? [he may explain].
A bhikṣu should act according to the circumstances and teach others so as not to contravene worldly customs.
Whether it be beneath the gate of the monastery or in front of the eaves of a room,
if there are women present, a bhikṣu should not remain there.
Having already renounced the objects of the five desires and no longer craving them,
one should therefore always apply the mind, maintaining mindfulness and diligently practicing cultivation.
This is the path of all Tathāgatas of the three times, as well as the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
All who follow this path are able to reach the city of Nirvāṇa.
A disciple should observe the virtue of the teacher before requesting him as a refuge;
the teacher, for his part, must inquire and ascertain whether he should accept the disciple.
If both parties commit a transgression, each incurs a fault;
therefore, you must both apply your minds with diligence and examine one another with care.
The teacher must possess complete conduct in the precepts and, when attending to the sick, not be stingy with the Dharma.
One should seek such a teacher who constantly provides instruction at all times;
a disciple likewise should be endowed with precepts, diligent in self-exhortation, gentle in nature,
respectful toward teachers and elders, and without fail in meditation and recitation.
If one departs on one's own business, or sees one's original teacher, or enters a non-Buddhist sect, or returns to lay life—in all these cases, one loses the formal reliance (*niśraya*).
Furthermore, if one follows another person with the thought of abandoning one's reliance; [in these instances as well, the reliance is lost].
This is what is called "renunciation"; one must know well when to advance or refrain.
When reprimanding a disciple, one must not immediately expel them;
allow them to remain temporarily within the monastery, and if they reform, command them to return to their quarters.
There are five kinds of censures:
not speaking and not instructing;
not accepting one's service; obstructing wholesome qualities; and causing one to relinquish robes.
Rebuke and the acceptance of confession must both be carried out in accordance with the teachings;
if these two are contravened, both will incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Those who are indolent and lack filial piety, who speak harsh words and associate with evil friends;
If one shows no respect for the teacher, that person shall not be granted absolution (*kṣamā*).
If a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is expelled, the teacher must carefully examine whether to provide him with his upper and lower robes, as well as a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*).
If one has already received full ordination, one should be provided with the six requisites;
if they are indeed difficult to tolerate, let them go and do not detain them.
If one is separated from one's original preceptor, one should not travel for even a single night [without him].
Furthermore, once five years have been completed, one must be well-versed in the Vinaya.
If one intends to go elsewhere, the conditions allow for a five-day leave;
one should diligently seek an *upādhyāya* (preceptor), for without one, one may not remain.
One should perform the washing and massaging of the teacher’s body at his own residence;
whether dyeing or sewing his robes, these are the duties of a disciple.
Regarding the performance of tasks, one should act with knowledge of moderation.
One should cultivate compassion for those who care for and protect one, yet not allow it to become excessive.
One should attend to and serve both the teacher from whom one studies and the preceptor upon whom one relies;
however, there is a distinction in the degree of reverence shown toward these two.
If there is no teacher to provide instruction, one may stay wherever one is without offense;
yet one should not dwell without a support, for one must maintain a twofold mind of reliance.
Even if one has severed all afflictions and is thoroughly proficient in the Tripiṭaka, [one must still rely on a teacher].
If one has not yet completed ten years of seniority, one must still remain in dependence upon a preceptor.
If the distance from the teacher is two and a half *yi* (approx. 15–20 li), one should pay homage once every half-month;
at a distance of one and a half *yi*, one should pay homage once every eight days; if residing in the same location, one must pay homage three times daily.
If, during the latter part of the summer retreat, the preceptor should pass away,
one should maintain self-restraint of mind and mutually oversee one another.
When the three months have reached their completion, if one remains in a place without a preceptor;
Regarding the second *poṣadha*: one should not remain here [in that state].
Since the matter of *pravāraṇā* has already been performed, do not perform another *poṣadha*.
The Great Sage, in accordance with the season, permitted this; it is therefore called *pāriśuddhi*.
They instruct one another, acting as sent by the Sage according to his will;
they constantly open the gate of Poṣadha to counteract the various karmas of transgression.
When guests arrive at the monastery, the hosts may sometimes be numerous.
If the number of monks is uneven, such as fourteen or fifteen, they should act according to the host.
If there are many guests present and the number of resident monks is few,
the host should follow the lead of those guests and perform the *poṣadha* together with them.
When the Saṃgha is not in harmony, one should maintain [the vow] in the presence of a single person;
if even a single person is absent, one should perform it through mental recitation and verbal expression.
By maintaining it in this manner, the robes and bowl of a bhikṣu are preserved.
One should know that both [the formal act] and the invitation are relinquished through analysis;
if the great assembly is in harmony, they may dwell together with virtuous persons.
It is reasonable to permit the recitation of the precepts, and the mental recitation (cittānuvartana) is likewise permitted.
If there are necessarily difficult conditions for the *pravāraṇā*, and one has a matter that disturbs the mind’s reflection;
one should know that regarding such matters of personal convenience, one should act accordingly based on this precedent.
The great assembly should be of one mind and should perform the *pravāraṇā* together.
If one departs otherwise than this, one must call for a fellow practitioner to act on one's behalf.
When departing at will, it may be for a period of seven or eight days;
one should announce the matter so that all people may know.

The ritual site should be governed by the Dharma; whether within the boundary or outside it, as long as one does not dwell separately within a single boundary, all communal affairs should be performed.
Whether there be twenty, ten, five, or even four bhikṣus;
There are these four types of Saṃgha, according to which one should uphold the various dharmas.
One must not include the World-Honored One in the count of those Saṃghas;
for the Jewel of the Buddha is distinct from the Jewel of the Saṃgha—this is what those who uphold the Dharma should know.
Twenty are required for the expiation of offenses; ten or more for full ordination (*upasampadā*);
five for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; and four for the *poṣadha*.
Wherever a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed, it is accomplished according to the Dharma through the motion (*jñapti*) and so forth.
One should know that this is called a proper dwelling; anything other than this is not a dwelling.
A bhikṣu should not remain silent; he should proclaim the words of the Dharma with his mouth.
These outsiders are foolish and deluded, seducing and deceiving those who lack understanding.
When a bhikṣu has completed the rainy season retreat, he should perform the three matters according to his own will;
if he does not do so, he must not depart unless there is an obstacle.
Even if there are grounds for seeing, hearing, or suspecting [a fault], if a separate circumstance of difficulty arises, [he may leave].
To protect one's body and life, one must travel even across the sea.
If there are kings, bandits, or others who wish to hear the bhikṣu precepts, they should be taught in times of difficulty;
however, they should not be taught when no such difficulties exist.
The poor man has faith, while the wealthy man lacks faith and respect;
being diligent and eager to hear the precepts, the World-Honored One opened the teaching for him to speak.
A bhikṣu well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, a Dharma-preacher, and a sick person—[to these he should teach].
The eldest among the assembly should all release the administrative officers.
Hearing that a Tripitaka Master of great renown has come from afar,
one should welcome him with drums, music, banners, and streamers for a distance of two and a half stations.
When the great assembly strikes the *gandi*, everyone should respond by going out to welcome [the guests] according to their ability;
with delicious food, they should relieve the fatigue [of the guests], and the order of invitation should be announced accordingly.
Lodgings and bedding are not subject to regular distribution.
Provide offerings to the *kappiyakāraka* (pure person), and do not delegate those who oversee communal affairs.
The training in the precepts was established by the Buddha; the regulations of the Saṃgha are observed collectively by the assembly.
It is better to deviate from the words of the assembly than to violate the teaching of the World-Honored One.
The inclinations of the multitude follow many paths; though established, they are often abandoned again.
How could there be anyone capable of altering them? Such is the word of the Great Teacher, who is without a second.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, one should enter the prior *anvāsaṇa* (the first retreat).
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, the bhikṣus enter the latter summer retreat.
Only on these two days may the formal procedures for the rainy season retreat (varṣā) be performed;
during the intervening period, one may dwell there only as a temporary resident, as the formal retreat is not permitted.
Within the three months [of the rainy season], a bhikṣu is not permitted to travel abroad;
even a flying bird during the summer does not leave its nest.
When the beginning of the fifth month arrives, one must be mindful as the summer draws near.
In that dwelling place, one should perform the necessary preparations and decorations.
When the fifteenth day arrives, all bedding and requisites must be collected;
then, a person endowed with virtuous qualities should be appointed as the distributor of bedding.
Free from desire, hatred, delusion, and fear, and devoid of all faults;
well-versed in what has been apportioned and what has not—such a person should be appointed.
Regarding the *vihāra-pāla*, one must inform them of the monastic regulations.
I hope you will dwell in peace and happiness, and never allow yourselves to fall into violation.
Those who wish to dwell in harmony should not engage in strife;
those who receive these voting tallies must examine themselves with care.
The formal announcement to the assembly:
"Today is the fifteenth day;
the Saṃgha shall together receive the voting sticks for the upcoming *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)."
Once the counting sticks have been distributed from the top down, the rooms and dwellings should next be divided;
as for the beds and bedding, they should all be assigned starting from the largest until the end.
When the time for the retreat (*varṣā*) approaches, one must carefully examine [the site].
In the area where one goes for alms, do not allow one's duties to be neglected.
If, at one’s place of residence, there are companions who are known to possess virtue and great learning, as well as being pure, good, and harmonious;
One should not allow afflictions to arise; if they do arise, one should immediately eliminate them.
Where such virtuous companions reside, it is fitting to dwell together.
Sickness, medicine, and alms-food—all these are easily obtained there.
A place where there are not many courtesans is called a suitable location for practice.
One should remain in a secluded spot, squatting before the bhikṣu;
reciting the text for the summer retreat, the ritual procedure should be performed in this manner.
I, the donor [Name], together with my attendants and laborers, now observe the preceding summer retreat at this place. Or, one may say:
"I observe the subsequent summer retreat; there are cracks and breaks here which shall be repaired."
I shall dwell here for this summer retreat; the rest is as previously explained.
If one observes the rains retreat here, one must not stay overnight outside the Dharma-realm;
there will be no benefit in the present life, and in a future life, one will suffer in hell.
If it is for the sake of the monastery or similar matters, as well as various miscellaneous meritorious deeds;
for the purpose of the *caitya* and communal meals, and for the expiation of offenses;
or when a nun violates the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*) and one wishes to eliminate her transgression.
Or for the sake of the three lower assemblies, one must observe the requirements for receiving the precepts and so forth.
If there are circumstances such as being summoned by laypeople,
the bhikṣu should examine the propriety of the time and respond by going when it is appropriate.
If there are matters concerning the Triple Gem, one's parents, or teachers and masters;
or due to the circumstances of various illnesses—one may request leave for seven days.
This may range from one or two days, up to forty nights.
The bhikṣu should depart so as not to let previous matters fall into neglect.
If there is a matter in accordance with the Dharma, and he has ascertained that it is not false,
and the Saṃgha collectively authorizes his dispatch, he may go at his own discretion.
Throughout a single summer retreat, one should not spend more than half of it outside;
for this reason, [the limit] is set at forty days, as exceeding this would constitute an offense and cause harm.
Furthermore, if there is a deficiency in food and drink, or if medicine is difficult to obtain, [one may stay longer].
If there is no one at all to provide service, departing does not constitute a violation of the summer retreat.
If a place is beset by the eight difficulties, or by such conditions as courtesans,
eunuchs, and predatory beasts, traveling under these circumstances incurs no offense of breaking the summer retreat.
If there is a person of evil deeds who comes to break the harmony of the assembly, it is better to leave for fear of unwholesome matters; one incurs no harm by departing.
If one hears of those engaged in strife and recognizes them as one's own kinsmen or friends, [one should likewise avoid them].
If one does not go to offer admonition, one incurs an offense; by remaining [without going], there is no fault of breaking the summer retreat.
If one makes an agreement with another to dwell in a certain place for the rains, yet fails to arrive at the appointed date, the bhikṣu incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a bhikṣu maintains his formal observance for seven days or more,
and encounters difficulties while abroad, he is permitted to remain there as long as necessary.
However, if there is no other valid reason, he must not stay for many days.
If one repeatedly transgresses the original limits, one incurs guilt and breaks the summer retreat (*varṣa*).
There are many ways to establish a boundary (*sīmā*); briefly stated, there are four types.
According to what is currently required, I shall now explain them according to their respective functions.
At most two and a half *yojanas*, or less depending on the circumstances;
one should set up markers in all four directions, using mountains, rivers, trees, and the like as signs.
These may be established within the aforementioned landmarks, or even within the dwelling place itself.
Excluding villages and their surrounding territories, one should know that a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) is established.
The entire assembly must gather, and a single person shall preside over the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
Through the unerring performance of the motion and the first proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), this is called the successful establishment of the boundary.
Furthermore, so as not to be separated from one's robes, one maintains the *karmavācanā* within the boundary;
this is intended to ensure a peaceful and happy dwelling, originally due to the conditions of old age and illness.
Even though one is separated from the three robes, one may stay overnight in a different location within the boundary.
Excluding the surrounding territory of the village, one may wander freely wherever one wishes.

If one intends to establish a small ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*) within the previously established great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), one should perform the formal act of notification (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to bind it; however, one must first dissolve the great boundary.
If one wishes to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), the markers should be placed as before;
this is called a *maṇḍala*, and within it one may perform the ritual acts at will.
First, establish the small precinct, and subsequently, establish the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).
One who establishes the boundary should understand this sequence:
when the entire assembly dies, changes their gender, or simultaneously renounces the precepts;
or when they all go outside the boundary and the dawn has passed without returning.
Sometimes it is performed by a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), and when the great assembly is of one mind, they relinquish it;
one should know that there are these five kinds of distinctions for relinquishing a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary).
Furthermore, those who wish to establish various boundaries must also understand the defining markers (*nimitta*).
A single tree should serve as two markers, with half of it designated for each boundary;
sometimes a single tree may serve as four boundary markers,
provided each of the four quarters is equal, but five divisions are not permitted.
Half a station downward, and the same distance upward;
reaching the treetops at the summit of the mountain, or even upon the fences and walls—
various kinds of ornamental objects are all present for one’s hearing as they follow.
Adorning the form of the Great Master serves to increase the merit of those who offer it;
yet one must not permit the wearing of earrings or tinkling anklets,
for these are ornaments of women and should not burden the form of the Great Master.
If you wish to disperse the multitude, the music may be silenced;
all ritual implements should be gathered up so that nothing is lost or damaged.
At times when the great assembly has gathered, there may be clamor and loud voices.
When the appointed time has arrived, one should sound the conch and beat the drum.
If the property of the deceased is to be distributed, it may be difficult for such a large multitude to manage;
therefore, let ten people form a single group, or even groups numbering in the hundreds or thousands.
Each shall take a large portion, and further subdivide it according to the number of people;
whether the portion has been divided or not yet divided, if death occurs, it must be distributed.
If death occurs only after the division is complete, the goods belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
If the items have not yet been divided, they should be shared among the companions.
Wherever there is an invitation for bhikṣus, one should also summon the bhikṣuṇīs;
when giving alms after the meal, one should place the wealth before the head of the assembly.
This should be divided into two parts, or according to the donor’s intention;
food and drink may be shared equally, for the Buddha has likewise ordained this.
When bhikṣus divide the offerings, they should give equal portions to the bhikṣuṇīs.
To a śikṣamāṇā, one should give two parts and [retain] one;
to one who is about to receive full ordination, likewise two parts and one;
for a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī, it should be known that one part is given out of three.
If there are many bhikṣus and few in the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, one should calculate by the number of heads;
it is not appropriate to divide the offerings equally between the two groups.
When the day of a great assembly arrives, one should invite the images into the village or city.
It can cause calamities and misfortunes to be dispelled, and its adornment brings forth merit.
Sprinkling [perfumes] everywhere upon the broad highways, it decorates the lanes and alleys;
scattering flowers and hanging exquisite banners, it is as elegant and beautiful as a celestial garden.
Sandalwood and camphor, and aloeswood incense, waft their fragrance everywhere;
carried by the wind, they reach every place, and those who smell them conceive deep reverence.
Conch shells are blown and small drums are struck; bells are tolled to announce [the news] to the four quarters.
Crowds gather as they hear the thunderous sound, and those who listen give rise to sympathetic joy.
The drums and music never cease, their loud resonance rising above the clouds;
banners and streamers are draped everywhere—this is called a Great Dharma Assembly.
There are five kinds of great banners: those of the whale, the ox, the garuḍa, the dragon, and the lion;
these painted pennants and flags are all held up as offerings.
The multitude of people all follow in attendance, with both the ordained and the laity relying upon one another.
With such supreme adornments, they led the Tathāgata into [the city].
Because the Buddha entered the village and town, the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas,
gave rise to offerings with reverent hearts and were able to eliminate all poisons and evils.
From this, one shall obtain wealth and profit; the assembly shall sell and divide the shares accordingly.
The Elder shall determine the value, carefully examining its quality—whether good or bad.
If there is anyone who requires it, they may offer a higher price according to their own inclination.
If the price has not yet been settled, one should not wear this robe.
One should respectfully offer it to one’s wife, children, or others, or give it as an offering to any one of the Three Jewels;
it must not be used to pay a price, but should follow the intention of the donor.
When a bhikṣu causes a place for song, dance, or music to be made,
those who guard the precepts should not say to him, "You are playing. Instead,
they should tell him, "O worthy one, you should apply your mind with care."
Make offerings to the Great Teacher and do not give rise to indolence.
When hanging banners on a stūpa, one should not use objects to nail them down;
at the time of its original construction, the insertion of stakes was permitted as appropriate.
When offering lamps upon a stūpa, a bhikṣu must not climb it himself;
if there is a necessary reason to ascend, he should have a śrāmaṇera do so.
If no one else is available, he may wash both his feet with scented water.
The bhikṣu should ascend himself, with a mind of devotion to make offerings to the Great Master.
He may build a monastery of three or five stories, or a fragrant terrace of five or seven;
or he may construct it according to his own inclination, such as a small temple of five or three rooms.
Briefly discussing the layout of the central monastery:
on both the eastern and western sides, there are three stories with nine rooms each; each room within is twelve feet wide.
Behind these are also three stories, occupying a space of three rooms in width.
In the central hall, one should intend to enshrine a sacred image; even before the eaves, the practice of circumambulation shall not be abandoned.
Alternatively, one may construct a multi-storied pavilion rising from the ground right here before the eaves;
there, one may install a great sacred image and offer incense and flowers every day.
For the two rooms at the front, construct a gate pavilion from the bottom;
the door should be situated between the lower tiers, made small yet sturdy.
Upon entering, turn toward a corner and ascend three stories via the gallery path.
The upper stories project outward and all have flat tops; the four sides are sheer cliffs.
Nunnery buildings are limited to three stories, while incense altars may extend up to five.
Regarding the architectural standards for rooms within the monastery, one should know that they correspond to those for *bhikṣus*.
If the form of a Buddha image is damaged or decayed, and the characters of the honored scriptures have been rubbed away or erased,
one may wipe them clean and restore them so that they become even more magnificent.
One must not step upon the stūpas, the sacred images, or the new altars.
If there is a necessity that requires one to pass through, one may recite the noble gāthās.
When a bhikṣu is begging for alms, if there is someone who makes no distinction [between a monk and a Buddha],
perceiving him as the Buddha and calling him "Buddha," they may offer their belongings as a gift.
The bhikṣu should question him, examining his intent with thorough scrutiny:
"When you call me 'Buddha,' do you mean the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings?
When you call me 'Dharma,' do you mean the Dharma that brings an end to suffering?"
Those whom you call the Saṃgha are indeed the assembly of true sages.
Once you have questioned them and gained certain knowledge, then according to their inclinations, the donor should accept [their guidance]; in this, there is no fault whatsoever.
Even if there is only a single nun who, having accepted an invitation, goes to another's house,
she should leave one seat behind upon departing for the sake of a bhikṣu’s arrival.
A bhikṣu should occupy this seat, and a śrāmaṇera may also sit there.
If one does not understand how to recite the verses of aspiration, a bhikṣuṇī may perform it for them.
If there is no attendant to manage affairs, one should go to a village as circumstances allow;
whatever profit is gained must be entrusted [to another], and only when a person is found should one send it to be carried.
The above clarifies various miscellaneous conditions, most of which concern matters while one is alive;
below we discuss what must be known regarding cremation and burial after the body has died.
Once a bhikṣu has passed away, one should inform the assembly and strike the *gaṇḍī*.
One must summon the corpse-bearers; for firewood, use the property of the Sangha.
With incense, flowers, banners, drums, and music, escort the body to the cremation forest;
relatives, acquaintances, and disciples shall follow along out of compassion.
One should carefully observe what may be burned; the fuel and fire must be abundant.
Use sandalwood and the like as aids, and pour ghee according to need.
If there are worms in the sores of the body, ensure they are not harmed when burying [the remains].
Or they may rest in the open air, their bodies covered by grass and leaves.
Within each and every body dwell eighty thousand kinds of worms;
they live and die together with the body, so that even when it is cremated, they pass away without exception.
One should take the upper and lower robes to cover the corpse, ensuring it is well-concealed;
as for the remaining robes, bowl, and other items, they may be distributed according to the Dharma.
While sitting wherever one is during the cremation, one should briefly recite the Sūtra on Impermanence.
With a focused mind, listen to these three expositions; each must give rise to weary detachment.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all things born of causes and conditions must cease.
They do not abide for even a moment, like dewdrops startled by the wind.
Surveying all the worlds, I see that nothing endures;
all flow toward the ocean of impermanence, together drifting upon the waves of death.
Even the solidity of the four great elements cannot be shifted.
That which is born must inevitably be impermanent; the power of the King of Death is great.
Impermanence makes no distinctions—whether one is virtuous or evil, observant of precepts or learned;
all alike return to death, regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or noble ones.
The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvaka disciples—even they must relinquish this impermanent body; how much more so for ordinary worldlings?
Having thus recited these verses on the Dharma, one should then recite the *Ṭakkiṇī*.
Upon returning, wash your hands and feet, and perform circumambulations around the *caitya*.
Alternatively, you may wash your entire body and then put on other clothes;
when departing, take your old garments with you, and do not damage your fresh flowered robes.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," etc., are the words spoken by the Muni;
as you walk back to the monastery, you should extinguish thoughts of stinginess and greed.
All clothing and requisites should be used in accordance with the Āgamas.
The sons of the Buddha share equally; the ritual procedures follow the established regulations.

When the *gaṇḍī* is struck and the three invocations are recited, when one pays homage at the *caitya* and casts the voting sticks (*śalākā*), and during the performance of the *karmavācanā*—at these five times, all may receive their shares.
One should not, while the assembly has not yet gathered, hastily divide the deceased's property;
the portion for the Elder and the one for the distribution at the end should be set aside as two separate shares.
Once this fixed record has been made, only then may the wealth be divided among the community.
"Should a guest arrive later, you must not share with him.
Only after my death shall you give it away"—with such words of stinginess he spoke;
since his intent was thus undecided, it is fitting that upon his death, the property should revert to the community.
Having resolved one's mind to be free from stinginess, one bestows [the gift] while still alive;
giving it away to another according to one's own will—such acts constitute the practice of the Dharma.
Worldly people harbor many expectations at death, but for those who have left the household life, this is not appropriate.
Just as attachment to worldly concerns increases birth and death day by day,
so too when a bhikṣu passes away, his own and others' belongings become intermingled and disordered;
one should therefore place his bowl and other requisites before the Saṃgha.
If one observes and knows these to be deceased property, they should be distributed according to the Dharma;
all such precious items and the like should be disposed of in accordance with the teachings.
If a bhikṣu dies, his belongings likewise belong to the bhikṣus to divide.
If at that time there are no bhikṣus, the community of bhikṣuṇīs should take possession.
If a bhikṣuṇī dies, the bhikṣuṇīs are entitled to it;
if there are no such bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣus should act as the masters.

When a bhikṣu dies in a layperson’s house, if there are no monks present, it is appropriate for the laypeople to give [the belongings] to those who arrived first; if they all arrived together, they should give them to those who requested them.
If two people request them simultaneously, they should be given to both.
Or, according to the donor’s intention, one who gives it should accept it. Or,
when there are many monasteries nearby and a bhikṣu of this household has passed away,
whichever direction his head points toward, he shall rightfully receive the deceased’s robes and bowl.
If a bhikṣu incurs a debt to another and suddenly passes away, one must inquire thoroughly into the matter;
the community shall provide for his needs using his deceased robes.
