If he was an administrator who took property belonging to others on behalf of the community, [the same applies].
One should give communal property [only] when it is appropriate; when repaying debts, one must deliberate carefully.
Whenever an administrator takes goods from another, they should inform the Elder (sthavira), so that the contract may be made clear.
If one brings funeral banners, robes, and the like to offer to a bhikṣu, there is no fault in accepting them; this causes their merit to increase.
Should the donor later feel regret and come back to reclaim these garments, [one should return them].
The bhikṣu should return it all; do not let him be oppressed by the fire of grief.
If one who has been suspended lives together with a virtuous person, they may die at the same time or one after the other;
the deceased’s robes shall be obtained by the virtuous person, and the one who performed the suspension shall not share in them.
If there is no one who upholds the precepts, and a person who has been suspended dies;
even though they have been suspended and have not yet received absolution, their belongings should be shared among the community.
Since there is a clear written document, the goods should be delivered to another person.
If one dies while serving the community, the community should seek [the property] according to the agreement.
That which belongs to the community should be given to the community; the same applies to the *caitya*.
If it is fit for the King, it should be sent to the King, provided that weapons such as swords and arrows are excluded.
One should employ such items to make knives and needles;
all other [excess] is to be divided among those present, for the original object is not subject to distribution.
If a person recites even a single verse according to the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, [he shall receive a share].
Wealth obtained through the Dharma should be accepted;
the Muni has two aspects: the teaching and the realization, which should be known.
The teaching is the Āgama; regarding the gift of the Dharma, one should request a portion.
If the summer retreat has passed its midpoint, and there is someone who renounces the precepts;
should a bhikṣu die at this juncture, one should share [the property] with that person.
Even for constructing a stūpa for the Buddha equal in size to Mount Sumeru;
The foundations on all four sides are firm, Extending even to the placement of the precious vases.
One, two, three, or four wheels— The corresponding fruits should be known in this order.
An ordinary person endowed with virtue Has a truncated head as its *caitya*.
If one constructs a caitya for a Buddha, the number of wheels and parasols is not fixed;
if it exceeds the height of Mount Sumeru by a thousandfold, the merit obtained will be boundless.
For a Pratyekabuddha who is like a rhinoceros, [the caitya] does not exceed thirteen *parvan*.
Upon the top of that harmikā, it is improper to place a jeweled vase.
Within the stūpa, the Buddha is installed; on both sides are the two disciples;
the other noble ones follow in succession, while all ordinary beings should be placed outside.
Next, the matter of attending to the sick is explained: members of the community should take turns providing care for one another.
If the patient lacks the funds for medicine, it is appropriate to provide them with items from the Sangha’s property.
If a sick person comes to beg, one should wash the bowl and fill it with pure water.
One should recite the Buddha’s gāthā three times, keeping the mantra in mind.
When a bhikṣu receives medicine for the sake of another, he may take it and give it to the patient;
if there is no one to administer it, he is permitted to take it himself and consume it.
One should not approach a sick person to teach them and take their robes and bowl;
even if they should offer them as a gift, the assembly must not divide them.
This is because both the donor and the recipient, as well as the teacher who instructed them, harbor greedy desires.
If all three are not pure in mind, these should not be used.
If a sick person so desires, they may offer fine robes and such to the Buddha and the Sangha;
they themselves should instead maintain coarse and worn clothing.
If they are poor and have nothing, one should still perform the work of teaching and transforming them;
by giving according to their means, whether much or little, cause their faith to increase.
Even a single plate of flowers, or perhaps a vessel of water may suffice.
One should follow the patient’s words and make offerings so as to gladden their heart. If,
regarding one's own wealth and possessions, the stingy mind finds it difficult to relinquish,
one should appropriately apply the mind to exhortation, causing them to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Alternatively, one may attend to the sick person by relinquishing robes, bowls, and other requisites;
by having them witness this offering, it will induce a mind of generosity.
If there is attachment toward any of these material necessities, they must be renounced.
One should bestow robes and alms bowls according to one's inclination upon those of virtuous conduct.
Although a bhikṣu may uphold the precepts, if he is so attached to his bowl that it follows him until death,
he will be reborn within that very bowl and suffer the retribution of a venomous snake.
If one suffers from hemorrhoids, fistulas, or similar ailments, do not allow untrustworthy persons to administer medical treatment in haste;
do not have them perform excisions that cause such suffering.
If treating for hemorrhoids, they may be cured through the application of medicine and incantations.
If there is no physician, one should not provide a prescription;

if there are no fingernails, one should not cut [the herbs]. If there is no attendant, no disciple, and no medicine, the great assembly shall all provide for it, for medicine comes forth from the Saṃgha.
This must be one who is solitary and alone, with no one at all to attend to them;
the entire community should look after them together, or perhaps take turns in shifts.
If they suffer from scabies or leprosy, do not defile the monks' beds and bedding.
It is appropriate to replace them with thick clothing, using entirely one's own private funds.
Within the eaves, halls, gatehouses, and latrines, those who tend to the sick should not remain;
they should instead dwell in a place of peace and security.
If the founder of the monastery dies, or is imprisoned, or departs for another land, one may reside there for five years; even if impoverished, one should not abandon it.
For another five years, one may share the same benefits as those residing near the monastery.
For the sake of the *poṣadha* ceremony, one must guard [the dwelling] so that it does not fall into ruin.
If, after ten years of keeping watch, the heart finds no pleasure in staying;
then one should take the bedding and other items and move them to a nearby monastery.
One should properly close the door and go elsewhere as one pleases;
if a bhikṣu wishes to dwell there, he may reside there at his own discretion.
Regarding items deposited in another monastery, they should be returned immediately when requested by the owner.
If there are indeed other circumstances, its use is truly without fault.
If the donor had a prior intention, saying, "I give this to this place and not another," yet it is diverted to another monastery, one ought to forcibly take it back.
If one wears monastic robes or garments of high value,
one should not wash or dye them, for in this way merit increases and they are not damaged.
During times of rain or snow, one should not leave them exposed on the open ground.
It is not appropriate to wear these robes while entering an impure room.
If the first watch of the night has passed, one should not share out the bedding;
however, if it is known that the guest will stay for a long time, it should be provided even during the middle watch of the night.
One should follow the order of seniority in providing beds and stools;
one should set aside a single room for visiting bhikṣus to reside in.
Even in an araṇya, one should distribute dwellings according to the preferences of those who are senior.
The ground, trees, and groves shall be distributed in due order;
even if one dwells in a secluded forest, one must still set aside space for guests.
To protect their robes and bowls, one must act accordingly; otherwise, one will incur an offense.
If one stays in a cramped place, one should share the floor space by the length of an elbow for lying down;
the water from the jar, tooth-sticks, and various medicinal vessels must all be shared.
If one intends to travel elsewhere, the room must be swept and wiped clean.
If one causes damage as before, the offense of *dukkaṭa* will invade the body.
When it is precisely the time for the distribution of rooms, if one goes outside without giving notice;
if one further causes others to proceed according to their order, even if they weep, one should not grant [the room] to them.
Regarding bedding and food and drink, those of lesser seniority shall share them equally;
the same applies to flowers, fruits, and so forth—such is the Master’s constant law.
If one is gravely ill and does not wish to leave their original room;
Until someone has been appointed [to oversee the matter], one should be exempted from their share of the duties.
If one sees bedding and furniture placed outside a monastic cell on the open ground, one should carry them inside;
for those who are elderly or infirm, one should have others lift them up.

If one sees the bedding and requisites of the great assembly being consumed by fire or swept away by water, one should protect them by rescuing and upholding them; one must not act with haste or negligence.
First, one must bring forth one's own wealth; next, one should bring forth the property of the Saṃgha.
In the future, one should handle the property of the Buddha; this sequence should be understood.
First, one must request permission; next, one may examine what is appropriate for the occasion;
only then, within the Tripitaka, may one inquire about points of doubt according to one's inclination.
For all who act as instructors, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—
amidst these four modes of deportment— it is not an offense to preach the Dharma.
All those who receive instruction must first give rise to reverence.
Except for the matter of lying down to sleep, the other three [postures] are not prohibited.
When instructing a student, if that person’s deluded mind has not yet been awakened, one should compassionately provide skillful analogies; one should not refuse even if asked a hundred times.
If a bhikṣu raises his hand to strike a pillar, a tree, or a wall, he incurs a transgression in each case; the wise should not do such things.
One should not wear bracelets on one’s arms, though one may wear protective cords as one pleases.
If there is a need for anything, one should tie [the amulet] on the arm so that it does not become visible.
When reciting various vidyā-mantras, one must not show reverence to other deities;
rather, one should pay homage to the Triple Gem and maintain the mantras and arts of the non-Buddhists.
One should not accept food, drink, bedding, or seats from a household whose bowl has been overturned,
nor go to that house to preach the Dharma or perform similar acts for them.
Only if they possess pure faith and spread exquisite garments upon the ground [should one do so].
A bhikṣu should step [on the mat], mindful that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
One who maintains only the three robes is permitted to keep only one *nivasana*;
if he keeps any additional garments, he deviates from the practice of *dhūta*.
If various grains such as wheat or beans have already been steamed or boiled,
even if they remain hard and ungerminated, all such firm seeds do not constitute an offense.
If food is vomited and exits the throat, one should spit it out and rinse the mouth clean.
Except for the power of past karma, there are two throats within the neck.
If there are painted or decorated fans, their possession for the sake of the community is permitted;
the robes worn by bhikṣus should not be of a single color.
If one is a mendicant, one should wear clothing that is coarse and simple;
under trees bearing flowers or fruit, one must not discharge excrement or urine.
The galleries at the corners of the monastery should be constructed of wood, not stone.
When suffering from a serious illness, one should neither pay homage to others nor accept the homage of others.
One should wait until the body has dried before putting on other clothes;
alternatively, one may dry it by fanning with the hand or wipe it with a towel.
If one obtains flowers or perfumed substances, one may smell them at will in a secluded place;
this can cause the eyes to become clear and increase the merit of the donor.
Sundarī beat her garment and sent it for Nanda to wear.
When the World-Honored One heard of this matter, he consequently prohibited the beating of robes.
If one obtains a robe previously beaten by another, one must sprinkle it with water and soften it before wearing;
to wear one that remains as radiant as before would incur the offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Knowing this to be what has been discarded by thieves, Or remnants of dead flesh left behind;
It is the same with sugarcane and other such things— One should not take them in the presence of the assembly.
If one carries items while traveling on the road, Whether across the head or on the back;
Having manifested suffering, one has already invited derision; in the future, one will be further oppressed.
If there is a cloak of great value, once it is lifted up and placed [there], it is pierced by insects;
if bitter wood leaves retain a lingering fragrance, they are wrapped in powder and thus not eaten.
On the day one's parents pass away, they leave a testament to the bhikṣus:
"These goods should be collected and used to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Even if they reside in another realm, they grant their consent for these items to be given to those bhikṣus.
This procedure is invalid and still incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
A costly and high-quality *cīvara* should be accepted when offered by others;
one may take a share from it after selling it, but one must not cut or tear it.
A bhikṣu did not see a snake; bitten by it, he passed away.
When he was crushed, the snake also died; for this reason, one must inspect the bed before lying down.
If one lies down without inspecting the bed, one immediately incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
One should not allow elephants, horses, chickens, or sparrows to fight while standing by and watching.
If one requires a waistband (ābandha), it is permitted by the Sugata;
those who are aged, infirm, or weakened by wind-disorders may use it as they see fit.
Whether departing from this dwelling or intending to return,
one should entrust the bedding before proceeding and sweep it clean.
The person to whom the entrustment has been made must maintain it with firm care.
If it is returned, it should be given back immediately; keep this in mind as a rule for its maintenance.
On the eighth and fifteenth days of the month, one must sun-dry and inspect the bedding and requisites;
this should be done regularly every half-month, for to act otherwise incurs a transgression of the Dharma.
Regarding the rooms for excrement and urine, as well as various utensils:
one should use those first arrived at, rather than choosing according to their size.
When using the household vessels of the community, one should act accordingly at the time of their use.
One should return borrowed items to their original owners so that their affairs are not neglected.
Exquisite rope beds and seats are permitted for communal use, not for private individuals;
however, leaning boards used to relieve fatigue are permitted for both the Sangha and private use.
If one has exceeded three summer retreats, it is permitted to sit on the same seat;
however, as with those who have not yet received full ordination, sitting together at the same table is never allowed.
If this occurs within a layperson's residence, one must not seek out a separate seat.
Even if one's preceptor permits a temporary sharing of the same seat, should there be circumstances involving difficulties, one may take the bedding of the community and depart.
The one who takes it may sleep [on the way], provided there is no fear; upon returning, he shall follow the established order.
If fear and distress have ceased, one may enjoy [the robe] as usual;
when it becomes tattered, torn, or riddled with holes, one should mend it according to the Dharma.
When it can no longer be used—even down to its inner lining—one [should discard it].
Torn apart to serve as wicks for lamps, or used as clay to fill up holes—
when utilizing them in such ways, one desires to bring peace and happiness to the body,
and furthermore, to cause the donor to constantly serve as a cause for meritorious deeds.
If another monastery has a fixed share, and others come to eat it indiscriminately, one must calculate the value and pay the price; such negligence is not permitted.
Regarding bedding and other items belonging to the *saṃghika* (the community), one must certainly keep records of them.
"This is the gift of so-and-so," written with clear and distinct characters;
a stool placed upon a stool, where bhikṣus sit one atop another;
the woman Black-Ear commits an evil deed, and is crushed toward the dark pass.
A śrāmaṇera who possesses faith and maintains a heart of reverence for the precepts may share in the distribution of the permanent bedding and requisites.
Regarding the use of leather bedding, it is not permitted in the Central Land.
In secular dwellings, sitting on them is temporarily permitted; lying down upon them is fundamentally not allowed.
While bear and *pārṣata* skins are generally permitted for sitting and supporting the feet, in frontier regions they are all allowed to be used as bedding.
Adorned with rare jewels such as gold, silver, and pearls,
And featuring ivory inlays— this is called a "great bed.
If a bhikṣu sits upon such a bed, His feet hang down and do not reach the ground.
This is what constitutes a high bed; those who uphold the precepts should recognize it.
These two types of large high beds are not permitted for bhikṣus to sit upon;
even among the laity, they are prohibited and not allowed, specifically when receiving the poṣadha.
It must be a sturdy seat, capable of accommodating two people;
a bed may also permit three, provided one inspects whether it is new or old.
If one intends to divide property, one should either announce it or strike the wooden gong.
Alternatively, one may distribute voting tallies to inform the entire Saṃgha collectively.
There are five kinds of *gaṇḍī*, each for different purposes;
their application depends on the circumstances at hand, provided they do not contravene the Great Teacher’s instructions.
Once the first strike has been completed, do not strike another;
this is an omen of misfortune, serving as a sign of the deceased's affairs.
If the ritual is performed with three strikes, one should deliver two blows with the clapper.
If one increases the number of *karaṇḍaka* staffs by one, this is called the constant rule for the assembly.
In times of urgent distress, there is no fixed rule for the staff; it is used to alert the multitude.
If, however, one wishes to alert those in meditative contemplation, one should shake and ring the *khakkhara*.
When a guest is about to enter the temple, they should wash their hands and feet outside the gate;
if water is difficult to find, one should use leaves to wipe them clean.
Once inside the temple, one should join the palms and approach the place of honor.
When the host has welcomed them with "Welcome," they reply, "Most welcome.
According to what is available, the host provides refreshments to relieve their fatigue;
he also offers non-time-appropriate drinks to bring joy to their hearts.
Having no leisure to wash my hands and feet, I immediately asked about the monks' regular regulations;
having heard them, I shall follow their practice, just as the Buddha himself spoke.
Whatever rules and ordinances have been established by the resident bhikṣus, [I shall observe].
All should rely on teachings that accord with reason, and not cause distress to others.
One must not address the Tathāgata, the Most Honored Great Teacher, by name or clan, nor by such titles as "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*) and so forth. Nor should one address a bhikṣu in such a manner.
A junior monk should address his seniors as "Venerable" (Bhadanta);
a senior should address juniors by their age as "Long-lived One" (Āyuṣmat).
Once assigned duties by the community, he should maintain the monastery grounds to the best of his ability.
On the eighth and fifteenth days, ring the wooden gong to assemble the disciples.
Should there be instances of defecating, urinating, spitting, or vomiting blood;
or when clearing the throat or snapping the fingers, one should do so two or three times to ensure they are alerted.
Do not discharge impurities upon living grass, nor into clear water;
likewise, one should not cast away filth upon fine trees or in pure fields.
When the body is at ease and free from the suffering of illness, one should not consume betel nut excessively.
When it is for the sake of illness, there is no transgression; a bhikṣu may eat and drink.
If one wishes to consume various fruit flavors at an improper time, although there is neither explicit permission nor prohibition, one should be thoroughly mindful of the brief instructions.
Just as one constantly consumes food to sustain the body day after day, so too must one apply eye medicine;
the Buddha taught that these things should be done regularly.
Within the pure grounds of the monastery, one must not shave the head haphazardly.
If one has an illness, it is permitted according to the circumstances; once finished, one must sweep and wipe clean.
When shaving the hair, one must follow the order of seniority;
once the shaving has begun, it is improper to call for someone to be moved.
The beard and hair are removed first and last; next, the hairs of the nose are plucked out;
only then are the nails of the hands and feet removed—one must know this sequence.
When a bhikṣu shaves his hair, he does not cut it like cow-hair.
If one has a wound or disease, one may trim the hair nearby provided it causes no injury.
Regarding the three private areas, one is not permitted to remove the hair arbitrarily;
however, if there is an illness, it is permitted, provided one informs a fellow practitioner of pure conduct.
Trimming the nails should be like the edge of an axe, or perhaps curved like a razor;
one may remove dirt from the surface of the nails, but it is not appropriate to seek a polished luster.
If staying in an araṇya (forest hermitage), the hair on the head shall not exceed the length of two fingers.
Using two fingers is not a fault; however, it is improper to do so in cities or villages.
When the shaving of the hair is completed, one should wash the entire body clean.
In cases where there is a specific reason, it is permitted, provided that at least the five limbs are washed clean.
One who shaves hair for those not of the secular world may do so within the dwelling;
if a bhikṣu is skilled and experienced, there is no offense in shaving them.
Whether it be at dawn when chewing a tooth-stick, or when preaching the Dharma, [one may act accordingly].
Furthermore, when the meal is finished, failing to perform [the cleansing rites] incurs an offense.
There are three distinctions regarding the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*): the long must be twelve finger-breadths;
the short is eight finger-breadths in measure; those between these two are collectively termed "medium."
Whichever wood branch it may be, it should be as thick as a small finger;
chew the tip until it becomes soft like cotton—those that are bitter and astringent are best.
Once the tooth-stick has been chewed, one must be mindful to scrape the tongue.
Copper, iron, red copper, or brass—scrape and polish them as desired.
If one dwells within a village or city, one may carry any one of these four;
wash them clean with ash and scrub them, so that no grime or filth remains.
If one must lack these, use the wood previously chewed;
split it in two and rub them together. For those who are poor, use it to scrape the tongue.
If tooth-sticks are suddenly difficult to obtain, the mouth and teeth must ultimately be kept clean.
The three powders may be used according to the occasion; even if one uses them as a provisional allowance, there is no offense.
In a previous life he was a venomous snake, and now he is the son of an elder;
because he left the household life due to his pure mouth, he must always scrape his tongue with a tongue-scraper.
Having cleared the impurities from one's tongue, if one places it on the ground, small insects may be killed;
for this reason, the Buddha gave rise to compassion and did not permit such casual disposal.
Whenever cleansing the mouth, one must wash the tooth-stick before discarding it.
Wiping dust with water that has not been strained invites the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
A fly may die upon the tooth-stick; one who eats this [leavings] loses his life as a lizard;
a yellow mongoose perishes by eating this; and a dog likewise passes away after consuming it.
A bhikṣu has three matters that should be performed in a secluded place:
namely, defecating and urinating, as well as chewing the tooth-stick.
A bhikṣu is permitted to wear leather footwear, provided it is only a single layer.
One is not permitted to wear multiple layers; they may only be worn if both the wearer and the recipient are laypeople.
If they make a sound when stepped upon, even if pure, they should not be kept.
For the sake of the community, one may follow the local custom; there is no offense in wearing them at such times.
If one is in a land of severe cold, where ice and snow fill the fields;
at such a time, one may open the *pūrvaka* (outer robe), and whether to wear it or not is entirely up to one's discretion.
However, the five skins—those of the lion, elephant, horse, and so forth—are not permitted to be carried.
Furthermore, these various tendons cannot be used for stitching.
As for other fanged and clawed beasts, such as jackals, cats, and wildcats—
one must not use their skins, for they are capable of causing harm.
If one is within a monastery (vihāra), the wearing of sandals is entirely prohibited;
however, it is permitted to move about after putting them on once one has reached a private room, and they are also allowed within lay dwellings.
It is not fitting for a bhikṣu to wear shoes made of materials such as reed or bamboo.
If one has a wind-blood disorder in the legs, it is permitted to wear [footwear] as required.
In places where there are no boats, one may rely on a cow’s tail to cross a river;
elephants, horses, bulls, and water buffaloes—none of these are prohibited.
When dividing the shares of rented fields, do not permit the cessation of agricultural work;
one should be diligent in guarding and watching them so as not to let the permanent property (sangha-ratna) suffer damage.
If one encounters difficult circumstances on a dangerous path, one may take [the goods] with oneself and carry them away.
If there are thieves within the monastery, you should respond to the commotion as appropriate.
If it occurs at the cow-pen, guard it with diligent care;
do not speak of the grain stores, but employ skillful means to manage them as usual.
When a śrāmaṇera seeks alms-food through meditative concentration, his body may become weak and he requires assistance;
one must not let his hands be released, so that there is no injury when lifting or lowering [the bowl].
If he is completely exhausted, the bhikṣu should carry it for him.
Tie a long cord to the top of the bag so that a śrāmaṇera may hold it.
If bandits come and flee in alarm, one may abandon it; or when crossing a river, one may likewise leave it behind.
When returning it oneself, there is no fault in eating [the food].
When loading the cart with grain, one fears the axle may break on dangerous ground;
the bhikṣus should push together, yet must remain vigilant at the front of the shafts.
When the boat is filled with grain, one must avoid the shallows and pass through the rapids and eddies with care.
One should assist the boatman by pulling him along, and must not touch his rudder.
Dyeing robes must be done on a clear day, and certainly not during the midday of a cloudy sky;
one should not do it on auspicious ground, for fear of staining it and inviting reproach.
If suddenly encountering wind and rain, one should fear that dust will soil the robes;
one may move them into the shelter of the eaves, and any soiled areas should be rubbed clean.
When fellow bhikṣus of the same Dharma see a quarrel, they ought to intervene and resolve it.
If they do not heed your words, abandon them and need not be looked upon.
One who breaks the precepts yet maintains faith, and one who maintains both—these are those who uphold what they have heard;
likewise, those who hear together and possess few desires, though their fewness of desire may differ in degree.
When these two are contending together, both their words may be trusted;
one should question that which has the least desire, for when both have reached the ultimate, there is no dispute.
If, however, they debate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), contention will then arise.
If such evil is not removed, one must perform the act of suspension (*pratikṣepaṇīya*).
When meeting at a place where etiquette is required, one should practice respect even if there has been a quarrel;
one should offer a greeting of "I hope you are well," for to violate this, both parties incur an offense.
When entering the bathhouse, have someone guard the door;
until the task of bathing is finished, do not allow those with little faith to enter.
If various colorful designs are used for painting, they may be done as permitted.
One must not paint sentient beings, yet one may still depict flowers and leaves.
If on the walls of a monastic dwelling, one may paint white bones and corpses;
or sometimes skulls, so that those who see them may give rise to revulsion.
On the panels of the main gate, deities are painted with relaxed countenances and joyful smiles;
some are depicted as yakṣas, holding staffs to ward off evil.
Scenes of great supernatural powers are illustrated, with the forms of Buddhas appearing amidst the flowers.
Furthermore, one may paint the wheel of birth and death on both sides of the door;
on the door-panels of the incense altar, yakṣa deities holding flowers should be painted;
and if it is the kitchen of the Saṃgha, deities bearing delicious food should be painted.
The yakṣa image at the treasury gate holds a *cintāmaṇi* pouch;
alternatively, he may hold a *bhadraghaṭa* (vase of fortune), from whose mouth various gold and jewels pour forth.
If it is in the hall of offerings and service, one should paint the image of an elderly bhikṣu.
One should expound upon the power [of the Dharma] to guide and lead sentient beings.
In the heated hall and the bathhouse, one should have paintings made of the five divine messengers;
regarding the bonds of birth, old age, sickness, and death, these matters should be executed according to the sūtras.
If it is in the infirmary, paint an image of the Great Master;
with his own hands of great compassion, he personally supports those who are gravely ill.
If it is in the water hall, carve and paint dragons and serpents.
If one is in a latrine or toilet, one should depict the image of a charnel ground.
On the walls of the eaves or corridors, one may paint the Buddha’s previous births (*jātaka*):
men and women performing difficult acts of giving, as well as those who sacrificed their bodies and practiced patience.
Such is the method for painting: the occasion occurred in the Jeta Grove;
when the Elder had completed the construction of the monastery, the World-Honored One personally explained it.
If one is in a room under the eaves, one must not allow smoke from fires to fume the area.
If there are indeed other circumstances, and no smoke can be carried forward,
one should not light a fire at will upon a fine brick floor;
if there is a pressing necessity, it should be done within a brazier.
The Buddha and those most venerable among the assembly, the king who benefits the myriad subjects,
and the two honored ones— the direct teacher and the preceptor— these five provide virtuous instruction that one must not transgress.
If there is a matter for which a bhikṣu acts, which the World-Honored One has neither permitted nor prohibited;
which is pure and not in conflict with worldly norms—this matter should be carried out without hesitation.
If it gives rise to worldly censure, a bhikṣu should not engage in such enjoyment;
this brief instruction can bring disciples to peace and also clarifies that the Buddha is omniscient.
If one cannot recall the specific origin story (*nidāna*) for a rule in the Vinaya or Sūtra, one may explain it according to the six great cities; even if there are discrepancies, there is no fault.
Śrāvastī and Sāketa, Vārāṇasī and Campā; Vaiśālī and Rājagṛha—these six great cities are mentioned according to their respective locations.
The elder is said to be Anāthapiṇḍada, and the King of Kośala, Prasenajit;
the woman is said to be Viśākhā—these names are assigned according to the occasion.
Within the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a sovereign king named Brahmadatta;
nearby lived a woman named Posadhā, and there was a great elder named Saṃtati.
It was first established in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where the Wheel of Dharma was initially turned to rescue the deluded masses;
there he preached the Dharma to deliver the five men, thereby repaying his former vow made in the past.
The second group of five was ordained in succession; for them, he taught that form and the other aggregates are empty and selfless.
By contemplating all the *skandhas* as being like floating bubbles, they were able to escape the cycle of birth and death.
Initially, five people wore their lower garments with uneven heights, which invited ridicule and shame;
he ordered them to wear them as perfectly round and neat as those of the Brahmā gods, and because of this, the śikṣāpada was subsequently established.

Subsequently, the Muni established the precepts; though Sujaṇṇa and others committed sexual misconduct, the origin of the training rule exempted the first offender. This is the path to rebirth in heaven and to Nirvāṇa.
How great are the six venerable elders! From them arose the extensive regulations concerning the *śikṣādattaka*;
all were preeminent in clear discernment of their time, and in the deeds they performed, there was no repeated transgression.
Although the training rules were established for these reasons, through them one may wash away impurities and restore broken morality;
like the Indus River in springtime, its waters flow across the plains and irrigate all the marshes.
Upānanda, Aśvaka, Channa, Nanda, Udāyin, and Punnava—
these six who are difficult to tame are the dregs within the teaching of the World-Honored One.
If one possesses the resolute mind not to transgress the precepts, such a person is called a person of supreme wisdom;
even if one transgresses but is able to repent, they are likewise of the superior class, whereas those who do not repent for a long time will be born in the evil realms.
The Buddhas can transcend the shore of all virtues; All their deeds are beyond measure.
They proclaim the discipline that liberates sentient beings, And guide superior and virtuous persons toward excellence.
Ordinary beings, accumulating ignorance since beginningless time, Revolve in constant delusion through the long night;
Only the Buddha can, with the hand of the True Dharma, Diligently pull them forth from the dark abyss.
During incalculable aeons, he constantly cultivated great compassion and perfumed his wondrous wisdom;
skillfully taming beings as he traversed the realms of existence, he necessarily performed the ten great deeds.
The so-called bestowal of predictions for future Buddhas, And the setting aside of the third portion for the sake of sentient beings;
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were the foremost pair, And all those whom the Buddha transformed and converted attained liberation on their own.
The rite of establishing the boundary must surely be performed; manifesting great supernormal powers, he descended from the celestial palace.
Having enabled his parents to attain the fruit, he explained the conditions of karma; to him who entered final nirvana, I pay homage with my life.
Homage to the Great Virtuous Ones who compiled [the teachings], Who could manifest the Sage’s hidden instructions;
They caused the precious ship that had sunk to float once more, Its radiance illuminating the boundless ocean.
I also prostrate to the attendant Ānanda, who has excellently gathered the treasury of sūtras through hearing and retention;
he causes all classes of beings to give rise to joy and delight, and brings about the removal of the fetters of affliction.
Next, I pay homage to the noble Upāli, Who can correctly proclaim and disseminate the Vinaya Piṭaka;
Like one who skillfully holds powerful mantras, He can eliminate the venomous serpent-kings of the evil realms.
Next, I pay homage to the Venerable Kāśyapa, Who was well-versed in the Maṭhara-piṭaka;
He caused the light to shine universally throughout this world, Causing all hidden meanings to be fully proclaimed.
Next, at the city of Rājagṛha, among the assembly of five hundred, those worthy ones compiled the Tripiṭaka;
once again raining down the Dharma to moisten the realm of sentient beings—to them all, I pay homage with the utmost sincerity.
With Śakra, King of Devas, as their leader, the hosts of Asuras all pay respectful homage;
filling the entirety of space, they gather like clouds, bowing their heads with profound hearts and praising his rarity.
At that time, by the side of the great city of Rājagṛha, celestial fragrances pervaded and filled the mountains and forests;
divine maidens scattered famous flowers, their drifting scents falling as far as the borders of Mount Mucilinda.
Subsequently, once again in that city of Vaiśālī, by the side of the Monkey Pond,
seven hundred arhats convened a second council to propagate the true path, hoping to cause the teachings of the Dharma to become even more radiant.

How great! The Buddha-sun has buried its light; Fearing that the remaining jewels of the Dharma might sink into obscurity, Fortunately, the various sages have compiled these subtle words, Enabling humans and devas to once again look up in reverence.
The Muni has long endured weariness through saṃsāra, seeking the True Dharma within birth and death;
wishing to rescue those who are without refuge, he hopes to bring all sufferings to complete cessation.
He gave away his head, eyes, hands, and feet; he saved those seeking aid even at the cost of his own flesh and blood flowing forth.
His love for his wife and children was like the first crescent moon; through joyful relinquishment of all, he returned to perfect stillness.
As proclaimed by the Great Master, the Muni, until the time the True Dharma has not yet perished:
one should eliminate indolence and sever ignorance, exerting oneself with earnest resolve and diligent application.
Among verbal teachings, Buddhism is supreme; among verses, the True Dharma is honored.
I, Viśākhā, having exhausted my humble mind, have composed this verse to provide an easy means for others to give rise [to faith].
If there be additions or subtractions in the teachings of the Sages, Or discrepancies and contradictions in their sequence;
May those of broad vision be mutually tolerant, So that the blind may follow the path without losing their way.
Within the Vinaya teachings for bhikṣus, I have briefly condensed the extensive texts into a few verses;
may all sentient beings together attain this, so that through it they may accomplish the deeds of merit and wisdom.
Feeling weary of and turning away from the mire of the five desires, May they always maintain pure faith as their adornment;
In birth after birth, may they constantly obtain the body of a bhikṣu, Firmly upholding the Buddha’s words until the ultimate limit of reality is reached.
If you aspire for the precepts to be ever pure, And proceed without doubt toward the palace of Nirvana,
Constantly recollecting and practicing these concise verses, Do not worry that this life will end in vain.
Even as the world is still scorched by the heat of birth and death, And even as the mind within is constantly burned by the fire of defilement;
May the teachings of the Great Sages flow like the Gaṅgā, Forever remaining to wash away the turbid stains of ignorance.
At Nālandā, I have already translated these verses; returning now to the capital, I have re-examined them to rectify any omissions or errors.
May all merit resulting from this cause reach all sentient beings, that they may earnestly aspire for liberation and swiftly emerge from the ford of birth.
